This PVDF/CNTs/BaTiO3 composite foam meets commercial EMI shielding standards (≥20 dB) with an absorption coefficient of 0.773. Its piezoelectric performance is also enhanced, with a maximum output voltage of 9.5 V. This research offers novel insights for human health monitoring applications while protecting individuals from electromagnetic radiation hazards.

title: One-step laser conversion of PASS into S-doped graphene on carbon fiber surface: Enhancing the interfacial property of carbon fiber/PASS composite
abstract: The application of carbon fiber-reinforced thermoplastic composite is often constrained by a key factor: their poor interfacial performance. Herein, we propose a novel, efficient, and industrially viable interfacial modification strategy: in situ growth of graphene on carbon fiber surface via laser induction. This study elucidates the mechanism of laser-induced graphene growth and enables precise control over graphene quality and polar group content through laser power modulation, thereby enhancing the physicochemical interactions between carbon fibers and PASS resin. SEM, TEM, XPS, FTIR, and Raman analyses confirm that high-quality graphene with abundant polar groups and strong interfacial bonding is achieved at 55% laser power. The modified CF/PASS composites exhibit significantly enhanced interfacial shear strength (IFSS), tensile strength, and interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) of 90.8 MPa, 505.1 MPa, and 46.3 MPa, respectively—representing increases of 68.9%, 30.6%, and 151.6% compared to desized CF/PASS. The interphase thickness expands to 835 nm, demonstrating that laser-induced fiber-graphene (LIFG) constructs a modulus-gradient transition layer via reinforced physical anchoring and hydrogen bonding, serving as a stress-transfer “bridge” between fiber and matrix. Fractography reveals a transition from interfacial failure to matrix/fiber fracture, corroborating the mechanical enhancement. Furthermore, the introduced graphene substantially improves electromagnetic interference shielding via enriched charge carriers and electric dipoles. This strategy simultaneously advances interfacial and functional properties, establishing a new paradigm for composite interphase engineering.

title: Micromechanical modeling for the stiffness of nanofiber composites: Synergistic effects of graded interphase, fiber waviness and distribution
abstract: Nanofibers are prone to waviness due to their extremely high aspect ratio, while their enormous specific surface area significantly amplifies the impact of the interphase. Previous studies often investigate these factors in isolation, despite the reality that a curved fiber is typically enveloped by a graded interphase with a similar curved shape. To bridge this gap, this study first divided the graded interphase into a sufficient number of sub-layers, each treated as homogeneous and isotropic. An iterative layering approach, combined with a bridging model, is then employed to derive the stiffness of the fiber-interphase system. Subsequently, the composites containing curved fiber are represented as an assembly of numerous composite material units of straight fibers oriented at specific angles relative to the fiber axis. The waviness effect is incorporated through an integration scheme. Furthermore, the established micromechanical framework is extended to the case of three-dimensional random fiber orientation, enhancing its applicability. The robustness of the theoretical framework is validated through comparison with existing experimental data, providing a reliable and precise approach for predicting the stiffness of nanofiber composites. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric analysis is conducted to elucidate the effects of fiber waviness and interphase properties on the composite stiffness, thus offering valuable insights for the optimization and design of nanofiber composites.

title: Significantly enhanced thermoelectric performance of carbon nanotubes through biomass hyaluronic acid for wearable thermoelectric engine and temperature monitoring
abstract: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have attracted considerable attention as a promising thermoelectric (TE) material due to their outstanding electrical properties, flexibility, and lightweight. However, their practical application is often hindered by the agglomeration tendency between nanotubes. Despite numerous dispersants that have been explored to improve the dispersion and TE performance of CNTs, biomass-derived hyaluronic acid (HA) remains rarely investigated to enhance the thermoelectric performance of CNTs. This study synergistically enhances the dispersion and thermoelectric properties of CNTs by biomass HA. The carboxyl groups in HA facilitate electron transfer with CNTs, which promotes the exfoliation and disentanglement of nanotube bundles, thereby significantly improving the dispersibility of CNTs. Combined with the doping effect of HA, the composite achieves a maximum power factor of 290.9 ± 11.9 μW m−1K−2 with an enhanced electrical conductivity of 1776 ± 71 S cm−1 at a HA content of 10 wt%, superior to pristine CNTs of 105.7 ± 10.2 μW m−1K−2. Furthermore, a flexible thermoelectric device consisting of five pairs of HA/CNTs films and nickel wires was fabricated. This device exhibits remarkable temperature sensing capability and generates a high output power of 470.1 nW at ΔT = 30 K, highlighting the potential of biomass HA in sustainable energy harvesting and flexible electronic sensors.

title: Molecular tailoring of imine-based liquid crystal epoxy resins for minimized interfacial thermal resistance in recyclable boron nitride composites
abstract: The development of advanced thermal management materials is crucial for next-generation electronics. While liquid crystal epoxy resins (LCERs) can achieve enhanced thermal conductivity through molecular ordering, their performance remains constrained by limited intrinsic conductivity and high interfacial thermal resistance when incorporating conductive fillers. Moreover, conventional thermosetting epoxies lack recyclability, posing environmental concerns. In this work, a series of imine-based LCERs with tailored molecular conformations, including varied bridging groups (ether or ester) and flexible spacer lengths, were synthesized and cured using imidazole to preserve the mesogenic order. The resulting LCERs exhibit highly oriented structures, showing intrinsic in-plane and out-of-plane thermal conductivities up to 2.54 and 0.40 W m−1 K−1, respectively. When blended with unmodified boron nitride (BN), the composites achieve a remarkable 211.8% increase in out-of-plane thermal conductivity over pure LCERs. Systematic characterization confirms that strong Lewis acid–base interaction between BN and ester-containing LCERs facilitate interfacial phonon transport. Moreover, the linear molecular conformation of ester-bridged liquid crystal monomer promotes dense molecular packing and reduces interfacial layer thickness. Owing to the dynamic reversibility and acid sensitivity of imine bonds, the resulting composites also gain excellent capabilities for recycling and controlled degradation. This work highlights the essential role of molecular architecture in minimizing interfacial thermal resistance and offers a strategic pathway for designing highly thermally conductive polymer composites with excellent recyclability.

title: Scalable structural supercapacitors with graphene-modified high-surface-area electrodes
abstract: Electrification, including emerging technologies such as structural supercapacitors, is critical in realizing carbon-neutral transportation. A fundamental challenge is the trade-off between mechanical properties and energy storage capabilities. We report the fabrication of structural supercapacitors with a novel fibre-fibre interface to improve the interlaminar strength and encapsulation while considering the effect of structural resin on energy storage performance. The synthesized graphene nanoplatelets-modified electrodes attain a high specific surface area of ∼231 m 2 ·g -1 - outperforming comparable carbon-based electrodes. We learned that the use of a gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) separator containing 60 wt% Li-salt eliminates the requirement of electrolyte infusion and showed the highest values for conductivity for the cell produced using GPE. The implementation of glass fabrics (GFs) into the GPE improved the flexural modulus by ∼22%, while retaining the mechanical strength of the cells. The multifunctional performance of the produced SSCs were on par or even outperformed the performances of SSCs reported in literature. A proof-of-concept prototype demonstrates that gel-polymer electrolyte cells can retain charges for longer than those with a glass fibre separator. Cumulatively, these offer the possibility of conventional composite manufacturing techniques to scale-up and eliminate delamination issues arising from different thermal expansion coefficients which also addresses the balance between mechanical stability and electrochemical performance. Our findings support the advancement of durable, lightweight energy storage and delivery systems for sustainable transportation, with potential applications in robotics and wearable technologies.

title: Biodegradable poly(glycolide-co-lactide) nanocomposites with functional-enzymatic cellulose for high-performance biodegradable stents
abstract: Although extensive studies have focused on the degradation of poly(glycolide-co-lactide) [P(GA-co-LA)] fibers, the preparation of high-performance and functional P(GA-co-LA) injection-molded products remains underexplored. In this paper, enzymatically-synthesized antibacterial cellulose (ECP) was incorporated into P(GA-co-LA) matrix for the first time. A series of P(GA-co-LA)/ECP nanocomposites with 0-3.0 wt% ECP were prepared by melt blending. The effects of ECP on mechanical properties, crystallization, antibacterial activities, morphology and in vitro degradation behavior were systematically investigated. Results showed that the composite with 0.3 wt% ECP exhibited excellent mechanical properties due to the effective energy dissipation of hydrogen bonding and the good compatibility and dispersion of the reinforcement ECP. ECP also acted as a heterogeneous nucleating agent, raising crystallinity and crystallization temperature. Degradation tests revealed that ECP slowed down the in vitro degradation rate, with the composite maintaining better structural integrity after 10 days in PBS, due to the enhanced crystallinity and interfacial hydrogen bonding. Antibacterial results confirmed that ECP effectively promotes bacterial death, owing to surface phenol groups. In conclusion, P(GA-co-LA)/ECP nanocomposites are a promising new material for high-performance biodegradable stents, combining improved mechanical strength, controlled degradation, and effective antibacterial functionality.

title: Enhancing interlaminar fracture toughness in 3D-printed multi-fiber composites via intra-bead hybridization
abstract: Material hybridization has emerged as an effective solution for balancing stiffness and toughness in 3D-printed continuous fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs). While recent studies on hybridization in 3D-printed CFRPs have predominantly focused on the inter-layer level hybridization, this research advances the understanding of hybridization mechanisms by introducing intra-bead hybridization. The method involves the simultaneous deposition of CF/PA6 and KF/PA6 filaments through a single nozzle, fabricating 3D-printed CKF/PA6 hybrid composites with a tailored stiffness–toughness balance. To determine whether this tailored balance was achieved, stiffness properties were systematically evaluated through longitudinal and transverse tensile tests, flexural tests, and fracture toughness experiments, including double cantilever beam (DCB) and end-notched flexure (ENF) for mode I and mode II, respectively. The key mechanism responsible for the significant enhancement of interlaminar fracture toughness in the proposed intra-bead hybridization approach was identified as the transition of fiber bridging from CFs to KFs. This transition promotes extensive fiber bridging within the fracture process zone, resulting in more ductile fracture behavior and greater energy dissipation through synergistic CF/KF interactions. Conversely, the observed reduction in stiffness stems from thermal property mismatches between CF-rich and KF-rich regions. Specifically, differential thermal conductivity induces localized thermal stresses during printing, leading to void formation and incomplete matrix diffusion, while mismatched thermal expansion coefficients cause shrinkage and interfacial sliding, ultimately leading to microcrack formation during solidification. These findings provide valuable insights for developing 3D-printed CFRP hybrid composite components that meet the demands of applications requiring a balance between stiffness and toughness.

title: Experimental–numerical phase-field modelling of ductile and fatigue fracture in short fibre-reinforced polymeric adhesives
abstract: Structural adhesives are essential in wind turbine blades, where bonded joints are subjected to complex static and cyclic loading and are prone to fatigue-driven failure. Recently developed short fibre-reinforced polymeric (SFRP) adhesives offer enhanced mechanical performance, but their fracture behaviour is strongly influenced by fibre orientation and anisotropy. This study presents an experimental-numerical framework for predicting quasi-static and fatigue fracture in SFRP adhesives using a phase-field approach. An experimental campaign, including quasi-static and tension-tension fatigue tests with full-field strain measurements, reveals pronounced anisotropic elasto-plastic behaviour, orientation-dependent fatigue life, and distinct damage mechanisms under monotonic and cyclic loading. Based on these observations, an anisotropic phase-field model for ductile fracture is developed and coupled with an invariant-based transversely isotropic elasto-plastic constitutive formulation with pressure sensitivity and non-associative plastic flow. Fatigue effects are incorporated through a thermodynamically consistent degradation of fracture toughness driven by accumulated energy dissipation. The model is implemented within a finite element framework and validated against experiments through simulations of dog-bone and single-edge notched specimens. The numerical results show very good agreement with experimental stress–strain responses, S-N curves, and crack initiation and propagation behaviour, demonstrating the capability of the proposed framework to predict the durability of SFRP adhesive joints under static and cyclic loading.

title: Construction of multifunctional carboxylated nitrile butadiene composite films: Integration of degradability, antioxidant and antibacterial functions
abstract: Aiming at the main application bottlenecks of long degradation cycle and poor antibacterial property of disposable carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) gloves, APS-iron (APS-Fe) chelate was employed as a multifunctional modifier to prepare XNBR/APS-Fe composite films through compounding and vulcanization processes. Utilizing APS-Fe's dual properties (metal-catalyzed aging and biodegradability), we established a “catalysis-biology” dual-driven rapid degradation system. The service life of the XNBR/1.5APS-Fe composite film to reach the 75% threshold of fracture retention at 25 °C was only 4.34 years, significantly shorter than its natural degradation cycle. With the synergistic effect of the active groups of APS and Fe3+, the composite film exhibited remarkably enhanced scavenging capacity for hydroxyl radicals and DPPH radicals, effectively addressing the shortcoming of weak antibacterial property of pure XNBR. The antibacterial capacity of XNBR/1.5APS-Fe against Escherichia coli was prominent, 11.4 times higher than that of pure XNBR. Additionally, the mechanical properties and solvent resistance of XNBR films were also improved. The novel composite film combines excellent properties such as degradability, antioxidant activity, and antibacterial safety. These findings provide a scientific and practical solution for the development of functional disposable rubber products.

title: Editorial Board
A bio-inspired interface modification strategy for suppressing insulation degradation of aramid fiber/epoxy composites
abstract: Designing effective interfaces for aramid fiber/epoxy (AF/EP) composites in electrical insulation applications is particularly challenging, given that interfacial failure is prone to occur at the AF/EP interface due to charge accumulation and inherent modulus mismatch. Inspired by mussel byssus and nacre, a bionic interface modification strategy is developed in this study, which integrates polydopamine coating and nanosilica (SiO2) onto the fiber surface through a hierarchical assembly approach. The results show that the interfacial shear strength and interlaminar shear strength of the composites are improved by 126.46% and 47.86% respectively, due to the synergistic effects of enhanced interface bonding strength, mechanical interlocking and successful construction of gradient modulus transition layer. Furthermore, more charge traps and energy scattering centers are introduced by SiO2. Consequently, interfacial insulation degradation process under high voltage is significantly suppressed in the channel length, cumulative damage area, and breakdown time. Compared to the unmodified AF/EP composites, the modified composites demonstrate exceptional dielectric properties with DC conductivity decreased by 83.38%, dielectric loss reduced by 10.36% and breakdown strength enhanced by 29.43%. This interface functionalization strategy provides novel insights into the performance improvement of AF/EP composites for high-end power equipment subjected to combined electrical and mechanical stresses.

title: An optimization strategy for carbon fiber composite electrodes toward high-performance V2O5-based zinc-ion flexible batteries
abstract: In integrated zinc-ion structural batteries, the design and fabrication of carbon fiber (CF) composite electrodes present considerable work, particularly because CFs exhibit inferior conductivity compared with traditional metal foils, which hinders their use as current collectors. This work employs silver-plated CFs as current collectors for both electrodes in zinc-ion flexible batteries for the first time and achieves electrodes with robust mechanical strength and substantial energy storage performance. For the cathode, commercial V2O5 is coated onto silver-plated CFs, which effectively leverages the electrochemical benefits of vanadium oxides to deliver a high specific capacity of 320 mAh g−1 and 87% capacity retention after 1500 cycles at 2 A g−1. On the anode, zinc is electrodeposited onto the CFs, where the silver layer improves deposition efficiency and yields a homogeneous coating. This work demonstrates an optimization strategy for CF composite electrodes, which holds potential value for structural energy storage and flexible electronic device applications.

title: Study on the initial damage in 3D woven composites using a novel high-capacity load-retention device suitable for in-situ CT
abstract: The onset of damage in 3D woven composites (3DWCs) is a critical factor in evaluating their structural performance. To eliminate the adverse effects of crack closure on initial damage detection while maintaining a high load capacity, a novel removable high-capacity load-retention (HCLR) device was developed for in-situ computed tomography (CT) systems. The HCLR device enables in-situ testing under loads of up to 200 kN, significantly surpassing the capacity of most existing in-situ CT setups. A testing method combing the HCLR device with acoustic emission (AE) technology was established to capture damage initiation in 3DWCs. AE technology serves as an effective indicator for identifying the onset of damage. Initial damage was investigated using both the HCLR and conventional ex-situ methods. The results demonstrate that the HCLR method allows for more accurate detection of initial cracks, which coincided with the appearance of the first high-energy AE signal. Notably, damage initiation occurred at only 35.8% of the material's ultimate strength, with matrix cracking identified as the dominant failure mode. These findings provide valuable guidance for the design and application of 3DWCs.

title: Physics-informed parameterised generative model for unidirectional fibre-reinforced microstructures with periodic boundaries
abstract: Accurate generation of realistic statistical volume elements is essential for predicting and optimising the mechanical behaviour of fibre-reinforced composites. Deep generative models that rely solely on imaging data often lack geometric accuracy and periodicity. We introduce a physics-informed deep learning framework based on diffusion models, which integrates multi-source experimental data: laser diffraction system measurements for ground-truth fibre diameter and computed tomography for image-derived spatial topology. The methodology features a novel parameterised microstructure grid that encodes spatial and dimensional attributes at each pixel, resolving fibre-order ambiguity. Augmented with a refinement module and physics-based constraints, our model generates realistic, overlap-free fibre arrangements that reflect representative diameter distributions and enforce periodic boundaries. Quantitative comparisons with real microstructures show that our method accurately captures key geometric features, including fibre spatial distributions and resin-rich regions. These results highlight the potential of physics-guided diffusion models to generate reliable microstructural representations, paving the way for accelerated microscale materials design and analysis.

title: Direct reconstruction of unit-cell models from micro-CT scanning for multiscale woven prepreg forming analysis
abstract: Forming prediction of woven composites is crucial for optimizing manufacturing parameters in the fabrication of large-scale and high-quality equipment across modern automotive, aerospace and marine industries. This work presents a systematic combination of multiscale forming simulation framework and the high-fidelity finite element (FE) model to predict non-uniform yarn orientation and laminate thickness distributions. Specifically, the high-fidelity FE model based on the unit-cell reconstructed directly via a deep-learning algorithm compatible with low-resolution CT images without manual adjustment is incorporated into the integrated mesoscopic simulation model previously developed for elucidating deformation mechanisms. The indispensable characterization experiments are simplified to only uniaxial tension and consolidation tests on orthogonal composites, minimizing experimental redundancy while preserving essential data integrity. Concurrently, the coupling deformation modes impervious to direct measurement can be reliably captured through virtual characterization based on the high-fidelity FE model, leading to exceptional predictive accuracy for stress-strain relationships with 2.1% average error compared to the idealized unit-cell model established before with 15.2% average error. Subsequently, these homogenized relationships were fed into the macroscale forming simulation, which was then validated through prepreg compression molding (PCM), resulting in strong consistency between experimental and simulation data on the deformed geometry, yarn angle and thickness distribution, exhibiting respective errors of 7.59%, 4.43° and 14.7%. Therefore, the proposed multiscale simulation framework not only mitigates experimental time costs and operational complexity but also augments forming process precision by accounting for the coupling effects between distinct deformation modes, addressing a critical gap in the efficient fabrication of high-performance woven composite components.

title: Multiscale damage analysis of 3D woven variable-thickness composite structures considering interlayer mesoscale yarn difference
abstract: The internal mesoscopic yarn characteristics of 3D woven variable-thickness composite structures exhibit significant variation, which strongly affects the macroscopic mechanical performance and failure behavior of structures. This paper aims to propose a multiscale method accounting for interlayer mesoscale yarn differences to efficiently and accurately predict the mechanical behavior of variable-thickness structures. Firstly, mesoscale geometric models are established using the digital element approach based on morphological characteristics from variable-thickness specimens with reduced yarns and varied weft sizes. Then, representative volume cells (RVCs) are selected in the thickness direction according to the woven yarn structure, including inner and surface RVCs. An R-V-A clustering scheme is developed to generate the offline database of self-consistent clustering analysis (SCA) for different RVCs. Finally, a concurrent multiscale framework coupling the finite element (FE) method with online SCA is used to investigate the damage behavior of two types of variable-thickness composite structures under cantilever loading. The predicted results are in good agreement with the experimental ones. Incorporating interlayer mesoscale yarn differences notably improves the prediction accuracy. The proposed concurrent multiscale method accurately captures the macro-meso failure behavior of composite structures. This study provides a theoretical basis and technical support for the structural design of complex textile composite fan blades.

title: Enhancing mechanical properties of CCF/PEEK composites by rotary 3D printing with Co-regulation of hot compaction and fiber tension
abstract: Continuous fiber-reinforced thermoplastic composites (CFRTPCs) fabricated by fused deposition modelling (FDM) methods often suffer from insufficient in-situ consolidation, resulting in interfacial voids, fiber waviness, and limited mechanical performance. In this work, a rotary 3D printing platform with real-time closed-loop co-regulation of hot compaction and fiber tension was developed to enhance the consolidation quality of CCF/PEEK composites. The closed-loop force feedback enables stable compaction control during deposition, significantly improving interlayer integrity compared with conventional fixed-height printing. The microstructural evolution is governed by the coupled competition between compaction-induced resin flow and tension-mediated anchoring. Hot compaction promotes matrix flow, effectively suppressing void defects and reducing porosity from 0.99% to 0.2%. However, excessive compaction induces strong hydrodynamic drag and fiber deviation, disrupting fiber alignment. In contrast, increasing fiber tension provides an axial stabilizing constraint, improving fiber collimation (misalignment reduced from 7.46° to 4.84°) and increasing fiber mass fraction from 17.51% to 24.81%. A friction-induced amplification mechanism further links compaction and effective tension, highlighting their intrinsic coupling during rotary consolidation. An optimal synergistic processing window was identified at 60 N compaction and 500 mN tension, delivering peak tensile strength, interlaminar shear strength, and modulus of 257.56 MPa, 31.37 MPa, and 3.24 GPa, respectively. These results establish a quantitative process–structure–property framework for compaction–tension co-regulation, providing guidance for high performance thermoplastic composite manufacturing of curved structural components.

title: A carbon fiber composite reinforced barrel shell with higher underwater pressure resistance performance
abstract: In this paper, the buckling properties of unreinforced and reinforced barrel shells of carbon fiber composite with positive Gaussian curvature under hydrostatic pressure are systematically investigated by combining theoretical, finite element simulation and experimental methods. The derived analytical formulas for buckling considering the effects of structural curvature and ribs are verified by finite element analysis to have a high prediction accuracy within 10%. Parametric analyses and failure mechanism diagrams of barrel shells and reinforced barrel shells are carried out to investigate the effects of factors such as length-to-diameter ratio, thickness-to-diameter ratio, layup angle, deformation, number and size of ribs on the critical buckling load of the shells. One cylindrical shell, two barrel shells and two reinforced barrel shells are designed, fabricated and measured under equal-volume conditions, prepared by integrated fiber winding molding using a split-flap mold. The test results show that the critical buckling load of barrel shells is enhanced by 32.03% on average compared with that of the equal-volume cylindrical shell, while the reinforced structure significantly improves the stability of barrel shells, with an average increase of 117.08% in the load carrying capacity. The results can provide relevant references for the structural design and preparation of composite pressure-resistant shells.

title: MOF-derived CoNi@C integrated into carbon nanotubes/aramid nanofiber hybrid aerogels for efficient and tunable electromagnetic wave absorption
abstract: The development of high-performance electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorption materials that are effective in harsh environments remains a significant challenge. Herein, a lightweight, flexible, and robust three-dimensional hybrid aerogel is fabricated for efficient broadband EMW absorption. The aerogel is constructed by integrating metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived magnetic CoNi@C nanoparticles and carboxylated multi-walled carbon nanotubes (c-MWCNTs) into an aramid nanofiber (ANF) framework. The synergistic effect between the components endows the composite with remarkable attenuation capability via conductive loss, dielectric loss, magnetic loss, and interfacial polarization. The optimized aerogel exhibits exceptional EMW absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of −59.66 dB at a thickness of 2.68 mm and a broad effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 7.96 GHz at a thickness of 2.94 mm. This work provides a promising strategy for designing advanced EMW absorption materials with integrated properties of strong absorption, wide bandwidth, and environmental resistance for use in aerospace, military, and electronic protection fields.

title: Amphiphilic terpolymer sizing enabling an interfacial toughening layer for enhanced interfacial and mechanical properties of CF/EP composites
abstract: The surface of carbon fibres (CF) was modified by chemical oxidation to introduce carboxyl and hydroxyl functionalities. A polymerization-induced self-assembly (PISA) approach based on reversible addition–fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymerization was adopted to prepare a functional amphiphilic terpolymer, poly (hexyl methacrylate-co-acetoacetoxyethyl methacrylate-co-[2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl]trimethylammonium chloride) (PHAM), by adjusting the monomer feed composition. The resulting PHAM was subsequently used as a sizing agent for carbon fibre/epoxy (CF/EP) composites. Leveraging the cooperative effects of hydrophilic and hydrophobic moieties, the PHAM sizing layer constructs a stress-buffering interphase with enhanced toughness at the fibre/matrix interface. This hierarchical structure facilitates efficient load transfer through chemical bonding while promoting energy dissipation via the physical entanglement of flexible polymer chains, thereby improving the interfacial properties and the macroscopic mechanical performance of the composites. Contact-angle measurements of carbon fibres with different degrees of modification in polar and nonpolar liquids indicate that oxidation of CF, together with the introduction of the highly polar PHAM, enhances chemical compatibility within the interfacial region and consequently increases the overall surface energy of the CF. As a result, the flexural strength and impact strength of the CF/EP composites were improved by 26% and 44.5%, respectively.

title: Designed intermittency in interlaminar fracture via kirigami-induced crack-front widening
abstract: Laminated composite materials remain vulnerable to Mode I delamination. Here, we demonstrate that kirigami-inspired through-thickness cuts can deliberately introduce and control crack-propagation intermittency in carbon-fibre/epoxy laminates by architecting the crack front. Tests on rectangular and trapezoidal patterns, supported by simulations, X-ray CT, and a crack front width model, reveal four distinct stages: baseline propagation; cut entry, marked by a load drop due to a reduced effective width; cut-controlled intermittent propagation, where coupled deformation widens the crack front, increasing its effective length and stored elastic energy; and post-cut propagation, which returns to the baseline trend. Trapezoidal cuts maximise crack-front widening and increase both the load and the apparent energy-release rate required for crack re-initiation by up to fourfold in the tested specimens compared with unpatterned laminates. Rather than relying on interfacial modification or material alteration, this study establishes a proof-of-concept geometry-assisted strategy for tailoring Mode I delamination behaviour in existing laminated composites. By converting delamination into designed, repeatable intermittency, this geometry-driven and material-agnostic approach opens a new design space for enhancing interlaminar resistance. However, broader structural applications require further validation to quantify stress concentrations, adherend failure risks, and associated in-plane performance trade-offs.

title: In-plane pure shear damage of ±45° CFRP Laminates using cruciform specimens under biaxial cyclic loading
abstract: The in-plane shear behavior of ±45° laminated composites in cyclic loading is pivotal to structural performance under complex loading. A clean in-plane pure-shear damage accumulation is achieved using a cruciform specimen in biaxial tension–compression cyclic loading in this work. The experimental investigation of the nonlinear shear response of ±45° carbon-fiber laminates is conducted. The experimental results indicate a smooth transition from linear elasticity to pronounced nonlinearity in large deformation, and accompanied by a progressive stiffness degradation under cyclic loading. The biaxial tension-compression tests with various loading levels are conducted to investigate the effect of stress level on shear damage accumulation, and reveal the relationship between shear stiffness degradation and fatigue life. The elastic, recoverable and irrecoverable nonlinear deformation are observed in the analysis of the experimental unloading–reloading processes. Accordingly, a model for the description of the relationship between the irrecoverable strain growth and the reduction of unloading tangent stiffness. The digital image correlation (DIC) and SEM are utilized to characterize the strain field and fractography in the gauge area of cruciform specimens. The damage mechanics including matrix shear deformation, interfacial sliding/debonding, and fiber-aligned crack–slip banding are observed in the experimental results. The methodology and findings provide a mechanism-informed basis for damage accumulation under cyclic pure shear loading.

title: Interphase construction via rigid-flexible segment modulation: poly(amic acid) sizing for strengthening carbon fiber/thermoplastic resin composites
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced thermoplastic composites (CFRTPs) exhibit substantial application potential owing to their low density and high mechanical robustness. Nevertheless, the inherently inert and smooth surface of carbon fibers leads to insufficient interfacial adhesion with polymer matrices, giving rise to inadequate interlaminar shear strength(ILSS) and fiber debonding, thereby restricting further performance enhancement. In this study, guided by the principle of “like dissolves like”, four novel self-emulsifying poly(amic acid) sizing agents (PAAs1–PAAs4) were designed and synthesized by tailoring the conformational disparities between rigid and flexible chain segments. These distinct segmental designs facilitated the construction of an interfacial layer with a “rigid-flexible” gradient between the carbon fiber and the matrix resin, thereby elucidating the interfacial reinforcement mechanism from the perspective of molecular segmental mobility and matrix compatibility. Furthermore, by employing a dual-component sizing strategy, the wettability variations induced by the Tg mismatch between the components were utilized to establish a characteristic interfacial architecture on the fiber surface, forming physical anchoring points analogous to those introduced by inorganic fillers. With PAAs1/PAAs4 blends optimized for each matrix, the ILSS of CF/PEI and CF/PEEK composites reached 99.08 MPa (+68.01%) and 90.89 MPa (+39.40%), while flexural strengths increased to 1093.46 MPa (+91.02%) and 935.11 MPa (+67.66%), respectively. Consequently, by synergizing chemical compatibility with physical interlocking, this dual-reinforcement strategy opens up new avenues for the interfacial design of high-performance thermoplastic composites.

title: The lightweight and hydrophobic PAN fiber/SiO2 aerogel-boehmite composite material can significantly improve thermal stability and flame retardancy while maintaining excellent thermal insulation performance
abstract: SiO2 aerogel is a highly promising thermal insulation material. However, its drawbacks of high preparation cost and poor mechanical properties limit its large-scale application. In this study, MTMS and boehmite (AlOOH) were used as precursors, and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) fibers were introduced as reinforcements to make up for the mechanical performance shortcomings of SiO2 aerogels. PAN/SiO2–AlOOH composites were fabricated using the sol-gel route, with the effect of boehmite concentration on the composite characteristics being comprehensively analyzed. Microstructural characterization indicates that SiO2 aerogel and boehmite particles can be uniformly distributed on the surface of PAN fibers. At a boehmite addition of 20%, a continuous coating layer and an inter-fiber three-dimensional network are formed, which significantly enhance the mechanical properties of the composite, with a tensile strength of 1.53 MPa and an elongation at break of approximately 40%. The results show that as the boehmite content rises, the composites maintain excellent thermal insulation performance (exhibiting thermal conductivity down to 0.023 W/(m·K)), good hydrophobicity (exhibiting water contact angles up to 139.12 °) and corrosion resistance, while their flame retardancy and thermal stability are also significantly improved. After calcination at 800 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C, the composites still retain high specific surface area, excellent thermal insulation and certain mechanical strength. The 1350 °C butane torch combustion test confirms their outstanding thermal insulation performance. Compared with conventional SiO2 aerogel processes, this method is more efficient and cost-effective, showing broad application prospects in thermal insulation.

title: Enhanced fusion prediction of composite material performance degradation via interval processes and machine learning
abstract: Predicting the performance degradation of composite materials is of paramount importance for ensuring the safe operation of composite engineering structures. Traditional experimental methods involve protracted, costly accelerated ageing tests, while theoretical methods also subject to their own inherent limitations. Physics-based methods face parameter-tuning difficulties and incomplete degradation descriptions, while data-driven approaches are data-dependent and may have low accuracy. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents an innovative methodology that integrates interval degradation progress models with Bi-LSTM (Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory) neural networks to enhance prediction performance. Specifically, the Grey System Theory (GST) is employed to quantify the interval process. By combining GST with physical information, a novel quantification method for the interval degradation process model is proposed. This model serves as a reference framework, enabling the mapping of experimental degradation data. The Bi-LSTM network then harnesses this nonlinear mapping to forecast the degradation trajectory of composite materials, leveraging its powerful sequential learning capabilities. The accuracy of the proposed method is verified using two different experimental datasets: stiffness degradation under hygrothermal conditions and fatigue damage under cyclic stress. The results clearly demonstrate that this fusion approach outperforms existing methods in terms of predictive accuracy, indicating its great potential for practical applications in the field of composite material performance degradation prediction.

title: Injection molding of segregated ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene/polyethylene wax/carbon nanotube composites with excellent electrical conductivity and mechanical properties
abstract: Conductive polymer composites (CPCs) with segregated structures can achieve excellent electrical conductivity at extremely low conductive filler contents. However, the processing of ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE)-based CPCs is largely confined to simple methods like compression molding, which leads to low processing efficiency. Meanwhile, the mechanical properties of CPCs usually deteriorate significantly with increasing conductive filler content. To address these challenges, UHMWPE/polyethylene wax/carbon nanotube (UHMWPE/PEW/CNT) conductive composites were fabricated via melt blending followed by injection molding using a specially designed screw-type injection machine. This strategy effectively improves processing efficiency while achieving a synergistic enhancement of electrical conductivity and mechanical performance. The experimental results demonstrated that the UHMWPE/PEW/CNT composites exhibit a high volume electrical conductivity of 4.2 S/m at a CNT content of only 4 wt%. When the CNT content increased to 6 wt%, the electrical conductivity was further enhanced to 26.2 S/m, accompanied by a high impact strength of 93.7 kJ/m2 and a well-maintained elongation at break of 131.5 %. This work provides a feasible and efficient approach for the large-scale fabrication of UHMWPE-based CPCs with segregated structures and high electrical conductivity.

title: Curing deformation prediction of aircraft-grade toughened composites based on the indirect characterization method
abstract: Accurate numerical simulation of curing deformation is essential for manufacturing high-quality thermoset carbon fiber composites. However, reliable material properties for constitutive modeling of aircraft-grade toughened prepregs remain challenging, primarily due to the extremely high viscosity of modified resin matrix, which hinders the preparation of low-porosity specimens critical for experimental characterization. To address this, we develop an indirect characterization method for resin’s curing characteristics using unidirectional composite prepreg as the test medium. Pure resin thermodynamic properties are derived from composite measurement data via reverse homogenization, enabling comprehensive evaluation of unidirectional composites with varying fiber volume fractions. The approach integrates the time-temperature superposition principle (TTSP) with Laplace-domain micromechanics, effectively circumventing complex viscoelastic convolution integrals in the constitutive model. Finally, a comprehensive material model of the composite material is integrated into a coupled constitutive model in Abaqus/Standard using a user-defined finite element analysis (FEA) subroutine, which considers the diversity of composite structure geometry, lamination sequence, and fiber volume fraction. Validation experiments on beam-shaped and L-shaped laminates show that the proposed method achieves a prediction accuracy of over 91.1% for curing-induced deformation, which is in good agreement with the finite element analysis results. This method not only provides a robust framework for characterizing and modeling high-viscosity resins and their composites but also enables efficient process optimization for complex composite components, thereby significantly reducing costly experimental expenses. • Proposed an indirect characterization method for highly viscous toughened thermoset resins. • Integrated TTSP with Laplace-domain micromechanics to avoid complex viscoelastic convolution integrals in constitutive modeling. • Established a coupled chemo-thermo-mechanical constitutive model implemented in Abaqus/Standard, achieving >91.1% prediction accuracy for curing-induced deformation of composite laminates. • Provided a systematic framework for next-generation aircraft-grade composites, reducing costly experiments.

title: Active-vinyl-graft MXene nanosheets modified high modulus carbon fiber /vinyl ester resin composites featuring mechanical-engagement and chemical-bond synergistic interactions in interphase for enhancing the interfacial performance
abstract: Endowing high-strength and high-modulus carbon fiber reinforced vinyl ester resin composites (HMCF/VE composites) with superior interfacial performance would produce advanced composites with great potential for applications in daily life and industry. Herein we report on depositing the reactive vinyl-group-graft MXene nanosheets (Vi@MX) on the surface of HMCFs through electrophoretic deposition (EPD) technology, achieving the Vi@MX-HMCFs with a surface presenting high roughness and containing the vinyl and hydroxy reactive groups similar to those in VE resin. As a result, the Vi@MX-HMCF/VE composites reveal a significant interfacial performance because of the synergistic interactions involving mechanical engagement, hydrogen bonding, and chemical covalent cross-link in the interphase. The Vi@MX-HMCF/VE composites’ interfacial shear strength (IFSS) and interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) are respectively 57.77 MPa and 69.85 MPa, an increase of 158.59 % and 45.95 % relative to the untreated HMCF/VE composites. In addition, the fracture toughness and interphase thickness of the composites are also greatly improved. This work provides a potential strategy to enhance the multiscale interfacial bonding capability, enabling more effective ways to enhance the interfacial properties of advanced HMCF/VE composites.

title: A bidirectional zero thermal expansion design method for carbon fiber composite structures
abstract: The invariance of structural dimensions during temperature changes is crucial for high-precision optical platforms, aerospace equipment, and metrological components. The adjustability of the effective coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) of traditional composite laminates is limited, and the existing concepts of zero thermal expansion (ZTE) are often constrained to one direction or dependent on porous mechanisms that reduce structural stiffness. This work presents a deterministic design method for bidirectional zero thermal expansion composite structures using a single material without introducing flexible hinges. The structure consists of a lower laminate and an upper laminate, forming a thermal-induced bending compensation mechanism. A combined thermal-moment model is established to characterize the coupling between axial strain, in-plane thermal mismatch, and layer-level bending. Analytical expressions for the effective CTE in the both principal directions are derived, enabling the identification of parameter ranges that simultaneously satisfy the ZTE constraints. The optimized design structure is evaluated using three-dimensional finite element simulation, and the predicted CTE is consistent with the theoretical results. In addition, the optimized structure is prepared using hot press molding process, and the bidirectional compensation mechanism is verified by measuring the thermal deformation between 20 °C and 200 °C. The proposed approach provides a fully manufacturable route to achieve bidirectional ZTE composite structures suitable for high thermal stability engineering applications.

title: Editorial Board
Structure and property relationships in thermally conductive flake filled composites
abstract: Dielectric materials filled with thermally conductive particles have undergone significant development as candidates for thermal management in computational, high-power, and radio frequency electronics and devices. Specifically, particle-filled systems including thermal interface materials and polymer-ceramic composite encapsulants offer cheap, easy, and customizable solutions. Understanding the relationship between the microstructural design and emergent thermal conductivity of such composites can inform processing routes that realize drastically higher heat flow. To investigate the large variable space associated with these materials, finite element analysis is leveraged to systematically explore representative microstructures and establish causal links with emergent property outcomes. Here, several key structural parameters are isolated and investigated including filler aspect ratio, filler volume fraction, filler conductivity both with and without anisotropy, filler orientation, filler-matrix interface conductance, and matrix conductivity. The relative importance of each variable is discussed in detail. These findings can be utilized to tune resultant composite microstructures by adapting processing techniques, thus enabling higher effective composite thermal conductivity.

title: Corrigendum to “Dielectric breakdown behaviors and high-voltage damages of 3D braided carbon fiber/epoxy resin composites” [Compos. Sci. Technol. 272 (2025) 111388]
Preparation of silica-coated recovered carbon black dual-phase filler and its regulation on the performance of solution-polymerized styrene-butadiene rubber composites
abstract: The annual global production of waste tires reaches tens of millions of tons, posing significant environmental and economic challenges. Thermal pyrolysis technology is an effective method for recycling and reutilizing waste tires, while recovered carbon black (rCB) is a main product of tire pyrolysis. But rCB exhibits low surface activity, leading to weak filler-rubber interaction, which limits its application. A novel dual-phase filler (rCB@SiO2) was prepared through the in situ reaction of tetraethoxysilane in aqueous suspension of rCB. rCB@SiO2 was designed to synergize the properties of both phases: the silica surface facilitates silane coupling for enhanced interface, while the rCB contributes its inherent structural reinforcement. This unique structure of rCB@SiO2 and the addition of Si69 lead to the significant improvement of the properties of solution-polymerized styrene-butadiene rubber (SSBR) composites in comparison to using rCB alone or a mixture of rCB and silica. When the silica content in rCB@SiO2 is 4%, SSBR/rCB@SiO2/Si69 (100/50/4) composite exhibited markedly enhanced properties relative to the SSBR/rCB (100/50) composite: 27% and 16% increases in moduli at 100% and 300% elongation, a 26% improvement in abrasion resistance, and a 22% reduction in rolling resistance, thus effectively balancing the tread “magic triangle”. This work not only provides a novel strategy for the high-value utilization of rCB, but also offers theoretical and practical foundations for designing high-performance and eco-friendly rubber composites.

title: A self-sensing plant fiber-reinforced composites based on piezoelectric effect for damage detection
abstract: Current self-sensing composites are generally incompatible with plant fiber-reinforced composites, failing to meet the requirements for their structural health monitoring. To address this issue, this study fabricated plant fiber piezoelectric composites via polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) functionalized matrix. By optimizing the material composition, 5% PVDF was identified as the optimal content to ensure the mechanical properties of the composites meet the service requirements. Sensing performance characterization confirmed that the composites exhibit stable self-sensing response capabilities based on the piezoelectric effect. Monitoring tests under three-point bending and impact load conditions verified that the proposed monitoring approach enables accurate localization of load-induced deformation and damage, as well as quantitative evaluation of damage severity. Finite element simulation provides theoretical validation for the monitoring mechanism, and the constructed structural health monitoring system realizes real-time damage localization. In conclusion, the self-sensing composites and associated monitoring technology developed in this study effectively resolve the compatibility issue of structural health monitoring for PFRCs, and can provide technical guarantees and support for the large-scale application of PFRCs.

title: Multi-physics coupled prediction method for the interlaminar performance of thermoplastic composites considering manufacturing-induced residual stresses
abstract: Thermoplastic composites exhibit high specific strength, weldability and re-formability, which gives them substantial engineering application potential in aerospace and related fields. However, existing studies mainly focus on the influence of processing parameters on crystallization behavior and mechanical performance, while the systematic role of manufacturing-induced residual stresses in governing interlaminar load-carrying capacity and failure modes has been largely overlooked, which prevents an accurate assessment of the structural performance. In this study, a multi-physics coupled prediction method was developed, in which manufacturing-induced residual stresses were explicitly considered based on a crystallization kinetics model and a traction–separation failure criterion. The method was able to effectively describe the interlaminar damage evolution and failure behavior of thermoplastic composites under the action of residual stresses, which was validated by experimental results. The results showed that, when manufacturing-induced residual stresses were included, the relative prediction error of the peak load was reduced by about 60% compared with the case without residual stresses. Furthermore, the study clarified the internal links among the crystallization process, cooling conditions, residual stress field, and interlaminar strength. These findings were of practical significance for forming-process optimization and structural design of thermoplastic composite components.

title: A Bayesian calibration method for quantifying interfacial fracture properties of 3D-Printed composites
abstract: Interfacial fracture properties largely govern the delamination resistance and structural reliability of 3D-printed composites. However, conventional calibration methods are typically established under linear-elastic and small-deformation assumptions, which can yield biased property estimates. Here, we develop a Bayesian calibration framework to quantify interfacial fracture properties from nonlinear large-deformation delamination while rigorously accounting for uncertainty. To this end, we designed 3D-printed composites (PS-CFRCs) with enhanced mechanical properties through phase separation and chemical grafting. A high-fidelity interfacial model is established by coupling the coincident element method with the fractional-order viscoelasticity, ensuring capture of time-dependent behavior and nonlinear delamination evolution. To accelerate inference, a shape-constrained surrogate model is constructed in a probabilistic framework that jointly estimates key interfacial parameters together with calibration error. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling is then performed to obtain the joint posterior distributions and posterior predictive intervals. The results show that chemical grafting enhances the delamination resistance of PS-CFRCs by promoting interfacial load transfer, increasing fracture toughness by about 2.7-fold. The calibrated model yields credible intervals that consistently encompass the experimental observations, demonstrating improved predictive robustness relative to conventional theoretical estimates. This framework provides a practical tool for interfacial characterization and reliability-oriented manufacturing of 3D-printed composites.

title: Precracking-guided anisotropic sensors via pressure-insensitive self-assembly design toward tensile strain monitoring
abstract: With the expanding applications of flexible strain sensors across various fields, their limitations in selective response and precise mechanical measurement under complex loading conditions have become increasingly evident. This work addressed these challenges by developing a pressure-insensitive anisotropic tensile sensor (PIATS) through the integration of aramid nanofibers and graphene nanosheets into an orientation structure (ANFG). The sensor was fabricated using directional freezing, followed by high-pressure compression, encapsulation, and pre-stretching strategies. The resulting PIATS exhibited extremely high sensitivity to radial tensile strain (with a gauge factor of 51.34). At 40% strain, the resistance change reached up to 2000%, and it also featured high linearity (R2 = 96.73%). Interestingly, owing to the exceptionally high modulus of the compressed ANFG in the Z direction, the electrical performance of the sensor demonstrated notable pressure insensitivity. More importantly, the sensor effectively decoupled pressure loads and achieved effective measurement of tensile excitation. By cross-stacking the conductive layers, we also achieved effective measurement of the tensile loading directions. Finally, a novel PIATS-based sensor array was designed to effectively measure the location and extent of impact. These results underscored the significant potential of PIATS in strain monitoring under complex environments.

title: Synergistic mechanical, EMI shielding, and deicing performance of CF/PEEK composites enabled by T-ZnO@MXene via electrostatic self-assembly
abstract: The escalating demand for multifunctionality in carbon fiber reinforced poly(ether ether ketone) (CF/PEEK) composites has intensified the need for next-generation structural materials. However, achieving a synergistic integration of functional performance and structural integrity—rather than a trade-off—remains a critical challenge. Herein, tetrapod-shaped ZnO whiskers decorated with 2D Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets (T-ZnO@MXene) were fabricated via electrostatic self-assembly and incorporated into CF/PEEK composites. This 3D conductive/enhanced network enabled the simultaneous enhancement of mechanical properties, electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding, and electrothermal deicing capabilities. The optimized CF/T-ZnO@MXene/PEEK composites exhibited a flexural strength of 1970.0 MPa, a flexural modulus of 142.3 GPa, and an interlaminar shear strength of 123.2 MPa, representing improvements of 33.4 %, 45.1 %, and 56.7 % over pristine CF/PEEK, respectively. Concurrently, the through-thickness electrical conductivity surged for 7.7 S/m, corresponding to a 76-fold enhancement, while the EMI shielding effectiveness attained 56.7 dB (a 40.7 % increase). In addition, the composites demonstrated efficient electrothermal conversion and reliable deicing performance. Overall, this work provides an effective route to harmonize structural robustness with multifunctional capabilities in CF/PEEK composites, opening new opportunities for advanced aerospace applications.

title: Photothermal dual-curing 3D printing of high-performance polymer composites with isotropic mechanical and thermal conductive properties
abstract: Digital Light Processing (DLP) 3D printing characterized by its high-speed and flexible manufacturing capabilities, holds great potential in the production of thermal conductive precision devices. However, its layer-by-layer stacking method leads to anisotropy in the mechanical and thermal conductivity properties, thereby reducing the reliability of the devices. Herein, composites were developed using a photothermal dual-curing resin system as the matrix and surface-modified hexagonal boron nitride (hBN-KH560) as the filler. During thermal curing, epoxy groups within the resin system crosslinked to form an interpenetrating network (IPN) and covalently bonded with epoxy-functionalized hBN-KH560, while the randomly distributed hBN-KH560 can penetrate different layers, effectively enhancing interlayer adhesion and interfacial compatibility between the filler and matrix, thus endowing the composites with high performance and isotropy. Specifically, with the addition of 20 wt% hBN-KH560, the composite achieved a tensile strength of 88.2 MPa, a glass transition temperature (Tg) of 165 °C and a thermal conductivity of 2.2 W m−1 K−1. The anisotropy of the tensile strength, elongation at break and thermal conductivity was significantly reduced to 2.6%, 2.4% and 0.5%, respectively, realizing isotropy in both mechanical and thermal conductivity properties. Besides, A heat sink with excellent heat dissipation performance was successfully fabricated by DLP 3D printing. This work will expand the application of photocurable 3D printing thermal conductive components in cutting-edge fields such as electronic technology.

title: Ultra-low filler loading flexible bamboo cellulose composite films with aligned structures for efficient thermal management
abstract: With the miniaturization and high-powerization of electronic devices, the demand for heat dissipation has increased sharply. However, traditional petroleum-based thermal conductive composites are characterized by high energy consumption, high pollution, and difficulty in recycling. Utilizing the three-dimensional network structure of natural bamboo cellulose, which is stretchable, highly flexible, and rich in easily cross-linkable hydroxyl groups, and transforming it into a two-dimensional network structure, further constructing one-dimensional ordered structures aligned in specific directions with the help of multiple orientation strategies, to promote the directional transport of phonons, is an effective strategy for preparing environmentally friendly polymeric composites while balancing thermal and mechanical properties. Experimental results show that with only 2 wt% MXene added, the in-plane thermal conductivity of the prepared MXene/bamboo cellulose (BMC) composite film reached 2.08 W⋅m−1⋅K−1, which was 160% higher than that of the pure bamboo cellulose film, and the tensile strength and Young's modulus were increased to 11.35 MPa and 71.77 MPa, respectively. After being stretched to 200% strain, the Herman orientation factor of MXene in the BMC composite film increased to 0.91, and the in-plane thermal conductivity of the BMC composite film was increased to 3.46 W⋅m−1⋅K−1. In addition, the heat dissipation simulation experiment results show that the BMC composite film has good heat transfer performance and heat dissipation capacity. This composite film fully utilizes the renewable and degradable properties of bamboo cellulose, providing a new idea for the development of high-performance, flexible, and environmentally friendly intelligent thermal management materials.

title: Aramid fiber surface activation engineering for long-term enhancement of AFEP insulation performance under mechanical cycling loads
abstract: Aramid fiber-reinforced epoxy composites are widely used in various fields, including electronics, electrical engineering, and aerospace, due to their high strength and low density. In the field of electrical power equipment, these materials must withstand harsh conditions involving long-term cyclic alternating loads, which require excellent fatigue resistance. Therefore, this study simulates a fatigue environment using tensile-tensile cyclic mechanical loads to investigate the degradation process and mechanisms affecting the material's insulation properties. Additionally, the study explores surface activation engineering for fibers, which may improve both the initial insulation performance and mechanical fatigue resistance of the material. The test results show that the untreated Pure-AFEP sample has an initial flashover voltage of 11.04 kV and a breakdown strength of 44.08 kV/mm. After optimal surface activation, the material's initial flashover voltage and breakdown strength improved to 12.51 kV and 52.64 kV/mm, respectively. After 1000 fatigue cycles, the Pure-AFEP sample showed a flashover voltage of 9.21 kV (a 16.58% degradation) and a breakdown strength of 23.57 kV/mm (a 46.53% degradation). In contrast, the M1-10%-AFEP sample, after the same fatigue cycles, exhibited a flashover voltage of 10.46 kV and a breakdown strength of 25.42 kV/mm. This showed improvements of 13.57% and 7.85%, respectively, compared to the Pure-AFEP material. These results demonstrate that surface activation enhances the material's resistance to mechanical fatigue.

title: Enhanced dielectric tunability at ultra-low bias in PVDF realized by ferroelectric–CNT core-shell structure
abstract: Polymer composites have emerged as promising tunable dielectric material in microwave devices owing to their low density, flexibility, and ease of processing compared to rigid ceramic counterparts. Nevertheless, their progress is constrained by limited tunability (Tu) and the requirement of high bias fields. Herein, we integrate ferroelectric Barium Strontium Titanate (BST) with electrically nonlinear Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) in core-shell configuration to achieve high Tu under ultra-low bias. The resulting nanocomposite exhibited high Tu of 38.92% at an exceptionally low DC bias field of 0.23 V cm−1, representing a 1.72-fold improvement over conventional systems. Importantly, dielectric loss (tanδ) is well-suppressed from 273.76 to 2.27 (at 100 kHz) due to effective charge trapping at the core-shell interface, which prevents direct electron hopping between conductive pathways. Furthermore, the dielectric breakdown strength (Eb) reaches 253.9 kV cm−1 at 1 vol% loading, nearly double of the uncoated conductive filler system (129.03 kV cm−1). These results highlight a new paradigm for combining nonlinear and ferroelectric materials within a core-shell architecture to realize low-bias, high-performance dielectric nanocomposites, offering significant potential for flexible electronics and next-generation microwave systems.

title: A unified modelling and experimental framework for microcapsule-mediated self-healing in epoxy composites
abstract: This study conducted a comprehensive investigation into the prediction of the effective elastic properties and fracture behaviour of self-healing epoxy composites reinforced with MWCNT/GY257/PMMA (containing MWCNTs in their cores) and AR2963/PMMA microcapsules. The methodology integrated an analytically modified Halpin–Tsai model to predict mechanical properties, accounting for MWCNT and microcapsule agglomeration, aspect ratio, and waviness, within a three-dimensional Representative Volume Element (RVE) progressive damage and healing numerical model under tensile, shear, and triaxial loading. Analytical core findings provided crucial numerical inputs, and the results were validated against experimental data. Damage mechanisms were analysed via Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and optical microscopy during Mode I and Mode II fracture tests. The present work utilises a MWCNT/GY257/PMMA epoxy-AR2963/PMMA amine microcapsules-based healing chemistry with the parent matrix LY556/HY951, achieving near-complete modulus recovery of ∼97% and superior fracture toughness recovery of 82%–93% at 7.5 vol%. Most notably, this system yields a 27% improvement in tensile strength relative to the damaged state, representing a significant advancement over the unreinforced or size-dependent systems reported in the literature. A broad parametric study, which examined factors like agglomeration cluster sizes, core diameters, MWCNT aspect ratio, and microcapsule concentration, concluded that the highest modulus and strength healing capability under various loading conditions is achieved with 45μm equivalent microcapsules (homogenised average form of MWCNT/GY257/PMMA and AR2963/PMMA microcapsules) at 7.5vol% concentration and an MWCNT aspect ratio of 1000. This enhanced performance underscores the efficacy of MWCNT-functionalised healing agents in optimising load-transfer mechanisms and structural integrity.

title: Cold atmospheric plasma modified multifunctional hydrogels with high electromagnetic interference shielding performance and good mechanical properties
abstract: Hydrogels have emerged as promising candidates for high-performance flexible electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding materials due to their strong absorption and attenuation of terahertz waves. The incorporation of conductive fillers, such as MXene, has been proven to significantly enhance the electromagnetic shielding effectiveness (SE) of hydrogels. However, this improvement often comes at the expense of mechanical strength, which may hinder their performance under complex conditions. Although chemical surface modifications can improve interfacial compatibility between MXene and the hydrogel matrix, these approaches usually involve complex procedures and environmentally hazardous reagents. Therefore, developing a simple and direct strategy for modifying MXene-based hydrogels to achieve balanced and improved overall performance remains a challenge. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) modification has recently attracted considerable attention for its rapid, direct, and environmentally friendly approach to tailoring material properties. In this work, a CAP treatment was applied to the hydrogel precursor, enabling the fabrication of a CAP-modified MXene/polyelectrolyte-chitosan hydrogel (CAP@MPC). The CAP-modification significantly improved the interaction between MXene and the polymeric matrix, thereby simultaneously reinforcing both the mechanical strength and electromagnetic interference shielding capability of the hydrogel. As a result, the gel achieved a tensile strength of 0.51 MPa (a ∼50% improvement) and an EMI SE of up to 57.9 dB (an increase of ∼12%) while maintaining excellent robustness. These enhanced properties render CAP@MPC gel a compelling candidate for EMI shielding in advanced flexible electronic systems. Furthermore, this work confirms the potential of CAP technology for application in polymer-based shielding materials.

title: Solvent-free phenolic oligomers with low viscosity and high char yield for resin transfer molding-processed composites
abstract: Conventional phenolic resins rely on solvent addition to enable resin transfer molding (RTM), which inevitably induces defects that degrade mechanical properties and ablation resistance of the resulting composites. In this work, solvent-free phenolic oligomers (SFPOs) with low viscosity and high char yield are successfully synthesized, rendering them intrinsically compatible with RTM for the fabrication of thermal protection composites. The key innovation of SFPOs lies in the precise pH regulation at a critical reaction stage that suppresses the phenol-formaldehyde addition and subsequent condensation reactions, thereby limiting the polymerization degree (MW < 300 g/mol). This endows the SFPOs with intrinsically low viscosity (0.036 Pa s at 70 °C) in the absence of solvents and excellent processability. Moreover, via deliberate regulation of reactant stoichiometry, SFPOs with a high proportion of ortho linkages and abundant reactive hydroxymethyl groups are obtained. These structural features enable multipoint thermally induced polymerization at relatively low temperatures of 100 °C, resulting in highly cross-linked networks and an exceptionally high char yield (72% at 800 °C under N2). Furthermore, SFPO-based composites reinforced by orthogonal three-dimensional quartz fibers were fabricated via RTM process. The SFPO-based composites exhibit superior ablation resistance with a low linear ablation rate of 0.047 mm/s under a 4.18 MW/m2 oxyacetylene flame, which is merely 70% that of commercial phenolic resin (PF)-based composites (0.062 mm/s). Additionally, the SFPO-based composites also exhibit outstanding mechanical performance with a high tensile strength of 371.0 ± 11.3 MPa, a 20% enhancement relative to commercial PF-composites (306.0 ± 31.1 MPa).

title: Improvement of dimensional precision in continuous carbon fiber reinforced composites by multi-filament co-deposition printing
abstract: This study introduces a novel method for improving the printing precision of continuous carbon fiber reinforced composites (CCFRCs) by a multi-filament 3D printer that employs a multi-channel, single-nozzle system with a rotatable printhead. The mechanical performance of triple-filament CCFRCs was evaluated across various inter-filament spacings and compared with that of single-filament specimens at equivalent spacings. The results demonstrate that triple-filament printing not only preserves mechanical properties of the CCFRCs comparable to those by single-filament printing but also increases throughput by approximately threefold. Additionally, turning precision was evaluated at equivalent volumetric build rates by comparing 1K triple-filament and 3K single-filament printing in terms of minimum turning radius and fidelity in tracking a 90° arc path. It was found that the 1K triple-filament configuration achieved a minimum turning radius of 4 mm, compared to 5 mm for the 3K single-filament printing. For 90° arc printing, turning accuracy decreases with increasing layer height. A zigzag-based path optimization significantly improved the turning accuracy of 1K triple-filament printing at small layer heights and radii, achieving a maximum improvement of 7.14% at a 5 mm radius. Feed-rate optimization further enhanced path-tracking accuracy, with a maximum improvement of 7.4% for 1K triple-filament printing, while at a layer height of 0.25 mm, feed-rate-optimized 3K single-filament printing achieved the highest improvement of 7.7%.

title: Thin-thickness 3D-printed dielectric loss multi-layer nested ultra broadband radar absorbing metastructure with wide incident angle
abstract: Efficient radar cross section (RCS) reduction under broadband and wide-angle incidence constraints is a core bottleneck for modern equipment stealth, yet existing absorbers face issues like excessive thickness, narrow bandwidth, and poor wide-angle performance. This study proposes an innovative multi-layer nested three-dimensional radar wave absorbing metastructure and introduces a cell random deflection parameter to expand the design methodology for absorbing metastructure. Based on a finite cellular electromagnetic model and the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II), a multi-objective optimization framework for wide-angle incident three-dimensional (3D) absorbing metastructure is developed. A high-dielectric-loss composite absorber filament were fabricated using polylactic acid/carbon black hybrid particles as raw material. An optimized, thin-thickness (9.6 mm) multi-layer nested square frame ultra-broadband radar wave absorber is produced via fused deposition modeling 3D printing, achieving a vertical reflection loss (RL) of less than −10 dB over the 2–40 GHz bandwidth. The random-deflection design significantly enhanced the multi-layer nested square frame's wide-angle absorption performance: average RL remained < −19.3, −18.5, −18.0, and −11.5 dB at 15°, 30°, 45°, and 60° incidence, respectively. Field and power loss contour analyses revealed the multi-scale ultra-broadband absorption mechanism of the multi-layer nested square frame metastructure absorber. This work advances thin wide-angle stealth structure design/manufacturing, supporting next-generation omnidirectional stealth technology and expanding 3D printing applications in electromagnetic devices.

title: Dynamic characterization of lightweight corrugated FRP tubes: Empirical modeling and probabilistic reliability assessment
abstract: : This study presents empirical formulas derived from finite element (FE) simulations for the dynamic characterization of lightweight corrugated fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) tubes, addressing the lack of reliable predictive tools for resonance-prone corrugated structures. Four surrogate models for predicting the first natural frequency are developed, among which the FE-calibrated analytical model and symbolic regression achieve high predictive accuracy ( ). The framework incorporates corrugation geometry and composite lamina architecture within a probabilistic design setting. Pareto trade-off analysis identifies lightweight woven composites as optimal configurations balancing mass efficiency and natural frequency performance. Global Sobol sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations reveal that convolution count, layer number, and crest radius dominate natural frequency variability, with a pronounced nonlinear interaction between convolution count and layer number governing stiffness-mass coupling effects. In contrast, trough radius, bellows outer radius, and fiber orientation exhibit marginal impact on Sobol sensitivity indices and natural frequency. These findings demonstrate that corrugation geometry exerts a stronger influence on dynamic response uncertainty than further composite tailoring. The proposed formulations provide quantitative guidance for the probabilistic design of resonance-tolerant corrugated FRP tubes, supporting resilient infrastructures in pipeline and aerospace applications.

title: Dynamic impact response and failure mechanisms of carbonene aramid composites: A combined experimental and finite element study
abstract: Aramid composites are widely used in transportation, aerospace, and protective equipment due to their high strength and lightweight properties. However, aramid composites are susceptible to internal damage from low-velocity impacts and exhibit inadequate protective performance under dynamic impacts, limiting their use in high-performance applications. The carbonene aramid fiber is prepared by polymerizing graphene oxide with aramid polymer monomers, followed by a wet spinning process. Currently, the dynamic mechanical behavior and damage mechanisms of carbonene aramid composites remain unclear. This study examines the dynamic impact behavior of carbonene aramid composites by evaluating their low-velocity impact, dynamic compression, and ballistic performance, with finite element simulations employed to support the analysis of low-velocity impact and ballistic performance. Experimental results show that under an impact energy of 140J, the carbonene aramid composites achieve a peak load of 18.65kN and an energy absorption rate of 86.18%, outperforming aramid composites by 54.64% and 34.24%, respectively. At a strain rate of 7000 s−1, the dynamic compression strength and specific energy absorption (SEA) are 1604.3 MPa and 8.18 MJ/m3, showing improvements of 13.8% and 22.46%. Under high-speed ballistic impact, the SEA is 32.05 J m2/kg, showing improvements of 13.25% over aramid composites.
