By precisely selecting curing agents, this work realizes controllable construction of BT resin crosslinked networks, deepens the understanding of multi stage curing mechanism, and provides theoretical and practical guidance for developing advanced BT based materials for next generation communication and electronic packaging.

title: Insights into biochar composition and its impact on the properties of natural rubber composites
abstract: Agricultural biochars offer a sustainable alternative to fossil-derived fillers in rubber composites, yet their performance depends strongly on feedstock-driven composition and structure. This study systematically examines biochars from corncob, bamboo, and tapioca incorporated into natural rubber vulcanizates, using N550 carbon black as a benchmark. Characterization revealed carbon-rich biochars retaining plant-derived hollow, multi-tubular architectures with varying mineral oxide contents. During high-shear mixing of the biochars and natural rubber, biochar particles fragmented into smaller agglomerates and aggregates comprising carbon-rich domains with surface-bound or embedded metal oxides. Filler–filler interactions prominantly occur within these agglomerates or large clusters, driven primarily by metal oxide polarity and carbon-carbon interfacial interactions, as evidenced by the Payne effect and elemental analysis. These structures governed filler–rubber compatibility, viscoelastic response, crosslink density, and mechanical properties. Biochar-filled compounds exhibited viscosity and processability comparable to the semi-reinforcing carbon black N550 for corncob and bamboo biochars, while tapioca-derived biochar showed higher viscosity due to stronger filler-filler interactions. All three biochars improved tear resistance through crack deflection. However, reinforcement efficiency was limited by poor compatibility between polar mineral components and non-polar rubber, as well as restricted rubber penetration into hollow biochar structures. Overall, biochar microarchitecture and inorganic content critically influence composite performance. The findings highlight opportunities to engineer high-performance, sustainable biochar fillers through mineral control, surface modification, and optimized processing for next-generation rubber composites.

title: Editorial Board
Unveiling the interplay between filler size and interface effects on the long-term durability of highly filled flexible elastomer composites
abstract: Highly filled elastomer composites are widely used in electronic packaging, where the high-volume fraction filler endows the material with special functions. However, the durability of those materials is becoming an important issue owing to the increasing power density of microelectronic. Due to its high filler content and heterogeneity, the long-term performance of highly filled elastomer composites has become a complex scientific problem involving the synergistic effects of the filler size and filler-polymer interface. In this study, we investigate the long-term durability (24h to 1000h) of highly filled elastomer composites under accelerated aging condition of 150 °C with varied interface proportion and the same volume percentage of 60 by the incorporation of three different-sized aluminum (Al) powders into polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix. Smaller filler spacing and the thickening of the interfacial thickness contribute to the more pronounced increase of Young's modulus (from 0.13 MPa to 16.98 MPa), yield stress (from 0.055 MPa to 0.87 MPa) in aged PDMS/Al elastomers with smaller filler size. Conversely, the aged PDMS/Al elastomer with large particle size shows a higher increase of thermal conductivity (from 2.0 W/(m•K) to 3.1 W/(m•K)) due to the increased interfacial thickness and lower interfacial phonon scattering. This work provides a valuable insight of the relationship among the filler size effect, interface effect and long-term performance of highly filled elastomer composites.

title: Enhanced compatibilization of aramid fibers with thermoplastic polyolefin via concurrent mechanical interlocking and surface functionalization
abstract: This study presents an effective approach for compatibilizing thermoplastic polyolefin, a polymer blend comprising polypropylene, polyethylene, and ethylene propylene diene monomer domains, with aramid fibers. It addresses the long-standing challenge of poor interfacial adhesion between non-polar matrices and inert fibers. Aramid fibers were modified using medium and high radio frequency (RF) power air plasma, which increased surface roughness and introduced amines and other polar functional groups. These functionalities enabled covalent bonding with polypropylene-graft-maleic anhydride (PP-g-MA), a compatibilizer, through stable amide linkages at the fiber-matrix interface. This compatibilization strategy leveraged both mechanical interlocking from surface roughness and chemical coupling through interfacial interactions. Combining these two mechanisms led to greater reinforcement than either approach alone. Mechanical testing revealed that the compatibilized composites exhibited significantly improved tensile and flexural strength and stiffness compared with both uncompatibilized systems and previously reported aramid/polyolefins composites. Dynamic mechanical analysis and rheological measurements confirmed enhanced stress transfer and energy dissipation, while differential scanning calorimetry indicated increased crystallization temperature and thermal stability. Scanning electron microscopy of fractured surfaces revealed distinct composite failure mechanisms between untreated fibers, plasma-treated fibers (mechanical interlocking only), and treated fibers with PP-g-MA (both mechanisms), with extensive fiber defibrillation observed only in the last case. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on this dual-mechanism compatibilization strategy based on plasma surface treatment. The findings establish a scalable and effective strategy for developing high performance, durable, and thermally stable composites from non-polar polymers and inert fiber systems.

title: Enhanced and accelerated self-healing performance of carbon fiber/epoxy composites with dual dynamic covalent bonds and graphene via near infrared response
abstract: The integration of photo-thermal fillers and dual dynamic covalent bonds remains challenging for the fabrication of high-performance self-healable carbon fiber reinforced epoxy (CF/EP) composites. In this work, graphene (GN) reinforced epoxy matrices with boronic ester and Diels-Alder (DA) bonds (GN/FBA-EP, GN/FBA-DA-EP) and corresponding CF/EP composites were fabricated, and their self-healing performance by near infrared (NIR) heating was compared to that of unreinforced epoxy matrices (FBA-EP, FBA-DA-EP) and composites by conventional heating. The presence of N–CO and a negative shift in CC binding energy verified successful integration of GN and dual dynamic covalent bonds in GN/FBA-DA-EP. Compared to thermal responsive FBA-EP (93.01%, 85.97%) and FBA-DA-EP (94.99%, 91.02%), NIR responsive GN/FBA-EP and GN/FBA-DA-EP achieved higher first and second self-healing efficiencies (95.07%, 88.76% and 96.46%, 94.16%). In contrast to GN/FBA-EP containing single boronic ester bonds, dual-dynamic GN/FBA-DA-EP exhibited rapid recovery of cross-scratches under NIR heating, indicating that high photo-thermal conversion efficiency of GN activated the exchange reaction of boronic ester bonds, thereby facilitating the dissociation and rearrangement of DA bonds. Correlative 2D and 3D morphologies revealed that CF/GN/FBA-DA-EP achieved the minimal scratch depth and fastest recovery time under NIR heating compared to CF/GN/FBA-EP, which confirmed the improved first and second self-healing efficiencies (96.98%, 93.15%) from the synergy between GN and dual dynamic covalent bonds. This work presents a strategy for synergistically enhancing and accelerating the self-healing performance of epoxy matrices and CF/EP composites.

title: Poly(amide acid)-mediated glass fiber fabric/Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 piezoelectric composites with high flexibility and sensitivity
abstract: Flexible piezoelectric composites have attracted increasing interest for sensor applications. However, for flexible fiber-based piezoelectric composites, constructing a continuous ceramic network with high loading and robust interfacial bonding on the fiber fabric remains challenging. In this study, we fabricated flexible glass fiber fabric (GFF)/PZT piezoelectric composites. Poly (amide acid) (PAA) was introduced as a molecular mediator on the GFF, where PAA forms hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl group and acetate groups of the PZT sol, enabling a 2.8-fold increase in PZT loading at an optimized PAA concentration of 8 wt%. The resulting GFF/PZT composite exhibits a continuous ceramic phase and retains good flexibility with a minimum bending radius of 15 mm. After encapsulation with interdigitated electrodes via epoxy resin (Ep), the GFF/PZT/Ep sensor achieves a minimum bending radius as low as 2.5 mm and exhibits enhanced electrical properties: a dielectric constant of 147, a low dielectric loss of 0.01 at 103 Hz, and an inverse piezoelectric coefficient of 119.5 p.m./V. As a bending sensor, it delivers a high sensitivity of 7.52 V per unit flexural strain and excellent durability over 1000 cycles. As a vibration sensor, it attains a sensitivity of 211.16 mV/g at 10 Hz and maintains stable output over 10,000 cycles. This work offers a promising strategy for developing flexible piezoelectric composites for energy conversion applications.

title: Achievable thermal conductivity of unidirectional carbon fiber composites limited by fiber breakage–induced thermal resistance
abstract: Unidirectional (UD) carbon fiber (CF) composites are theoretically expected to exhibit high thermal conductivity because longitudinal heat transport is governed by highly conductive fibers aligned in parallel, and the parallel model predicts direct proportionality to fiber thermal conductivity and volume fraction. However, actual composite thermal conductivity is often limited by defects such as fiber breakage, which introduces additional thermal resistance at fracture surfaces of CFs. We investigated how the properties of CF affect the efficiency of achieving the ideal thermal conductivity of UD composites. First, we examined anisotropic thermal conductivities of two types of CFs, pitch-based CFPitch and polyacrylonitrile-based CFPAN, using time-domain thermoreflectance. CFPitch exhibited longitudinal thermal conductivity of (430 ± 80) W m−1 K−1 and transverse thermal conductivity of (13.6 ± 1.8) W m−1 K−1, while CFPAN shows (10.6 ± 1.1) W m−1 K−1 and (3.7 ± 0.6) W m−1 K−1, respectively. Despite these high intrinsic values, the corresponding UD composites achieved only 29% (70.5 W m−1 K−1) with CFPitch and 63% (2.4 W m−1 K−1) with CFPAN of the thermal conductivities predicted by the parallel model. Finite element analysis incorporating fiber breakage revealed that interruption of continuous fibers substantially increased thermal resistance, with the effect being more severe in the more brittle CFPitch-based system. These findings demonstrate that fiber breakage is the dominant factor limiting the achievable thermal conductivity of UD CF composites and highlight the need for processing strategies that minimize fiber damage to realize high-performance thermal interface materials.

title: Influence of irregular R-curve behaviour on failure prediction of interface-toughened composite joints
abstract: Interlaminar toughening is increasingly used to enhance the fracture toughness and strength of composite bonded joints. However, certain toughening strategies can introduce irregular fracture resistance behaviour during debonding, such as falling–flat or rising–falling–flat R-curve characteristics, whose influence on joint performance prediction remains unexplored. This study investigates the effect of such irregular R-curve behaviour on the modelling and strength prediction of interface-toughened composite joints by simulating debonding in single-step joints toughened with core–shell rubber (CSR) nanoparticles, polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) micro-fibre veils, and hybrid CSR–PPS systems using a bilinear cohesive zone model, validated against existing experimental results. Fracture energies are assigned to cohesive elements along the bondline using either experimentally measured crack-length-dependent fracture energies or crack-length-independent constant values. The results demonstrate that irregular R-curve behaviour introduced by PPS-veil toughening significantly influences the predicted debonding process and joint strength, and neglecting this behaviour leads to unreliable modelling. Furthermore, a selective local PPS-veil toughening strategy is explored, exploiting the elevated fracture resistance at early stages of crack growth. Appropriate localised toughening is shown to alter the debonding process and achieve improved joint strength compared with full-length toughening.

title: Core-shell fillers with interacting cores in sandwiched composites for high-temperature energy storage
abstract: Polymer dielectrics for energy storage at elevated temperatures are often limited by the trade-off between polarization and breakdown strength, together with thermally activated charge transport. Herein, a sandwich-structured composite incorporating interaction-enabled core–shell fillers in the middle layer is designed to achieve coupled regulation of micro-interface and macro-spatial structure. Al2O3 NSs are introduced as insulating outer layers, while CDs@AO NWs with interaction-enabled CDs are incorporated into the middle layer to construct a transport-regulating framework. The combination of CDs and high aspect-ratio AO NWs introduces multi-level trapping sites and heterogeneous interfaces, while interactions among CDs induce micro-capacitive effects, enabling enhanced interfacial polarization. Through regulation of the middle-layer composition and thickness ratio, the optimized 1–4–1 composite with balanced polarization and breakdown strength is achieved. Consequently, it delivers an Ud of 8.1 J/cm3 at 150 °C and 4.2 J/cm3 at 200 °C with η above 90%. This work provides an effective strategy for dielectric energy storage at elevated temperatures.

title: Revealing penetration mechanism of cross-ply CFRP via experiment and high-fidelity simulation: From quasi-static to dynamic
abstract: Assessing the penetration behavior of carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates is crucial for their engineering applications. The work presents a comparative investigation into the penetration behaviors of thin cross-ply laminates under quasi-static indentation (QSI) and low-velocity impact (LVI). Experimental results reveal the divergences that a lower peak load, smaller failure displacement and less severe intralaminar damage (as indicated by a higher residual stiffness) under dynamic penetration when compared to QSI. A Puck criterion-based critical strain criterion is developed within the element deletion strategy, enabling the capture of matrix splitting. Subsequently, high-fidelity simulations replicated both the experimental mechanical responses and fracture morphologies under both QSI and LVI loading conditions. This proves the robustness of this validated framework for extending from quasi-static to dynamic regimes, confirming that the CFRP dynamic penetration behaviors can be effectively predicted using the critical strain calibrated under quasi-static penetration. As revealed by simulation, the observed divergences are attributed to the earlier fiber breakage in the backside plies caused by the dynamic inertia effect. A parametric analysis evaluated the influence of critical strain on the predictive accuracy. In particular, a low critical strain value results in excessive element deletion, leading to premature failure and a smaller delamination area. In addition, a positive correlation exists between intralaminar element deletion area and interlaminar delamination area. This work further demonstrates the applicability of the strain-based element deletion strategy and offers mechanistic insights into CFRP penetration.

title: Synergistic enhancement of dielectric properties in PVDF/BT/BNNTs composites for miniaturized antenna sensors with improved crack detection sensitivity
abstract: Current antenna sensors encounter size mismatch challenges when monitoring cracks in precision metallic components. Herein, a miniaturized microstrip patch antenna sensor was developed using pneumatic-electric synergy printed polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF)/boron nitrate nanotubes (BNNTs)/barium titanate (BT) composite films as the dielectric layer. Systematic investigations were conducted on the synergistic effects of BNNTs and BT on the composites' dielectric properties, antenna performance, and crack detection sensitivity. Results demonstrate that electric field-pneumatic pressure guidance coupled with BT-BNNTs synergy promotes the formation of the β-phase in PVDF. This β-phase enhancement and the abundant interfaces from BT/BNNTs facilitate polarization and space charge accumulation, significantly optimizing the composite's dielectric properties. Concurrently, the three-dimensional network constructed by BNNTs effectively suppresses electron migration, reducing dielectric loss. At 1 kHz, the PVDF/10 wt%-BT/0.15 wt%-BNNTs composite film exhibits a high relative permittivity (ε′) of 16.89 and a notably low dielectric loss of 0.042. Benefiting from the enhanced dielectric properties, the antenna achieves a compact size of 5.86 mm × 8.36 mm (62% area reduction vs. PVDF-based antenna) and a high crack detection sensitivity of 22 MHz/mm. This work highlights the synergistic enhancement of dielectric properties in PVDF/BT/BNNTs composites, providing a strategy for miniaturized high-sensitivity structural health monitoring (SHM) sensors.

title: Small-data machine learning-assisted design of synergistic phase change composites for advanced thermal management
abstract: Electronic devices may face electromechanical performance degradation or even failure during long-term service. This is because continued miniaturization and integration of devices intensify heat accumulation caused by the Joule effect. Recently, functional phase change composites have been developed to alleviate device heating. Although significant progress has been made in enhancing the thermal conductivity of phase change composites and suppressing leakage, maintaining both flexibility and excellent thermal management performance remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose a synergistic enhancement method to develop a leakage-free flexible functional composite (FFC) by using hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) as the thermal conductivity phase and microcapsule phase change material (MPCM) as the thermal storage phase. Herein, the incorporation of thermal conductivity phase forms a continuous heat conduction network within the polymeric matrix, enhancing heat dissipation of composites. Meanwhile, it can rapidly direct heat flow to the thermal storage phase, improving the heat absorption efficiency of composites. Besides, cross-linking inhibition and non-contact external force constraint can enable the effective fabrication of high filler concentration FFC. The fabricated FFC exhibit excellent flexibility and can sustain tensile strains exceeding 150% under twisting of up to 720°. Furthermore, we utilized the limited experimental data to obtain performance curves within specific filler content ranges based on the Attentive Neural Process (ANP) network and a two-stage “pretraining-fine-tuning” strategy. The results indicate that the small-data machine learning approach can effectively predict material properties, and numerical simulations also verify experiment data, thereby reducing experimental iterations. Finally, the outcome of this work can provide guidance for innovative design of multifunctional phase change composites.

title: Crystallization and permittivity engineering with polar electron-deficient molecules for enhanced energy storage in polypropylene capacitor films
abstract: Polypropylene (PP) is a state-of-the-art dielectric material for capacitor films owing to its high breakdown strength, excellent processability, and intrinsic self-healing capability. However, its low energy density and poor thermal stability limit its application in next-generation power electronics. Here, a physical blending strategy is developed by incorporating a highly polar, electron-deficient molecule—2-(2,4-Dihydroxyphenyl)-4,6-bis(2,4-dimethylphenyl)-1,3,5- triazine (DBDT)—into PP via extrusion casting. DBDT, owing to its high electron affinity, serves as an effective charge-trapping agent under elevated electric fields and temperatures, thereby significantly suppressing leakage currents while enhancing both breakdown strength and thermal stability. In addition, DBDT functions as a heterogeneous nucleating agent, facilitating crystal refinement and enhanced crystallinity, which collectively contribute to improved mechanical strength. The incorporation of polar DBDT enhances dipolar polarization, thereby increasing the dielectric permittivity. These synergistic effects yield significantly improved energy storage performance. At an optimized DBDT loading of 0.50 wt%, the composite film delivers a high discharged energy density of 5.87 J/cm3 at 650 MV/m, coupled with a discharge efficiency exceeding 87%. This study demonstrates a scalable, physically driven strategy to concurrently tailor crystallization behavior and dielectric performance in PP films, offering a promising design paradigm for high-performance, thermally stable polymer dielectrics.

title: Flexibility, thermal properties and tribological performance of epoxy resin-based phase change composites films regulating via polyethylene glycol mixture synergy with boron nitride nanosheets
abstract: Commercial epoxy resin (EP) has been restricted in electronic packaging due to intrinsic brittleness and poor tribological performance. Herein, facile strategy for fabricating flexible, excellent thermal properties, mechanical property and tribological performance of EP-based composite film is proposed. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) mixture fabricated by polyethylene glycol 6000 (PEG6K) and low molecular weight PEG (PEG0.8K, 1K, and 1.5K) and high thermal conductivity fillers hydroxylated boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS–OH) were introduced into EP (EPPB). The effects of PEG addition amount and molecular weight of low molecular weight on flexibility, mechanical, thermal and tribological properties have been systematically investigated. Non-covalent crosslinking EP and PEG mixture polymer network structure endows EPP with flexibility, stretching stress attained 21.04 MPa. Surprisingly, latent heat of EPPB can reach 62.28 J/g, few papers have been reported commercial EP that possess both flexibility and thermal storage properties. In addition, the results of tribological experiment indicated that average friction coefficient (COF) of EPPB achieve 0.1854 and ultralow wear rate of 19.79 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m), demonstrating outstanding tribological performance. This work offers fresh method to obtain phase change composite films utilizing commercial EP in thermal management of flexible electronic packaging devices.

title: Enhanced transverse and longitudinal compressive strength of micro-/nano- aramid pulp interleaved unidirectional CF/PEEK composite laminates
abstract: Carbon fiber-reinforced polyetheretherketone (CF/PEEK) thermoplastic composites are increasingly used in biomedical implants and are attracting attention as potential alternatives to carbon fiber-reinforced epoxy (CF/epoxy) thermosets due to their superior toughness and biocompatibility. However, delamination in CF/PEEK composite laminates, arising from the absence of fiber reinforcement in resin-rich regions, remains a critical limitation. This study demonstrates the interfacial toughening effect of micro-/nano- aramid pulp (AP) interleaving in unidirectional CF/PEEK laminates, as well as comparing the AP interleaving effect in CF/epoxy counterparts. AP-interfacial toughening led to notable improvements in CF/PEEK composites, with up to 21% higher longitudinal compressive strength, 27% higher transverse compressive strength, and 15% higher short-beam shear strength. A comparison further revealed that AP-interfacial toughening exhibits distinct behaviors in CF/PEEK and CF/epoxy under different loading modes. While AP interleaving enhanced compressive strength in both systems, its effect on flexural strength diverged: CF/epoxy benefited due to compression-driven failure, whereas CF/PEEK, governed by tension-driven failure, experienced flexural strength reduction when interlayer thickness exceeded 10 μm. Overall, this work establishes AP-interfacial toughening as an effective strategy to enhance CF/PEEK compressive performance by promoting fiber bridging in resin-rich layers and reducing delamination between carbon fiber plies.

title: Porosity evolution and fractal–energy modeling of cutting-induced damage in CFRP
abstract: Carbon fiber–reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites, renowned for their exceptional specific strength and stiffness, have been widely employed in aircraft structures and aero-engine components to perform critical load-bearing functions. Given that these components must withstand extreme service conditions such as impact loading, machining—an essential stage in CFRP application—imposes stringent requirements on process stability and structural integrity. However, the intrinsic anisotropy of CFRP readily triggers complex thermo-mechanical coupled damage and pore-structure evolution during cutting operations. Such damage degrades load-carrying capacity and accelerates fatigue crack initiation, constituting a major bottleneck in CFRP machining. In response to this challenge, this study establishes an energy-dominated, temperature-modulated structural damage modeling framework for CFRP cutting. By integrating cutting-force and temperature measurements, differential scanning calorimetry, and mercury intrusion porosimetry, a semi-analytical predictive model is established, in which equivalent force–thermal coupled input energy is defined as the driving variable, while porosity and fractal dimension are used as the response variables. The model elucidates how cutting parameters influence the evolution of pore damage via force–thermal coupled energy, thereby uncovering the underlying mechanisms governing machining-induced structural degradation. Results show that, compared with baseline models, the proposed model achieves improved prediction performance within the tested parameter range (R2 ≥ 0.99, with the root mean square error (RMSE) reduced by approximately 77%). This work provides a pore-structure-based perspective for the quantitative characterization and modeling of machining-induced damage in CFRP composites.

title: An adaptive clustering FE2 multiscale framework for heterogeneous materials with localized damage
abstract: An adaptive clustering FE2 (ACFE2) method is developed to accelerate the multiscale damage and failure analysis of heterogeneous materials. Firstly, a feature vector which is composed by the strain components and damage rates of each macro integration point is applied for macro model reduction. Then based on the feature vector, an elbow-based k-means clustering method is used to find the optimal number of clusters for macrostructure in each numerical increment. Once local damage behavior appears, an adaptive local enhancement scheme is applied in the region where damage evolves rapidly, so that the corresponding elements are directly coupled with RVE calculations, improving the accuracy of localized damage prediction. By comparing with the experimental and numerical results, the accuracy of ACFE2 method for predicting the damage evolution of heterogeneous materials with various microstructures and microscale constituents is validated. Regarding the computational costs, the ACFE2 method is about 10-50 times more efficient than the traditional FE2 method, and 3-5 times more efficient than the k-means FE2 (KMFE2) method, which demonstrates a great improvement in computational efficiency for multiscale problems.

title: Rapid evaluation of electromagnetic damage tolerance for microwave-absorbing honeycomb sandwich structures
abstract: A rapid evaluation approach is developed for impedance mismatch and electromagnetic damage tolerance (EDT) in low-velocity impact–damaged microwave-absorbing honeycomb sandwich structures. Experiments and simulations are conducted to characterize impact-induced damage morphologies and to relate damage geometry to frequency-dependent changes in reflection and impedance mismatch. To enable fast and interpretable assessment, a physics-guided neural network is established to predict impedance mismatch directly from frequency and nondimensional damage parameters. An EDT criterion is then defined based on the deviation of the normalized impedance response from the intact state, and the corresponding EDT surface partitions within-tolerance and beyond-tolerance states in the frequency–damage parameter space, providing direct visualization of frequency-dependent damage sensitivity and supporting repair-related decision-making. In addition, an explicit analytical expression is derived for impedance mismatch, providing a closed-form alternative for rapid evaluation. The proposed methodology offers an efficient and extensible route for EDT assessment of impact-damaged microwave-absorbing composite structures.

title: An ultra-broadband pyramid-grid composite absorber structure inspired by biomimetic moth-eye arrays
abstract: Multifunctional microwave-absorbing structures have been widely adopted in the aviation and maritime industries due to their combination of excellent wave-absorption performance and load-bearing capacity. Inspired by the anti-reflection mechanism of moth-eye nanoconical arrays, this study combines the broadband wave-absorption characteristics of three-dimensional impedance gradient structures with the load-bearing advantages of grids to propose a novel pyramid-grid composite absorber structure (PGCS). The structure employs Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) technology and an impregnation process to fabricate the absorptive pyramids, which are then integrated with absorptive grids prepared via screen printing and interlocking processes to form the composite absorber structure. Based on this, the influence of geometric and electrical parameters on the reflection coefficient was systematically investigated. Bow-type method testing indicated that the effective absorption bandwidth (−10 dB) of the PGCS reaches 37.15 GHz (2.85–40 GHz), with a maximum absorption peak of −66.54 dB. Furthermore, the structure, composed of glass fiber composites and nylon, achieves a lightweight design while maintaining a compressive strength of 25.16 MPa. The PGCS proposed in this paper offers a new approach to the design of multifunctional absorption structures that combine broadband absorption with load-bearing capabilities, and holds broad application prospects in fields such as stealth aircraft skin.

title: Ti3SiC2 modified carbon fiber/phenolic aerogel composite with low density, high strength and excellent thermal protection performance
abstract: Lightweight, high-strength, ablation-resistant and thermally insulating carbon fiber/phenolic aerogel composite (CF/PAC) is crucial for thermal protection for hypersonic vehicles and deep-space exploration spacecrafts, yet it is prone to oxidation failure at elevated temperatures. Herein, we report the surface modification of Ti3SiC2 ceramic using the silane coupling agent KH-560 and incorporation into a CF/PAC system. The novel ceramizable aerogel composite (CF/PACC) with a nanoporous structure was fabricated via a facile solvent-exchange-free sol-gel/ambient drying route. The results demonstrated that surface modification significantly enhanced the interfacial compatibility between Ti3SiC2 and the matrix. Consequently, CF/PACC maintained a low density of 0.43 g/cm3 and a low thermal conductivity of 0.162 W/(m·K), while achieving substantially improved compressive strength and modulus of 8.3 MPa and 88.9 MPa, respectively. It exhibited excellent ablation resistance when subjected to an oxyacetylene flame of 1.5 MW/m2 for 60 s, with linear ablation rate (LAR) and mass ablation rate (MAR) as low as 0.0390 mm/s and 0.0093 g/s, respectively, with reductions of 32.8% and 25.0% compared to pristine CF/PAC. It demonstrated remarkable long-term high-temperature insulation performance, maintaining a backside temperature of 224.5°C during 1200 s exposure to 1300°C butane flame. The outstanding thermal protection performance originates from a dynamically coupled mechanism involving competitive oxygen consumption effect, in-situ formation of a molten oxide barrier, and carbothermal reduction and phase transformation of Ti3SiC2 with oxygen and pyrolytic carbon (PyC). This work provides a novel design strategy and theoretical foundation for developing large-area thermal protection materials that are lightweight, high-strength, and resistant to high-temperature oxidation.

title: Editorial Board
Inter- to intra-laminar crack bifurcation in aerospace-grade carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites due to aligned carbon nanotube reinforcement
abstract: Here, we examine vertically aligned carbon nanotube (VA-CNT) interlaminar reinforcement of aerospace-grade epoxy carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composite using short-beam shear (SBS) and Mode I&II fracture testing, together with peridynamics modeling, to elucidate inter- to intra-laminar crack bifurcation. SBS testing revealed clear evidence of more diffuse (intralaminar) cracks in postmortem imaging for CNT vs. baseline laminates, along with interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) retention. By contrast, Mode I and II fracture testing demonstrated pronounced interlaminar toughening with sustained crack bifurcation away from the interlaminar region and into the intralaminar region. Mode I and II cracks deflect from CNT-reinforced interlaminar regions into adjacent intralaminar plies, then propagate as sustained intralaminar Mode I cracks parallel to the interlaminar plane. The bifurcation distance into the adjacent ply from the midplane is ∼10 μm greater in this 190 gsm system than the ∼24 μm distance in the prior 130 gsm system. Peridynamics modeling at two scales in Mode I further elucidated bifurcation mechanisms: a global laminate model matching macroscopic results (load, deflection, toughness), and a microscale submodel predicting crack bifurcation consistent with experiments for bond strengths at least 2.5× higher in CNT-reinforced regions. This corresponds to ∼200% toughness increase due to the A-CNTs and shows the bifurcation distance into adjacent plies remains constant beyond a 2.5× bond strength threshold. With new mechanistic insights and a novel predictive capability for crack bifurcation and propagation, future work can extend to design studies and applying VA-CNT reinforcement to other interfaces, such as woven composites and composites with interlaminar microparticle tougheners.

title: Characterization of flexure-induced through-thickness fracture in tape laminate composites using ex-situ computed tomography
abstract: This study characterizes through-thickness interlaminar and intralaminar fatigue-driven crack growth in tape-laminate composites using ex-situ X-ray micro-computed tomography (μCT). Notched specimens were fatigue loaded in four-point bending at 5 Hz. Two layups were investigated: a large-angle (LA) laminate with 45° angle changes between adjacent plies and a small-angle (SA) laminate with 15° angle changes. Five specimens from each layup were tested continuously, while one specimen per layup was interrupted and imaged under load at six damage states using an X-ray transparent fixture. Structure tensor analysis and deep learning-based segmentation were used to identify ply structure, local fiber orientation, and crack morphology. Fatigue flexure produced planar transverse cracks in 90° plies and stitch cracks in off-angle plies for both layups. Delamination was observed at 90°/45° and 45°/90° interfaces in the LA specimens, whereas no visible delamination occurred in the fatigued SA specimens. Crack coarsening occurred in the off-angle plies of both layups, where many stitch cracks initiated but only a subset propagated through the ply stack. The interrupted ex-situ methodology produced damage morphologies consistent with continuously tested specimens, indicating that the interruption and imaging protocol did not measurably alter fatigue damage evolution. The resulting cycle-indexed three-dimensional datasets provide information suitable for validation of progressive damage analysis tools.

title: Mechanical response of carbon fiber pyramid-honeycomb under combined shear-compression loads
abstract: In this paper, the mechanical response of continuous carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) pyramid-honeycomb was studied under combined compression-shear loads. An improved semi-fixed Arcan fixture was developed to precisely control the direction of the combined stress. The strength envelope showing a competition trend between parabolic and linear forms was proposed to describe the combined performance of the honeycomb. Experiments and simulations were conducted with the honeycomb inclination angle and loading angle as variables, yielding results consistent with theoretical predictions. The results indicated that two differently performing sidewalls within honeycomb cause the shape-uncertain strength envelope. The buckling failure of low-angle (45°) pyramid-honeycomb was governed by thicker double-layer wall, while for higher angles it was governed by single-layer wall. The variety of envelopes suggested that pyramid-honeycomb with designable inclination angles can flexibly meet engineering requirements. At the same time, the shear test of honeycomb in L direction was carried out to supplement the honeycomb performance data. The experimental and theoretical approach was considered applicable for predicting the strength of complex (CFRP) structures under combined loading.

title: A highly sensitive wearable sensor from conductive core-spun yarn for monitoring body motion
abstract: Flexible wearable sensors have attracted considerable interest owing to their versatile applications in areas such as electronic skin, health monitoring, and smart wearable systems. Herein, a highly sensitive strain-sensing yarn (PMC@CTY) is fabricated by constructing a conductive core-spun structure, in which an MXene-coated cotton yarn sheath (MCY) is helically wrapped around a wet-spun MWCNTs/TPU elastic core (CTF) and subsequently coated with a conformal PEDOT:PSS layer. The conductive materials residing in the core yarn, the sheath yarn, and the coating layer form a multilayered conductive network that generates sequential resistance changes under strain, thereby imparting good strain-sensing performance to the yarn. The PMC@CTY integrates excellent mechanical elasticity, exhibiting an elongation at break of 426% and a tensile strength of 15.19 MPa. It demonstrates a broad detection range from 0.2% to 200% strain, a high sensitivity of up to 366.4 in the 120-200% strain range, and remarkable long-term cycling stability over 4000 cycles. When attached to the body, PMC@CTY accurately captures physiological signals and joint motions. Furthermore, a smart glove integrated with multiple PMC@CTY sensors and a 1D-CNN model achieves a gesture classification accuracy of 97.62% across 13 gestures, demonstrating its significant potential for advanced wearable human-machine interaction.

title: Cactus-spine inspired aligned CNT-electrospun fibers for interlaminar toughening of CF/PPESK composites: Guiding, arresting, and enabling 3D propagation for energy dissipation
abstract: Conventional carbon fiber reinforced high-performance thermoplastic (CFRHPTP) composites suffer from inherent dispersion deficiency and alignment challenges of carbon nanotubes (CNT) in high-viscosity matrix, leading to suboptimal interlaminar toughening efficiency. To address this critical issue, a bioinspired multiscale toughness and reinforcement paradigm for carbon fiber reinforced poly(phthalazinone ether sulfone ketone) (CF/PPESK) composite was proposed. Specifically, drawing inspiration from the geometric microstructure of cactus spines (high aspect ratio and directional growth), the vertically aligned CNT-anchored electrospun fiber veils were developed by the synergistic electrospinning-electrospraying protocol, and were strategically inserted into the interlaminar zones of CF/PPESK composites. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterizations confirmed that the electrospun fibers were firmly anchored with CNT, successfully constructing a three-dimensional reinforcement network. Furthermore, this architecture significantly enhanced the toughness of CF/PPESK composites, with the initiation and propagation values of mode I fracture toughness increased by 51% and 44%, respectively, while mode II fracture toughness improved remarkably by 178%. Notably, flexural strength, flexural modulus, and interlaminar shear strength were enhanced by 25%, 24%, and 18%, respectively. Microstructural analysis revealed that the excellent toughening effect originates from a three-dimensional crack deflection, guidance, and arrest mechanism formed by the synergistic interaction between electrospun fibers and aligned CNT. This micro-nano synergistic mechanism significantly promotes fracture energy dissipation and simultaneously enhances the in-plane strength of the composite. This work provides an innovative and efficient pathway to overcome the interlaminar toughness limitations in high-viscosity resin-based composites.

title: Enhancing interfacial adhesion and mechanical properties in quartz fiber composites via sydnone-modified phthalonitrile resins
abstract: Phthalonitrile resin (PN) exhibits great potential in the field of high-performance composite materials. However, its practical application is often limited by its high curing temperature and poor interfacial adhesion. To address these challenges, a novel curing agent, Sydnone, was introduced. Through a solution-based prepolymerization strategy, a high-performance resin prepolymer was synthesized, effectively reducing the curing temperature of PN. Upon catalytic interaction with cyano groups, sydnone undergoes electronic redistribution, leading to the transformation of its carbonyl moiety into hydroxyl groups, which significantly enhance the polarity of the resin. These hydroxyl functionalities further react with quartz fibers to fabricate fiber-reinforced composites with outstanding mechanical properties, including a flexural strength of up to 917 MPa and an interlaminar shear strength of 92.2 MPa. XPS results confirmed the formation of covalent bonds between the hydroxyl groups in the resin and the surface silanol groups on the fibers, substantially improving interfacial adhesion. SEM analysis of the fracture surface revealed a predominant tough fracture mode, supporting the enhanced interfacial strength.

title: Numerical failure mechanism analysis on integrated braided bolted joints of three-dimensional braided carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites
abstract: Three-dimensional braided carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites (3DBC) show strong potential for load-bearing structures due to their high delamination resistance and design flexibility. To avoid yarn cutting caused by drilling holes during connecting 3DBC parts, molded-in holes were introduced herein to fabricate 3DBC bolted joints, thus enhancing their load-bearing capacity. A verified macro-mesoscopic finite element model and single-lap tensile tests were conducted to investigate the key geometric parameters affecting the failure evolution of 3DBC joints. Drilled-hole control specimens were further tested to directly compare the effect of the hole-forming method. The width-to-diameter ratio affects both the load level and the transition between fastener-controlled and composite-dominated failure. Increasing the lap ratio prolongs the load plateau stage and improves post-peak stability. The high-strain zone initiates at the bearing contact region and propagates along the loading direction over a range of approximately twice the braiding angle. Failure is dominated by bearing extrusion, accompanied by interfacial cracking, interfacial debonding, and fiber/resin breakage. This study provides mechanical insights for the parameter optimization and structural safety design of 3DBC bolted joints.

title: Accurately obtaining effective mechanical parameters of primary bearing layers for pressure vessels considering realistic defects
abstract: The structural performance and burst behavior of composite pressure vessels (CPVs) are primarily governed by the effective mechanical properties of their load-bearing composite layers. Accurate determination of these properties across multiple length scales, particularly in the presence of manufacturing-induced defects, is essential for reliable structural prediction. This study proposes a defect-aware multiscale modeling framework to characterize the effective mechanical parameters of prepreg tape wound laminates (PTWL) and plain-weave reinforcement laminates (PWRL), providing reliable material inputs for subsequent macroscopic CPV simulations. Realistic void morphologies were experimentally characterized using scanning electron microscopy and optical microscopy. Based on these observations, microscale damage models explicitly incorporating void defects and interfacial behavior were developed to simulate damage initiation and evolution under key loading conditions, including longitudinal and transverse tension/compression as well as in-plane and out-of-plane shear. A customized UMAT subroutine was implemented to enable consistent parameter transfer from the microscale to the mesoscale, allowing progressive damage simulations of PTWL and PWRL within a unified multiscale framework. The predicted effective mechanical properties were validated against macroscopic experiments, yielding tensile strength prediction errors of 1.13% for PWRL and 3.24% for PTWL. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can accurately capture defect-sensitive effective mechanical parameters of PWRL and PTWL composites and provides a solid basis for high-fidelity structural simulations of composite pressure vessels.

title: Decoding the trap-regulated dielectric breakdown and energy storage of polymer nanocomposite films: A multiscale carrier dynamic analysis
abstract: The pursuit of high-performance energy storage devices with superior dielectric breakdown strength serves as a primary focus for modern electronics. However, it remains a challenge to clarify the dynamic dielectric breakdown mechanism of polymer nanocomposite films (PNCFs). To address this issue, a multiscale charge carrier dynamic model considering Joule heating effect is developed to predict the dielectric breakdown strength and ultimate energy storage density of PNCFs. The charge carrier dynamic simulation, including migration, trapping, detrapping and recombination, is integrated into a hierarchical homogenization method. Nanofiller- and trap-dependent electrical and thermal interface effects are considered, including imperfect interfacial connection, electron tunneling, Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars polarization, interfacial thermal resistance and interface overlapping. The free volume breakdown criterion is adopted to evaluate the ultimate energy storage performance in PNCFs. The predicted dielectric breakdown strength, ultimate energy storage density, and deep trap density show good agreement with two experiments of MgO/polypropylene nanocomposites and graphene/low density polyethylene nanocomposite films, respectively. The findings demonstrate that the dielectric breakdown strength and ultimate energy storage density of PNCFs can be simultaneously enhanced by elevating the deep trap density and energy level via surface modification and defect engineering. A reliable multiscale mechanism on the optimal design of dielectric breakdown and energy storage performance is achieved for MgO/PP and graphene/LDPE nanocomposite films.

title: Electrospun graphene oxides reinforced polylactic acid /polycaprolactone shape memory membranes for antibacterial tracheal stents
abstract: Electrospun shape-memory polymer (SMP) membranes were engineered from polylactic acid/polycaprolactone (PLA/PCL) reinforced with graphene oxide (GO) for potential antibacterial tracheal stent applications. This research integrated shape memory behavior with drug release kinetics to achieve on-demand antibacterial response, specifically tailored for the infection-susceptible tracheal microenvironment. GO served as both a reinforcing nanofiller and a carrier for vancomycin (VAN) and silver nanoparticles (AgNPs). The effects of GO content (0.1, 0.5, and 1 wt%) on fiber morphology, mechanical properties, thermal behavior, hydrophilicity, and shape-memory performance were systematically investigated. The results indicated that the incorporation of 0.1 wt% GO yielded optimal mechanical reinforcement and shape recovery efficiency (100% fixity/recovery ratio, recovery time ∼8 s). Notably, the shape memory effect (SME) actively enhanced membrane hydrophilicity with a decreased contact angle from ∼127° to ∼87° and facilitated a more rapid release of VAN. The drug-loaded membranes exhibited sustained release profiles and potent antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Biocompatibility tests confirmed the enhanced adhesion and viability of rat tracheal epithelial cells on GO-reinforced membranes, with Ag@GO showing better cytocompatibility to VAN@GO. This work demonstrated an antibacterial strategy for advanced tracheal stents.

title: Balancing graphene integrity and interfacial coupling for ultrahigh electrical conductivity in graphene/copper composites
abstract: Graphene-reinforced copper (Gr/Cu) composites are promising candidates for next-generation electrical and thermal applications; however, their performance is often limited by graphene agglomeration, structural damage during processing, and weak interfacial bonding. Herein, we report a synergistic strategy combining electroless copper plating of graphene with an improved wet ball-milling process, followed by high-temperature and high-pressure (HTHP) sintering, to simultaneously achieve uniform dispersion, structural preservation of graphene, and enhanced interfacial coupling. As a result, the composite exhibits a remarkably high electrical conductivity of 130% IACS (75.4 MS/m), representing an improvement of approximately 30% over pure copper. Microstructural analyses reveal that structurally preserved graphene is preferentially located along copper grain boundaries, where semi-coherent Gr(0002)//Cu(00 2‾), and a high density of low-resistivity Σ3 twin boundaries jointly facilitate efficient electron transport and suppress interfacial scattering First-principles calculations further demonstrate that moderate graphene defect densities optimize interfacial charge transfer through C-2p and Cu-3d orbital hybridization, whereas excessive defects introduce strong electron localization and scattering, thereby deteriorating conductivity. This work establishes a clear structure–processing–property relationship and provides a scalable and generalizable route for fabricating high-performance graphene/metal composites with exceptional electrical properties.

title: Evaporation-induced alignment of boron nitride nanofillers in supramolecular polymer composites for integrated thermal management, self-healing, and recyclability
abstract: The rapid development of flexible electronic devices and intelligent robots urgently requires elastomeric thermal management materials that integrate high thermal conductivity, mechanical flexibility, self-healing capability, and environmental recyclability. However, it remains challenging to achieve these multifunctional properties simultaneously, due to inherent conflicts between thermal conductive network construction, dynamic supramolecular stability, and mechanical robustness, as well as the complexity and high cost of conventional fabrication methods. Herein, we report a green, facile, and scalable ethanol-mediated strategy to prepare phosphotungstic acid stabilized poly (lipoic acid)/boron nitride (P-PLA/BN) supramolecular composites by coupling concentration-induced ring-opening polymerization (CIROP) and evaporation-induced self-assembly (EISA). This one-step approach realizes in-situ PLA synthesis and directional BN alignment in one go, effectively overcoming PLA's inherent depolymerization and random filler–induced severe phonon scattering, thus endowing the composite with a high in-plane thermal conductivity of 2.2 W m−1 K−1 at only 30 wt% BN loading. Dynamic disulfide bonds and reversible hydrogen bonds contribute to a high self-healing efficiency of 76% and balanced mechanical elasticity (Young's modulus = 1.65 MPa, elongation at break = 115%). Meanwhile, the P-PLA/BN30 composite exhibits outstanding electrical insulation (2.9 × 1013 Ω m), multi-surface adhesion, and full recyclability via ethanol dissolution. Distinct from traditional thermal conductive composites, this work breaks through the bottleneck of integrating high thermal conductivity, self-healing, and recyclability in a single material, offering a new design paradigm for next-generation sustainable flexible thermal management materials.

title: Evaluation of the mechanical properties of nanocomposites prepared by varying the degree of orientation of bio-nanofillers using a modified rule of mixtures
abstract: The mechanical properties of nanocomposites largely depend on the orientation of their fillers. However, fillers are often randomly dispersed, limiting the ability to maximize their effects. In this study, we used cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), which have attracted attention as fillers, and employed a magnetic field processing technique to control their alignment, thereby fabricating alignment-controlled nanocomposites. The reinforcing effect of the CNC alignment was systematically evaluated, and a modified rule of mixtures was developed to quantitatively describe the alignment-dependent mechanical properties. Nanocomposites were prepared by dispersing CNCs derived from tunicate cellulose into a poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) solution, followed by casting under magnetic fields ranging from 0 to 6 T. X-ray diffraction analysis confirmed that higher magnetic field strength significantly enhanced the CNC alignment. Tensile testing revealed that incorporating 20 wt% randomly aligned CNCs increased the elastic modulus and tensile strength of the PVA films by 374% and 44.4%, respectively. Magnetic field-induced alignment of CNCs further boosted the nanocomposite film's elastic modulus by 74% and tensile strength by 88% compared to randomly oriented (0 T) samples. To rationalize these improvements, a modified rule of mixtures was proposed that incorporates the anisotropic mechanical properties of CNCs alongside stress transfer losses caused by changes in CNC contact points during alignment. The proposed model demonstrated good agreement with experimental results under all alignment conditions, demonstrating that magnetic field-induced alignment is effective in tuning the mechanical properties of CNC nanocomposites.

title: Homologous interface constructed via covalent anchoring of P-CNPs onto C-Ti3C2Tx for enhanced EMI shielding and mechanical synergy in CFRPs
abstract: Achieving a synergistic balance between electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding and mechanical robustness in carbon fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs) remains a fundamental challenge due to the long-standing trade-off between electrical conductivity and mechanical integrity. Here, we report a homologous interfacial reinforcement strategy to engineer a hierarchical architecture via the atomic-scale anchoring of C-Ti3C2TX and polyimide/polydopamine-derived carbon nanoparticles (P-CNPs). The formation of Ti-O-C covalent bonds yields a continuous hybrid network that effectively suppresses MXene restacking. This hierarchical configuration acts as electromagnetic-wave confinement walls, inducing pronounced Maxwell-Wagner polarization and extending energy-dissipation pathways through multiple internal reflections. The composite achieves a high EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of 75.44 dB at a low filler loading of 4 wt%, while maintaining an excellent tensile strength of 215.4 MPa. The homologous interfacial engineering strategy presented here offers a transformative route for simultaneously integrating mechanical robustness with absorption-enhanced EMI functionality, providing new design insights for integrated materials in aerospace and microelectronics.

title: Corrigendum to “Structure tensor-based analysis method for quantitative assessment of fibre waviness in fibre-steered laminates manufactured by continuous tow shearing” [Compos. Sci. Technol. (2025) Vol. 270: 111270]
MXene reinforced CMC-P(AA-co-AM)/PANI hydrogel for high-performance all-in-one supercapacitors and flexible sensors
abstract: Conductive hydrogels with sandwich-structured have been developed as promising candidates for wearable power sources and sensing devices. However, the applications of hydrogels are often hindered by poor adhesion to active electrode materials and high interfacial impedance. To address these challenges, we report a high-performance sandwich-structured hydrogel (CMC-MXene/P (AA-co-AM)/PANI). This sandwich-structured hydrogel is prepared from polyaniline electrodes integrated with P (AA-co-AM) hydrogel electrolytes, and it significantly enhances the interlayer bonding strength between the electrode and the separator, thereby reducing the interfacial impedance between them. Moreover, MXene nanosheets form an interconnected three-dimensional conductive network within the hydrogel that further consolidates the mechanical strength and significantly strengthens the adhesive properties and ionic conductivity of the sandwich-structured hydrogel. Benefiting from this distinctive three-dimensional structure, the CMC-MXene/P (AA-co-AM)/PANI hydrogel exhibits superior mechanical properties, with the tensile stress, tensile strain, compressive strength, and adhesion strength being 139 kPa, 1697%, 1.39 MPa, and 2.25 MPa, respectively. Besides, the sandwich-structured hydrogel can be used as a supercapacitor as the electrode made from hydrogel delivers a remarkable areal capacitance of 527.6 mF cm−2 (at a current density of 1 mA cm−2) and an energy density of 94.86 μWh·cm−2. Importantly, such a supercapacitor demonstrates outstanding ability to store electric energy, retaining 96.61% of its ability after 5000 cycles, and maintains good electrochemical performance under various mechanical deformations. Furthermore, the hydrogel competently functions as strain gauges, demonstrating high conductivity of 152 mS cm−1 and the gauge factor of 3.01, which enables the strain gauges to be applied in the monitoring of diverse human motions. Based on these excellent performances, this work provides viable approaches to fabricating the conductive hydrogels suitable for both supercapacitors and smart wearable electronics.

title: Enhanced thermal properties of epoxy composites through nanowire-bridged SiO2@ZnO core–shell fillers
abstract: With the advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the demand for high-performance electronic devices has surged. However, device miniaturization and high integration have led to severe heat accumulation, degrading performance and reliability. In this paper, a thermally enhanced epoxy composite was developed using a dual-filler system consisting of zinc oxide–modified silica spheres (SiO2@ZnO) as core–shell fillers and zinc oxide nanowires (ZnONWs) as bridging structures. This dual-filler architecture effectively functionalizes conventional silica fillers and promotes improved heat transport within the epoxy matrix. The enhanced performance arises from the combined contributions of the silica core, the increased crystallinity and interconnectivity of the ZnO shell induced by calcination at 800 °C (SiO2@ZnO-800), and the ZnONW-bridging networks that establish continuous thermal pathways between adjacent fillers. The epoxy composite containing 40 vol% of SiO2@ZnO-800 fillers and 0.54 vol% ZnONWs exhibited a thermal conductivity of 0.5064 W/m ⋅K, representing 131 % enhancement compared to neat epoxy. In addition, the epoxy composite has favorable thermal stability and enhanced heat-spreading performance in infrared thermography tests. These results demonstrate the effectiveness in overcoming the intrinsic limitation of epoxy, offering potential as an advanced material for electronic applications.

title: Additive manufacturing of high-temperature GF/TPI composites for extreme environment applications
abstract: This study presents a novel GF/TPI (glass fiber-reinforced thermoplastic polyimide) composite, developed through melt-mixing and FFF (fused filament fabrication) additive manufacturing, targeting high-load-bearing structures that are lightweight and exhibit exceptional energy absorption in extreme environments, such as advanced transportation and aerospace systems. The GFs were infused at 5, 10, and 15 wt% into TPI, resulting in printable filaments. The SEM analysis confirmed uniform GF distribution and good interfacial bonding in GF/TPI-5% and GF/TPI-10%, whereas GF/TPI-15 wt% showed agglomeration and higher viscosity, leading to voids and delamination in the 3D-printed structures. The comprehensive mechanical evaluation demonstrated an optimal performance at 10 wt% GF: bending strength reached 86.02 MPa (↑32.8% compared to the TPI-64.79 MPa) and compressive modulus of 1.375 GPa (↑34.2%) due to enhanced crystallinity and interlayer bonding. The fracture mechanisms transitioned from interlayer-dominated failure in the TPI to fiber pull-out and void compression in the GF/TPI, showcasing enhanced toughness and energy dissipation. Critically, the post-processing (annealing) eliminated interlayer raster voids, delamination, and weak interfaces in the GF/TPI-10%, boosting strength in bending to 100.03 MPa (↑54.4% compared to the TPI) and modulus to 2.51 GPa (↑38.7%), with the compressive strength enhanced to 105.66 MPa (↑21.8%) and the modulus to 1.592 GPa (↑55.3%). Such a performance can lead to higher payload capacity and fuel efficiency. It establishes a robust framework for high-temperature composite preparation, filament development, 3D printing, and annealing-enhanced performance in extreme environments, with future research pathways for large-scale robotic additive manufacturing to realize components of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

title: Synergistic dual-dynamic networks combining Diels-Alder and hydrogen bonds enable a high-performance and efficient self-healing interface in carbon fiber/bismaleimide composites
abstract: Carbon fiber/bismaleimide (CF/BMI) composites are prone to interfacial debonding, microcracking, and related damage modes during service, which compromise structural integrity and long-term reliability. To address these problems, this study engineered a self-healing and durable high-performance interface by incorporating dual-dynamic networks formed by Diels-Alder (DA) and hydrogen bonds into composite interface via chemically grafted furan-terminated hyperbranched polyester (FHBP) onto CF surface. Comprehensive characterizations confirmed that the synergistic effects of dual-dynamic networks contributed to efficient self-healing at the interface in CF-FHBP/BMI composites, achieving an initial healing efficiency of 95.8% and maintaining 90.5% efficiency over five consecutive healing cycles. In particular, the dual-dynamic networks also acted as an “interfacial binder” for composites, resulting in a significant improvement in interfacial and mechanical properties. As compared to the untreated CF/BMI composites, the IFSS, ILSS, bending strength, and bending modulus for CF-FHBP/BMI composites were increased by 89.4%, 34.9%, 28.1%, and 32.7%, respectively. The strategy of constructing dual-dynamic networks (incorporating both reversible DA bonds and hydrogen bonds) at composite interface, will provide inspiration for fabricating high-performance self-healing carbon fiber reinforced composite with extended durability and reliability.

title: Programming mechanical response in smart composite shells: Synergistic piezoelectric actuation and graphene-origami auxetic metamaterials
abstract: Programmable mechanical response in adaptive smart structures requires materials whose stiffness, Poisson's ratio, and thermal expansion can be tailored independently from geometry. This study addresses that need through a comprehensive electro-thermo-mechanical stress-strain analysis of sandwich cylindrical shells composed of a functionally graded graphene-origami enabled auxetic metamaterial (FG-GOEAM) core integrated with two oppositely-poled piezoelectric face layers. The novelty of the present work is fourfold. (i) For the first time, four distinct through-thickness graphene-origami (GOri) distribution patterns — Uniform (U), X-type, O-type, and Asymmetric (A) — are systematically evaluated for piezoelectric-actuated cylindrical shells under coupled pressure, thermal, and electric loading. (ii) A refined eight-parameter higher-order shear deformation theory (HSDT) with cubic expansion of both axial and transverse displacements is adopted, which preserves the full three-dimensional elastic σz coupling rather than enforcing the artificially incompressible normal direction of classical or first-order theories. (iii) The governing equations are recast as a quadratic eigenvalue problem (QEP) admitting an analytical clamped–clamped solution, avoiding the discretisation error of purely numerical approaches. (iv) A consolidated design map quantifying the relative roles of wall-thickness ratio, average GOri weight fraction, and distribution pattern is provided, identifying a Pareto-optimal region for practical actuator/sensor cylinders. Detailed through-thickness distributions of displacements, strains, and stresses are obtained with particular emphasis on the coupled effects of GOri weight fraction, folding degree, distribution pattern, temperature change, and applied electric voltage. Results demonstrate that the synergistic interaction between the architected FG-GOEAM core and the piezoelectric layers provides significant tunability of bending deflection, hoop stress, and transverse shear stress. At fixed GOri weight fraction the distribution pattern acts as a stress-redistribution lever rather than a strain-reduction lever: the mid-surface hoop stress varies by more than a factor of two between X-type and Asymmetric distributions, and the maximum axial displacement varies by a factor of nearly three between the (X, A) and (U, O) pattern groups, while the radial deflection remains essentially pattern-insensitive. These findings establish a robust theoretical basis for the design of next-generation smart, adaptive, and multifunctional composite shell structures with programmable mechanical response.

title: Tailoring highly dense and homogeneous networks via site-specific electronic effects in epoxy monomers for CFRPs with high compressive strength
abstract: Tension-compression asymmetry remains a critical bottleneck for carbon fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs), as the polymer matrix often cannot provide sufficient lateral support for high-performance fibers when subjected to external compressive loads. Given this challenge, novel epoxy monomers, methyl 3,5-bis(glycidyloxy)benzoate (BIDE) and 3,5-bis(glycidyloxy)acetophenone (BKDE), featuring polar side groups with distinct electronic effects were designed to fabricate high-strength and high-modulus resin matrices. For BIDE, the ester side group can form an auxiliary hydrogen-bonding network alongside the primary epoxy crosslinking. In contrast, alongside forming a hydrogen-bonding network, the BKDE ketone carbonyl utilizes its pronounced local electrophilicity to trap curing-induced oxyanions, effectively suppressing side reactions and sustaining network homogeneity. Consequently, the BKDE-DDM (4,4′-diaminodiphenylmethane) system achieves a simultaneous leap in tensile strength (122.9 MPa) and modulus (5220 MPa), outperforming typical high-performance epoxy systems (e.g., AFG90MH, AG80, and TDE85) while maintaining a superior char yield (49.4%). At the composite level, the BKDE-DDM-T800 system reaches a compressive strength of 1303 MPa, confirming that the highly homogeneous and robust network architecture effectively suppresses premature fiber microbuckling. This work provides a potent molecular design paradigm for developing high-performance, compression-critical composites.

title: Dynamic flexible interface engineering for synergistic enhancement of mechanical, insulating, and self-healing properties of AF/EP composites
abstract: Aramid fiber-reinforced epoxy resin (AF/EP) composites are widely used in high-voltage insulating components due to their excellent mechanical and insulating properties, with interfacial integrity being critical to overall performance and reliability. However, the inherent chemical inertness of aramid fibers results in weak interfacial adhesion, leading to property degradation and the formation of irreparable micro-defects such as cracks and delamination under stress. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a dynamic reversible mechanism into the AF/EP interface layer. Combined with siloxane, a flexible interface optimization engineering is designed to achieve the improvement of AF/EP from static to dynamic reversible. To enhance the mechanical, insulating, and self-healing properties of AF/EP composites. Specifically, Furan groups were linked to the resin via siloxane segments in the epoxy chain extender, while maleimide was grafted onto aramid fiber surfaces to increase roughness and introduce polar groups. Composites fabricated via dual-layer curing were systematically investigated under different oxidation conditions. The optimally modified 85%120min-AF/EP sample demonstrated significant improvements: The mechanical properties, transverse fiber bundle tension(TFBT) increased by 71%, and interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) by 49%. The insulating performance, flashover voltage, breakdown strength, and partial discharge inception voltage (PDIV) were enhanced by 35.6%, 66.3%, and 51.4%, respectively. Self-healing efficiencies reached 72.3% for TFBT, 81.5% for ILSS, 83.7% for dielectric loss, and 88.8% for PDIV. This dynamic flexible interface design achieves multi-scale synergistic enhancement, potentially overcoming application bottlenecks in insulation pull rods and providing theoretical support for improved insulating reliability and service life.

title: Damage analysis of panel sandwich reinforced with different fiber type under high-velocity projectile impact
abstract: This study presents an experimental–numerical investigation of the ballistic response of asymmetric sandwich structures with aluminum–ceramic composite foam cores, aluminum face sheets, and intermediate fiber-reinforced composite laminates with various stacking sequences. Particular emphasis is placed on the measurement methodology and quantitative evaluation of impact parameters. Ballistic tests were performed using 5.56 × 45 mm NATO M193 and SS109 projectiles and 7.62 × 51 mm NATO M80 bullets. Projectile velocities were determined using synchronized optical gates and high-speed camera imaging, enabling accurate pre- and post-impact velocity measurements and energy calculations. The recorded signals were processed to determine projectile velocity reduction, absorbed kinetic energy, and specific energy absorption, with repeatability verified through multiple trials. The results indicate that the laminate architecture significantly affects projectile destabilization and energy dissipation. Hybrid carbon–glass configurations provided the highest ballistic efficiency, reaching velocity reductions of up to 100 m/s for the M193 projectile. Finite element simulations conducted in Abaqus/Explicit with Johnson–Cook and Hashin damage models were validated against experimental data, showing residual velocity discrepancies below 3%. The proposed measurement framework enables reliable quantification of ballistic performance and provides a validated basis for the design and optimization of lightweight protective sandwich structures.

title: Thick/thin/thick or thin/thick/thin gradient: which one is effective for improving tensile strength in open-hole CFRP composites?
abstract: Inspired by the gradient layered structures of biomineralized tissues, thickness gradient hybrid designs combining thick and ultra-thin plies have become an effective strategy for enhancing composite performance. According to our previous research, thick/thin/thick gradient structures have been proven to exhibit better performance under out-of-plane loadings (impact and bending). However, it is unclear whether the thick/thin/thick design is optimal under all load conditions, such as in the case of open-hole tensile (OHT). Two gradient laminates were designed and investigated via experiments and finite element analysis, with progressive failure, damage distribution, and stress evolution analyzed. We comprehensively discuss the mechanical mechanisms of gradient structures under OHT. An unexpected experimental result was observed that for OHT performance, the thin/thick/thin design (H-1661) is even better than the thick/thin/thick laminate (H-6116) which has been proved effective under out-of-plane loading. Results show that the H-1661 delivers 12.9% higher OHT strength than the H-6116. The high interlaminar normal stress S33 zone is confined to the middle region in H-1661, while it extends through the entire thickness in H-6116. Placing thin plies on the outer surfaces effectively suppresses delamination. The failure mode of outer sides dominates OHT performance, and H-1661 features fiber-fracture-dominated failure with higher load-bearing capacity. Finally, thickness gradient design strategies are summarized for different loading conditions. This work highlights the potential of gradient design and the necessity of matching gradient configurations to specific loading environments.

title: In situ 3D visualization and quantitative analysis of damage evolution in carbon fiber-reinforced plastic laminates under static flexural loading using synchrotron X-ray microtomography
abstract: Carbon fiber-reinforced plastics (CFRP) are widely used in aerospace applications owing to their high specific strength and stiffness. However, under out-of-plane flexural loading, CFRP laminates exhibit complex internal damage mechanisms that threaten their structural integrity. Conventionally, high-resolution in situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT) observations during static flexural loading have been challenging to obtain because of fixture interference with the X-ray beam. In this study, we focused on an eccentric flexural loading mode and developed a compact compression–flexural fixture that enables unobstructed X-ray imaging throughout the flexural loading. Static flexural tests were performed on CFRP laminates with a [45/90/−45/90]s stacking sequence, and deep learning-based segmentation was used to extract 3D distributions of matrix cracks and interlaminar delaminations from CT images. In situ 3D observations revealed that matrix cracks initiated at the specimen ends and propagated at an inclination of approximately 36° to the thickness direction. This is consistent with the results from finite element analysis using the LaRC05 criterion. Interlaminar delaminations initiated at the 45°/90° and 90°/−45° interfaces once matrix cracks in the 90° ply reached these interfaces, and then grew rapidly along them, highlighting the strong coupling between intralaminar cracking and interlaminar delamination under flexural loading. The proposed methodology thus enables the high-resolution time-resolved 3D characterization of damage evolution in CFRP laminates under out-of-plane flexural loading.

title: Mechanical response of the negative electrode in structural batteries with nonuniform microstructure
abstract: A proposed structural (negative) electrode consists of carbon fibres embedded in a Structural Battery Electrolyte (SBE). The carbon fibers swell during lithiation, causing internal stresses in the composite. Geometrical features such as e.g. interfibre distance affect the resulting stresses in the SBE. For proper functioning of the structural battery, it is important to ascertain that the compressive stresses generated in the SBE do not result in material degradation. This study investigates how the nonuniform distribution of fibres inevitably caused by the battery manufacturing process affects the local stress field variations in the SBE matrix. For this, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) images of the processed battery composite are produced and are used to calculate statistics of interfibre distances. A procedure for reconstruction of statistically equivalent Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) is developed and the generated RVEs are analyzed in a boundary value problem with specified chemical expansion of fibres and a recently developed constitutive model for the SBE matrix. The calculated extremes in the local compressive stress show approximately 25% higher values than those in an idealized reference model with a uniform (hexagonal) fibre pattern. The importance of considering manufacturing induced nonuniform microstructure in structural batteries is thus demonstrated.

title: Ultrahigh local stiffening-sensitivity in mechanical metamaterials enabling automatic performance reprogramming with few actuators
abstract: Integrating tunable building-blocks, control, and actuation systems in mechanical metamaterials enables automatic, precise, and fast performance reprogramming for physical intelligence. However, limited by the mixing rule of composite materials, large-range and precise reprogramming typically requires manipulating each building-block, dramatically increasing the complexity of control and actuation systems. Here, an ultrahigh local stiffening-sensitivity mechanism is revealed in the rotating-squares-based structure with quasi-single degree-of-freedom, and is harnessed to drastically reprogram the mechanical performance by manipulating only few local points. The metamaterial's macroscopic modulus increases up to 23.5× by stiffening only 2.5% of local points, corresponding to a tuning sensitivity that is two orders of magnitude higher than that of conventional materials. Guided by the structure-performance relation established with a neural network, the metamaterial's performance can be automatically adjusted to match different targets, using ≤4 built-in stiffening actuation switches within 0.1-0.5 s.
