This work presents local stiffening-sensitive mechanical metamaterials and establishes a new design strategy for efficient mechanical performance reprogramming.

title: Large nonlinear flexural behavior of curved sandwich beams with flexible honeycomb cores
abstract: This paper experimentally and numerically investigated the large nonlinear flexural behavior of carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) curved sandwich beams with flexible honeycomb cores. Based on curved beam structural mechanics, a semi-analytical model for displacement-controlled boundary value problem was established to capture full-range nonlinear load-deflection evolution. After parameter calibration using the test data of specimen R100, the established model predicted the ultimate bearing load of specimens R150 and R200 with error less than 4.83%. Experiments reveal that the dominant failure modes are face sheet fracture and interfacial debonding. With the curvature radius increasing from 100 mm to 200 mm, the ultimate load is decreased by 38.46%, and the deflection-to-radius ratio at peak load drops from 0.2982 to 0.0354. Parametric analysis reveals a non-monotonic relationship between the rise-to-span ratio and the bearing capacity, and the optimal rise-to-span ratio is approximately 0.35. Benefiting from freely deformable flexible CFRP honeycomb, the proposed curved sandwich structure achieves remarkable large flexural deformation performance.

title: Longitudinal fracture resistance of Double–Double composites without 0o plies
abstract: Double–Double (DD) laminates, composed of repeating unit blocks in the form of [±Φ,±Ψ], simplify composite design and manufacturing through their homogenized layup. The configurations without 0o plies are of central concern for practical application, as the longitudinal tensile fracture behavior governs a fundamental failure mode under primary loading. This study investigates the translaminar fracture behavior of such DD laminates using two-tapered compact tension (TTCT) tests, with fracture toughness evaluated through the compliance calibration method. The fracture process is simulated using a trilinear cohesive zone model, and the experimentally measured R-curve is incorporated into a finite fracture mechanics (FFM) framework to predict the open-hole strength of DD laminates. The results show that DD laminates exhibit a clear rising R-curve behavior, in contrast to conventional quasi-isotropic laminates. Despite the simplifying assumption that the translaminar damage is modeled as a cohesive crack, the numerical predictions agree well with the experimental results. In addition, an empirical approach based on the principal fracture angle is proposed to predict the propagation fracture toughness of DD laminates, reducing prediction errors to within 10%. Overall, these findings provide a valuable reference for the damage tolerance design of DD laminates, underscoring their potential for advanced composite structures.

title: High thermal conductivity, low dielectric constant and good processability of epoxy composites achieved by boron nitride/hollow glass microsphere heterostructured particles
abstract: The growing demands of high-power-density and high-frequency electronics require epoxy (EP) composites that achieve a simultaneous balance of high thermal conductivity, low dielectric response, and low viscosity. This study reports a heterostructured particle design, where hollow glass microspheres (HGM) are coated with boron nitride (BN) nanosheets through electrostatic self-assembly, achieving functional partitioning. The BN shell forms continuous thermal pathways, the hollow HGM core introduces air to reduce dielectric polarization, and the confinement of BN nanosheets on spherical HGM suppresses viscosity rise of composites. As a result, the 30 B N@M-HGM/EP achieves an optimal balance among performances, with a thermal conductivity (κ) of 2.4 W/m·K, a dielectric constant (Dk) of 3.7 at 1 MHz, and a viscosity of 12.43 Pa s, outperforming the conventional composite prepared through physical compounding. Encapsulation tests of electronic components further confirm the good thermal management of the composites, reducing the maximum operating temperature by 27.1 °C. These results demonstrate that the heterostructured engineering of composite particles offers an effective and scalable approach for the simultaneous optimization of thermal, dielectric, and rheological properties in epoxy-based electronic packaging materials.

title: High-fidelity modeling of yarn nesting in plain-woven composites using virtual fiber and voxel methods
abstract: Compaction-induced yarn nesting in multilayered plain-woven composites leads to complex mesostructures, which complicate accurate mechanical property prediction. This study develops an integrated virtual fiber method (VFM) and voxel-based finite element framework for nested multilayer plain-woven composites. The compacted yarn geometry is first obtained through virtual-fiber compaction simulation. The deformed virtual-fiber information is then converted into voxel-level material fields. In this virtual fiber-to-voxel conversion, the local fiber volume fraction and local fiber orientation are calculated for each voxel and used to assign spatially varying yarn properties and material orientations. The framework is further combined with progressive damage analysis to study the effect of yarn nesting on stiffness, damage evolution, and tensile strength. An automated software platform is developed to connect virtual fiber generation, compaction simulation, virtual fiber-to-voxel conversion, material assignment, and finite element model generation. A parametric study of 64 nesting configurations shows that nesting patterns affect both elastic modulus and tensile strength, with a stronger effect on tensile strength. The random nesting simulations using 4-layer periodic models and a full-thickness 11-layer model show good agreement with tensile experiments, with the 11-layer model giving relative errors of 1.2% for modulus and 3.9% for strength.

title: Bifunctional surface modification for corrosion inhibition of carbon fibers from electrolyte in structural batteries
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced composite structural batteries that integrate both mechanical load-bearing and energy storage capabilities will be prone to failure at the fiber/matrix interface. However, the interactions between carbon fiber (CF) electrodes and liquid (or polymer) electrolytes remain rarely explored. In this study, we examined the corrosion behavior between CF and liquid electrolyte, based on the assembled CF-based coin cell after cycling. Then, a surface modification strategy was employed to construct a bifunctional layer with carbon nanotubes and polytetrafluoroethylene (CNTs/PTFE) on CF surface. Mechanical flexural testing results for the modified CF composites exhibited ∼17% greater strength values, along with a 28% increase in modulus compared to those of unmodified. Furthermore, the electrochemical performance of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP)||Li half cell with modified CF as current collector was tested with a specific capacity of 163.4 mAh g−1 at 0.1 C (∼6% greater than unmodified sample). Also, excellent cycling stability was obtained, with 90.02% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 2 C (representing the highest values reported to date for structural half cells). Finally, a structural battery of Graphite||LFP with modified CF as current collector exhibited stable capacity under cyclic loading ranging from 100 to 250 MPa and could be used in electrical devices. This work demonstrates the importance of fiber surface architecture for material-level innovation of structural batteries to achieve high performance.

title: Unravelling the microstructural organization of recycled thermoplastic composites made from unidirectional carbon fibre tapes through novel descriptors
abstract: The stochastic microstructure of recycled carbon fibre-reinforced composites poses significant challenges for process optimization and performance prediction, due to the disparity in scales between fibre diameter and fibre agglomerates size. This study establishes a comprehensive quantitative characterization framework to evaluate the microstructural evolution of recycled carbon fibre thermoplastic tapes processed under two distinct melt-compounding regimes with contrasting processing conditions. Utilizing a deep learning-based EfficientNet-B4 model and computer vision for robust fibre segmentation, we analysed the interplay between fibre morphology, orientation, and dispersion on large-field high-resolution micrographs. A novel quantitative approach revealed microstructural notions, hard to detect otherwise, and uncovered a critical trade-off governed by shear mixing history: while a shorter processing scenario preserved fibre length ( > 600 μ m ), it resulted in a planar-random orientation state driven by the tumbling of large aggregates. Conversely, the longer processing scenario induced significant fibre fragmentation but facilitated a transition toward uniaxial alignment. To identify these changes in microstructure, novel homogenization factors (Cluster Prevalence Indicator (CPI) μ and Intra Cluster Density indicator (IDI) κ ) and a Collective Similarity Index (CSI) were introduced. These metrics demonstrated that extended mixing transitions the material from a state dominated by volumetrically large, internally dense super-clusters to a locally dispersed microstructure, without altering the invariant global spatial periodicity ( d ∗ ≈ 260 μ m ). Furthermore, a comparative evaluation of statistical descriptors highlighted that while conventional topological metrics (e.g., Voronoi statistics) proved insensitive to processing variations, the proposed cluster-based metrics and eigenvalue-based orientation tensors successfully captured the structural nuances. This framework provides essential methods for tailoring the processing-structure relationships in recycled discontinuous fibre composites.

title: Bio-based (E)-β-farnesene as an efficient curing co-agent and interfacial bridge for butyl rubber composites: Enhanced vulcanization rate and gas-barrier properties
abstract: Butyl rubber (IIR), which possesses the most excellent gas impermeability among rubber species, suffers from an inherently low vulcanization rate. Although some recent grafting techniques have improved the curing rate of sulfur or peroxide curing systems, the gas-barrier properties of the rubber composites were compromised. In this study, bio-based (E)-β-farnesene (Eβf) was employed as an efficient curing co-agent and interfacial bridge to improve the vulcanization rate and gas-barrier properties of IIR/CB composites. Benefiting from the high reactivity of conjugated double bonds and abundant crosslinking sites, together with the good compatibility with IIR, a portion of Eβf was in-situ grafted onto the backbone of IIR during mixing, and the added Eβf was fully involved in the crosslinking process. An inserted crosslinking and a grafting structure of Eβf were proposed to explain the improvement of thermal stability, the variation of crosslinking density, and glass transition temperature (Tg) of the composites upon Eβf addition. Grafting and curing of Eβf, coupled with robust interactions between Eβf and CB, markedly improve the dispersion state of CB and strengthen interfacial adhesion between the IIR matrix and CB fillers. As a result, compared with IIR/CB composites, the optimum curing time (T90) of the IIR/CB/Eβf composites was shortened by 57.8%, while gas-barrier properties improved by 31.3%. This work provides IIR/CB/Eβf composites with a high curing rate and gas-barrier properties, which hold significant value for the industrial applications of IIR.

title: Damage evolution and localization in carbon fiber 3D woven composites under repeated low-velocity impact via electrical resistance tomography
abstract: Electrical resistance tomography (ERT) presents a promising nondestructive solution for structural health monitoring (SHM). However, its application to three-dimensional (3D) woven composites remains challenging due to the materials' inherent electrical anisotropy and intricate damage mechanisms. This study investigates the damage evolution and electromechanical response of 3D woven carbon fiber/epoxy composites subjected to repeated low-velocity impacts (LVI). To facilitate precise damage localization and imaging, a self-sensing framework employing a Bayesian-optimized hybrid regularized (L1-IRL2) ERT technique was developed. Digital image correlation (DIC) and micro-computed tomography (μ-CT) were integrated to characterize the macroscopic deformation and internal damage evolution under repeated impacts. Multi-channel resistance measurements indicate that the disruption of the conductive network induced by sequential impacts leads to a resistance increase and exhibits pronounced direction-dependence. Owing to the inherent electrical anisotropy of the woven architecture, the damage monitoring sensitivity of the weft direction resistance surpasses that of the warp direction. The proposed ERT framework effectively identifies the progressive damage evolution. Quantitative μ-CT validation demonstrates that the ERT-reconstructed damage area exhibits a growth trend highly consistent with the crack volume fraction under repeated impacts. The proposed ERT framework achieved a centroid positioning error of less than 5 mm. These findings confirm that the proposed Bayesian-optimized hybrid regularized ERT technique can serve as a quick, non-invasive method for preliminary damage assessment of advanced 3D textile composites.

title: Full-scale finite element modeling of compressive behavior and damage evolution in 3D6d braided composites
abstract: Mastering the compressive mechanical characteristics of three-dimensional six-directional (3D6d) braided composites is crucial for their stable service in aerospace engineering. In this paper, a novel parametric full-scale modeling method was proposed for 3D6d braided composites, which fully considers the mutual extrusion and spatial interleaving effects of multi-directional yarns. The compressive mechanical properties and progressive damage evolution of the composites under longitudinal, transverse and out-of-plane loading were systematically investigated. The results show that the longitudinal compressive strength decreases from 425.68 MPa to 265.26 MPa as the braiding angle increases from 20° to 35°. Small braiding angles mainly induce local yarn damage, while large angles cause simultaneous damage at yarn ends and middle accompanied by interlaminar failure. The transverse compressive strength declines regularly from 281.71 MPa to 185.59 MPa. Small angles only damage four-directional and six-directional yarns initially, whereas large angles lead to synchronous failure of all yarn components. Differently, the out-of-plane compressive strength increases steadily from 206.89 MPa to 331.78 MPa with the rising braiding angle. Small angles initiate damage at the ends and interior of four- and five-directional yarns and gradually spread to six-directional yarns, while large angles induce internal damage of four-directional yarns, fracture of five-directional yarns and compression-shear failure of six-directional yarns, eventually forming continuous damage bands. These findings provide valuable insights into the structural design and performance prediction of 3D6d composites. Compared with 3D4d and 3D5d composites, larger braiding angles deflect yarns to transfer excess load into the matrix under longitudinal compression and accelerate damage initiation. All three configurations follow angle-dependent damage evolution despite distinct failure modes. Under out-of-plane compression, increased angles induce premature yarn rupture and interfacial debonding in 3D5d yet retard initial damage in 3D6d, endowing 3D6d with superior out-of-plane damage tolerance.

title: Molecular dynamics simulation and experimental investigation of glass transition temperature reduction in shape memory composites via GO alignment and flexible chain modification
abstract: Shape memory polymers (SMPs) facilitate ice removal by undergoing stimulus-induced deformation that weakens the ice–substrate interface. However, the high glass transition temperature (Tg) of epoxy-based SMPs increases the activation temperature and limits low-temperature use. In this study, Tg was regulated through a dual strategy combining flexible-chain modification with field-assisted alignment of graphene oxide/magnetic graphene oxide (GO/MGO) nanosheets. Neopentyl glycol diglycidyl ether (NGDE) was introduced into the epoxy network as a reactive aliphatic modifier. GO/MGO nanosheets were aligned to form interfacial regions and preferential heat-transfer pathways. Thermal analysis, shape-memory tests, and de-icing experiments were performed to evaluate the composites. Molecular dynamics simulations using the COMPASS III force field were employed to analyze changes in specific volume and free volume and to clarify the underlying molecular basis of Tg regulation. The combined GO/MGO alignment and NGDE modification lowered Tg from 64.9 to 38.2 °C while maintaining a shape recovery ratio of 91.1%. De-icing tests at −15 °C show that the modified EP composite reduces both de-icing time and energy consumption by 58% compared with pristine EP, indicating its potential as a low-temperature shape memory de-icing material.

title: Impact on CFRP adjacent to adhesively bonded hybrid joints: Residual strength assessment and competing failure mechanism
abstract: Carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites and their adhesively bonded hybrid joints are increasingly employed in engineering applications, yet impact damage incurred during service can severely degrade their mechanical performance. Existing studies have mainly focused on impacts directly striking a bonded joint, whereas in realistic cases, impacts are more likely to occur on the large exposed composite area. Under the condition that the impact occurs on the CFRP adjacent to its bonded joint, the interaction between impact-induced CFRP damage and debonding during subsequent loading remains poorly understood, and a dedicated assessment method is lacking. To address this gap, a symmetric double-lap CFRP-Titanium bonded configuration was designed, and low-velocity impact (LVI) and post-impact tensile tests were conducted. Through integrated experiments and simulations, the effects of impact energy and unbonded CFRP size on residual mechanical performance were investigated. The results reveal that LVI induces four distinct damage modes: impact-side debonding, back-side debonding, CFRP delamination, and intralaminar fiber-dominated fracture. Under subsequent tensile loading, the fracture sequence is governed by a competition among the residual strengths of these damage modes. Increasing impact energy intensifies both composite and adhesive damage, thereby reducing the residual load-carrying capacity, while varying the length of the unbonded CFRP region modulates the extent of delamination propagation, thus causing failure mode transitions. Notably, the back-side debonding is identified as the most critical and likely failure mode, as it typically occurs first. This study elucidates the mechanical origin of performance degradation in the CFRP-metal adhesively bonded structure with CFRP subjected to impact.

title: An anisotropic phase-field fracture model for fiber-reinforced composites within an FFT-based computational framework
abstract: In this study, we propose an FFT-based computational framework for solving anisotropic phase-field fracture (PFF) problems in fiber-reinforced composites. Based on the classical phase-field formulation, strain energy density is decomposed into fiber- and matrix-dominated components in order to capture orientation-dependent failure mechanisms. A penalized structural tensor is introduced into the phase-field evolution to promote crack propagation along the fiber direction. The coupled mechanical and phase-field equations are solved iteratively in Fourier space. The proposed anisotropic PFF model is incorporated into a solid-plate coupled framework. In this framework, damage evolves in a three-dimensional solid representation, while the mechanical equilibrium is solved in a plate model by transferring damage-dependent stiffness resultants and reconstructing the three-dimensional strain field from plate kinematics. This coupling strategy enables efficient fracture analysis of thin laminated plates governed mainly by in-plane intralaminar damage, while retaining layer-wise through-thickness damage information. The accuracy, convergence, and efficiency of the proposed framework are assessed through several numerical examples, including a single-edge notched tension test, an open-hole tension test of a unidirectional composite lamina, and an open-hole tension test of a composite laminate. The numerical results reproduce very accurately fiber-orientation-dependent crack paths and layer-wise damage patterns. The proposed solid-plate coupled framework reduces the final cumulative computational time by around 20 times compared with the full three-dimensional FFT-based PFF model.

title: Scale-dependent evolution of transverse electrical conduction and electro-thermal stability assessment in 3D braided composites
abstract: The electric conductivity of 3D carbon fiber braided composites is an important factor to applications in electrical environments. However, anisotropic conductivity, especially the transverse electrical conductivity lacks a precise investigation. Here we report an analytical geometric model to derive transverse electrical conductivity based on minimum physical span of through-transverse yarns. The scale effects on temperature-dependent conductivity and electrical-thermal fields were investigated. We found that the electric conductive mechanism transits from a non-uniform interface contact-dominated mode to multi-yarn contact mode as the scale increases. The randomness of interface contact is the primary factor inducing local field non-uniformity, while through-yarns establish continuous bulk pathways that balance the discrete contact conduction mechanisms. When the representative length reaches four times the through-yarn span, the transverse conductivity converges to a scale-independent value, accompanied by the simultaneous convergence of the electric, thermal, and heat flow fields. This span criterion provides a quantitative basis for the scale selection and stability design of 3D braided functional composite devices.

title: Investigation on electrothermal co-curing bonding and integrated forming-damage monitoring in CFRP stepped repairs using CNTFs
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) structures require efficient and reliable repair after sustaining local damage. This paper proposes an electrothermal co-curing bonding stepped repair method for CFRP by embedding a carbon nanotube film (CNTF) into the adhesive layer, endowing the repair with both Joule heating and self-sensing functionalities. The electrothermal and sensing properties of the CNTF are first discussed, followed by analyses of curing monitoring and forming quality, mechanical performance and damage sensing. The influence mechanism of the curing cycle on repair performance is then clarified. Results show that the CNTF exhibits not only rapid, stable, and uniform electrothermal performance but also a sensitive electrical resistance response to strain. Compared with conventional repair, electrothermal repair shows superior performance in temperature control and energy consumption, and both methods produce no obvious defects in forming quality. The resistance signal of the embedded CNTF can be used both to infer the cure evolution of the resin during the co-curing process and to detect damage initiation and propagation in the repaired structure under three-point bending loads. The embedding of the CNTF alters the local failure behavior of the stepped repair structure and slightly weakens its bending performance, though the effect is not significant. Furthermore, extending the holding time optimizes the distribution of curing-induced residual stress (CRS). When the holding time increases from 90 min to 150 min, the ultimate load recovery ratio rises from 75.89% to 83.34%, albeit with a diminishing beneficial effect. This study demonstrates that the CNTF holds promise as an integrated heating and sensing unit for in situ curing repair and condition monitoring of CFRP structures.

title: Hybrid design of graphene oxide-coated polyurethane foam with air layers and a membrane for broadband sound absorption: Poroelastic modeling and experimental validation
abstract: Multilayer hybrid sound absorbers that combine porous materials with structural designs offer a promising strategy for achieving high sound absorption, yet predictive frameworks for optimizing such systems remain limited. Here, we develop an integrated acoustic modeling and optimization framework for multilayer absorbers composed of graphene oxide-impregnated polyurethane foam (PUGO), air layers, and a membrane. The framework quantitatively predicts acoustic performance using poroelastic theory and multilayer boundary conditions, enabling the multilayer sequence to be determined for a given thickness and number of layers. The optimized structure achieved an average sound absorption of 0.896 at a thickness of 105.3 mm, demonstrating improved performance compared to previously reported values by 7.7% ± 4.0%, primarily due to enhanced low frequency absorption enabled by the multilayer hybrid design. Predicted sound absorption curves show excellent agreement with measurements across a wide range of thicknesses and configurations, with a mean prediction deviation of 5.67% ± 3.56%, confirming the framework's reliability. These results establish a predictive design strategy that integrates material modification with structural optimization, providing a practical pathway for lightweight and highly efficient multilayer absorbers in advanced noise control applications.

title: Interfacial engineering via optimized co-deposited polyethyleneimine-polydopamine structure toward gaining carbon fiber composites with high interfacial strength and toughness
abstract: To solve the limitations of uncontrollable polydopamine (PDA) deposition morphology and the lack of rigidity in polyethyleneimine (PEI). Herein, by jointly adjusting the PEI content and the addition sequence of PEI and dopamine, we obtained a co-deposited PEI-PDA coating with uniform distribution and optimized structure, which resolve the interfacial strengthening-toughening trade-off of carbon fiber composites. In the case where PEI was added first at 50% content, a highly cross-linked and compact PEI-PDA coating was formed, featuring a unique architecture of flexible PEI backbone and rigid PDA side chains. This resulted in a 21.2% growth in carbon fiber tensile strength, along with elevations of 49.1% and 255.9% in interfacial strength and toughness, relative to untreated CF composites. Enhanced dual-interface (fiber–coating and coating–resin) bonding, wettability, and crack deflection drive the interfacial reinforcement, whereas PEI stretching/slippage and tortuous crack paths are the key mechanisms for improved interfacial toughness. Reversing the addition sequence led to a low-cross-linked PEI-PDA coating, causing the increment in interfacial properties was far inferior to that of fibers with the PEI-first sequence. This work presents a green and easy-to-implement strategy in acquiring high-performance composites.

title: Bridging atomistic simulations and experiments: A potential-energy-landscape-based analytical model for the strain-rate-dependent mechanical behaviour of epoxy resins
abstract: Nanoparticle-reinforced composites can improve stiffness, strength and thermal stability, but nanoscale defects such as particle agglomeration can reduce performance. This behaviour is hard to study because simulations and experiments work at very different strain rates. Conventional molecular dynamics (MD) is limited to very high strain rates and nanosecond times, while experiments use much lower rates. To reduce this gap, this work develops a coarse-grained potential-energy-landscape (PEL) framework for epoxy deformation. In this study, a PEL–Eyring model is proposed. In this model, autonomous basin climbing samples a spectrum of metastable stress states, and an Eyring-type activated-process model turns this spectrum into the rate- and temperature-dependent response. All model inputs are physical constants, independently reported literature values or PEL-derived quantities, and no parameter is fitted to the validation curves. The coarse-grained model is first checked against all-atom simulations at high strain rates and is then validated against independent low-rate tensile experiments. It reproduces both rate hardening and thermal softening, with yield-stress errors of 2.7–3.6%, normalized area errors below 0.10 and R 2 ≥ 0.938 across two strain rates and three temperatures. It also matches an independent tensile strength scale without adjustment. The work gives a parameter-free and physically clear link from molecular-scale PEL information to experimentally accessible mechanical behaviour. It shows that the nonlinear, rate- and temperature-dependent tensile response of epoxy can be predicted beyond the time limits of conventional MD.

title: Efficient recycling of epoxy resin composites via ionic-liquid-promoted amine enrichment
abstract: Benefiting from their well-balanced properties, epoxy resin composites are extensively employed in coatings, electronic packaging, structural components, and various other high-value applications. The growing consumption of epoxy resins has made the recycling of epoxy-based composites increasingly significant. However, current recycling and disposal methods mainly rely on incineration and landfilling, which may cause environmental pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Moreover, most existing recycling methods require epoxy composite panels to be crushed before treatment, which increases processing complexity and limits the recovery of intact fibers. Thus, it is essential to establish recycling routes that combine environmental sustainability with economic feasibility. Herein, we report an ionic-liquid-assisted chemical recycling strategy for the simultaneous recovery of epoxy resin and intact fibers. In this system, the ionic liquid promotes interfacial MXDA enrichment, resin swelling, amine diffusion, and selective aminolysis of ester linkages in the epoxy network. Notably, the recycled carbon fibers showed high performance retention, with tensile strength reaching 96% of that of the original fibers. The recycled epoxy resin exhibited a tensile strength of 80.5 MPa, a break elongation of 5.27%, a flexural strength of 107 MPa, and a flexural strain at break of 9.94%. The recycled epoxy-derived materials were also used to prepare oil-water separation adsorbents, successfully achieving selective separation and adsorption of oil from water. Overall, this study demonstrates an ionic-liquid-assisted chemical recycling strategy for the efficient recovery of carbon fibers and the value-added reutilization of resin-derived degradation products from epoxy resin composites.

title: Highly thermally conductive polydimethylsiloxane composites with bidirectional thermal conduction pathways
abstract: Constructing ordered thermally conductive pathways within polymer-based composites can optimize heat transfer routes, thereby significantly enhancing the thermal conductivity of the composites. In this work, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) was employed as the matrix, while magnetically responsive boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS@Ni) and surface-functionalized gallium-indium liquid metal (f-LM) were utilized as hybrid thermally conductive fillers to fabricate H-‍BNNS@Ni/f-LM/PDMS composites with bidirectional thermally conductive pathways in both the in-plane and through-plane directions via magnetic field orientation. At a H-BNNS@Ni to f-LM mass ratio of 4:1 and a total filler loading of 50 wt%, the in-plane thermal conductivity (λ∥) and through-plane thermal conductivity (λ⊥) of the H-‍BNNS@Ni/f-LM/PDMS composites reached 6.31 W/(m·K) and 0.98 W/(m·K), corresponding to 33.2 and 9.8 times those of pure PDMS, respectively. The H-BNNS@Ni/f-LM/PDMS composites also exhibited outstanding thermal stability (thermal resistance index of 261.8°C), photothermal conversion capability (surface temperature reaching 161.4°C after 30 s of near-infrared light irradiation at 0.95 W·cm−2), and hydrophobicity (water contact angle of 120.0o), indicating their considerable potential for applications in next-generation flexible electronic devices.

title: Multi-scale optimization design of topology and fiber orientation with path planning method for additive manufactured continuous fiber-reinforced polymer structures
abstract: The development of additive manufacturing (AM) has created more opportunities for fabricating complex topology and fiber distributions, which are essential for fully exploiting the performance benefits and design flexibility of continuous fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRP). However, the complexity of the geometry and fiber orientation in CFRP structures poses challenges for multi-scale optimization and their direct application in AM. This paper develops a multi-scale collaborative optimization method for CFRP structures. A compliance minimization model with structural volume constraint is constructed to simultaneously optimize the topology and local fiber distribution. To address the critical issue of fiber discontinuity in optimized designs, we propose an improved fiber orientation filtering strategy that enforces smooth and continuous fiber distributions, thereby enhancing both structural performance and manufacturability. Building upon this optimization foundation, we introduce a complementary fiber path planning algorithm that translates the optimized fiber orientation fields into continuous, collision-free printing paths suitable for AM processes. Numerical examples and experimental validation are conducted to assess the validity and robustness of the developed method, wherein the fabricated specimens with complementary fiber paths exhibit substantial improvements in structural stiffness and load-bearing capacity relative to conventional path planning strategies. Collectively, this work establishes a unified paradigm bridging multiscale optimization design with manufacturing-oriented path planning, thereby offering a robust and scalable pathway toward performance-driven design of additive manufactured CFRP structures.

title: Microstructure-failure interactions in continuous carbon- and glass-fibre reinforced nylon 3D-printed composites under compression
abstract: Continuous fibre-reinforced nylon produced by fused filament fabrication (FFF) offers great potential for lightweight structural applications; however, process-induced defects such as porosity, fibre misalignment and inter-bead discontinuities can significantly reduce compressive performance. This study investigates the role of these microstructural features in governing damage evolution and collapse in continuous carbon fibre-reinforced (CFRP) and glass fibre-reinforced (GFRP) nylon under uniaxial compression using in-situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (XCT). XCT scans recorded before and after compression are analysed using a deep learning-based segmentation framework to quantify phase fractions, fibre orientation and void morphology. CFRP exhibits higher void content (11%–12%) and lower fibre volume fractions (30%–33%) than GFRP with approx. 70% and 50% of fibres oriented within 2.5° of the extrusion direction. For both CFRP samples and one GFRP sample, kinking was observed out-of-plane of the printed layers, accompanied by fibre fracture and delamination. In the other case, the GFRP exhibited more distributed deformation characterised by fibre reorientation, bending instability and interlaminar damage. This was ascribed to a reduction in lateral constraint arising from interlaminar voids, but the lower degree of fibre alignment for that sample may also contribute. These results show how compressive failure in continuous-fibre FFF composites is controlled by the coupled interactions between fibre architecture, void morphology and nonuniform local stress field, providing a basis for microstructure-informed process optimisation and improved structural performance.

title: Editorial Board
Interlayer bonding enhancement via conformal graphene oxide coating in FDM additive manufacturing
abstract: Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is a widely used 3D printing method due to its low cost, material versatility, and design flexibility. However, FDM-printed parts often suffer from poor mechanical strength caused by weak bonding between layers. Coating filaments with graphene oxide (GO) has been shown to improve these mechanical properties. In this study, ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used to investigate how GO coatings enhance interfacial strength in FDM printing. The results show that the degree of GO oxidation, the covalent bonding rate and spatial distribution of interfacial bonding sites significantly affect the bonding strength between layers. Using the Taguchi method, the theoretical optimized molecular-scale interfacial strength was predicted to reach ∼40.54 GPa under the simulated conditions. Furthermore, an idealized interface with uniformly distributed covalent bonding sites was predicted to achieve a theoretical upper-bound interfacial strength, corresponding to a ∼65.46% improvement over the optimized configuration. The simulation results qualitatively reproduce the experimental strengthening trend, providing molecular-scale insights into interfacial reinforcement mechanisms and a rational basis for optimizing GO coating characteristics and printing parameters to enhance the mechanical performance of FDM-printed parts.

title: Enhancing silica dispersion and interfacial adhesion in natural rubber composites via a novel synergistic liquid-phase modification strategy
abstract: The preparation of high-performance "green tires" via liquid-compounding is hindered by the phase incompatibility between hydrophilic silica and lipophilic silane coupling agents in water, which limits silanization efficiency. A novel liquid-compounding strategy based on the synergistic modification of silica by fatty alcohol polyoxyethylene ether-9 (AEO-9) and Bis-(γ-triethoxysilylpropyl)-tetrasulfide (Si69) was proposed in this study. During liquid-phase modification, AEO-9 rapidly adsorbed onto the silica surface, constructing a favorable lipophilic microenvironment. This interface not only disrupted the hydrogen-bonded silica network for exceptional slurry stability but also drove the localized enrichment and subsequent covalent grafting of the lipophilic Si69. Consequently, the nanocomposites exhibited uniform silica dispersion and strong interfacial interactions between silica and the rubber matrix. This microstructure resulted in a lower Payne effect and balanced mechanical properties. Compared to conventional dry-mixed counterparts, the co-modified composites exhibited exceptional dynamic performance and higher wear resistance. This study not only reveals a novel synergistic modification mechanism but also offers a low-pollution process for fabricating advanced rubber nanocomposites. This approach has great promise for the development of sustainable, high-performance tires.

title: Magneto-mechanical properties of high-loading MRE with NR/SBR mixed matrix and application in profile multi-point stretch-bending
abstract: This study designed and developed a functional material reference system for profile stretch bending - a magnetorheological elastomer (MRE) with an interfacial locking mechanism, based on a natural rubber (NR)/styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) hybrid matrix highly filled with carbonyl iron powder (CIPs). By leveraging the high elasticity of NR and the wear resistance and thermal stability of SBR, a dense secondary percolation network of carbon black (CB)/carbon nanotubes (CNTs) was constructed over a CIPs content range of 60–80 wt%, approaching the congestion threshold. This configuration effectively addresses the challenges associated with the preparation and dispersion of high-content heterogeneous filler systems. The static compressive mechanical properties of the MRE under varying magnetic fields were systematically investigated, uncovering the nonlinear regulatory mechanism of the interfacial locking effect on the magneto-induced stiffening behavior in highly congested systems. Results indicate that both increased CIP content and enhanced magnetic field strength lead to a monotonic increase in the magneto-induced stiffening effect and the normal stress response of the MRE. Experimental and numerical simulations confirmed that the proposed MRE, when used as a flexible mold, significantly improves the uniformity of stress and strain distributions within profiles and enhances forming accuracy.

title: Synergistic interface tailoring and low temperature curing toward high strength wave-transparent PBO/CE composites via PDA-ZIF67 activation and thiol catalysis
abstract: PBO fiber and cyanate ester (CE) resin are essential candidates for integrated load bearing and wave transparent composites, but their inherently poor interfacial adhesion and the ultra-high curing temperature of CE significantly limit their practical application. A dual strategy was proposed to simultaneously optimize the resin curing behavior and the fiber matrix interface in this study. Specifically, a polydopamine zeolitic imidazolate framework-67 (PDA-ZIF67) multilayer assembly was constructed to activate the surface of the PBO fiber, while a thiol polysulfide catalyst (PSC) was introduced to achieve low temperature catalytic cross linking of the CE resin. The PDA -ZIF67 modification increased the surface energy of the PBO fiber from 24.7 mN/m to 33.4 mN/m, substantially enhancing its wettability to the CE resin. With 6.0 wt% PSC, CE resin reached 98.3% crosslinking at 150 °C, and the cured resin exhibited high tensile strength (79.8 MPa), flexural strength (134.8 MPa), glass transition temperature (268.8 °C) and low water absorption (0.32%). The PBO@PDA-ZIF67/CE-PSC composite achieved an interfacial shear strength of 59.4 MPa, 60.5% higher than the unmodified system. It also displayed a low dielectric constant (2.48), low dielectric loss (0.0082) and high wave transmittance (92.6% at 10 GHz). Moreover, benefiting from the PSC and ZIF67, the composite exhibited remarkable UV aging resistance and excellent mold-resistant antibacterial performance, meeting the stringent environmental requirements for aerospace radomes. This work paves the way for the fabrication of high-performance PBO/CE wave-transparent composites, providing a viable solution for next-generation aerospace radome applications.
keywords: Thiol polysulfide catalytic cyanate ester resin

title: A sandbag-inspired 3D elastomeric skeleton for leakage-free and flame-retardant flexible phase change composites in battery thermal management
abstract: Flexible phase-change composite materials (FPCMs) are highly promising for battery thermal management (BTM), but mitigating liquid leakage, low thermal conductivity, and flammability simultaneously remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a multifunctional FPCM featuring a robust "sandbag-like" 3D skeleton fabricated via the in-situ cross-linking of a silicone rubber matrix. This resilient elastomeric network securely microencapsulates the palmitic acid (PA) core, thoroughly eradicating leakage risks while preserving exceptional mechanical flexibility. To address thermal and fire safety bottlenecks, 2D boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS) and a reactive flame retardant, triallyl phosphate (TAP), were synergistically integrated. Crucially, TAP covalently grafts onto the polysiloxane backbone, coupling with the continuous BNNS network to trigger a dense condensed-phase charring mechanism that significantly suppresses combustion dynamics (peak heat release rate reduced to 125.8 W/g) without hazardous melt-dripping. The optimized composite delivers a robust latent heat of 91.7 J/g and an enhanced thermal conductivity of 0.613 W/(m·K) (a 107% improvement). Demonstrating outstanding thermomechanical reliability over 200 cycles, the FPCM effectively regulates battery temperatures. Under a severe 3C discharge, it restricts the maximum battery surface temperature to 58.9 °C (a 20.8 °C reduction versus natural convection) and narrows the interfacial temperature gradient to 7.44 °C, demonstrating substantial engineering potential for safe BTM systems.

title: Machine learning design of electronic packaging materials: A phonon spectrum continuity matching framework for high thermal conductivity
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing chips has posed significant challenges to thermal management in advanced electronic packaging. Conventional epoxy packaging materials struggle to meet the thermal dissipation demands of high-power chips due to their low thermal conductivity (<0.5 W m−1 K−1). This study introduces a phonon spectrum continuity matching strategy for multiple functional fillers integrated with a machine learning framework to develop high thermal conductivity composites. Through high-throughput screening, we identified three high performance composites. Experiments demonstrate that the composite achieves through-plane and in-plane thermal conductivities of 2.22 and 11.18 W m−1 K−1, while maintaining excellent process adaptability (viscosity: 16.1 Pa s). Device-level thermal management validation using an Allwinner H133 platform demonstrated a 5.1 °C reduction in chip temperature. The Arrhenius analysis further suggests that the improved thermal management capability may contribute to enhanced reliability and extended service lifetime of electronic devices. The synergistic interaction between the high frequency phonon characteristics of diamond, the mid-to-high frequency characteristics of expanded graphite, and the mid-to-low frequency characteristics of SiO2 enhances the thermal conductivity of the composite. Machine learning effectively explores the multi-component formulation space, overcoming the limitations of trial-and-error methods. This study establishes a systematic paradigm for the development and validation of high-performance composites in advanced packaging.

title: “Thermal locking” enabled by carborane nanocages in waterborne poly(amic acid) salt sizing for high-temperature interfacial reinforcement of carbon fiber/polyimide composites
abstract: Developing waterborne sizing agents that combine aqueous processability, polyimide compatibility, and high-temperature stability remains a key challenge for carbon fiber/polyimide (CF/PI) composites. The water-based sizing technology is a widely adopted and effective strategy, yet it faces the challenge of balancing water solubility and heat resistance. Here, carborane-functionalized waterborne poly (amic acid) salt (PAAS) sizing agents with a rigid-flexible architecture were designed to address this limitation. Flexible ODPA-containing segments improved aqueous stability and promoted uniform coating formation on carbon fibers, while rigid carborane nanocages were introduced to restrict high-temperature chain relaxation in the PI interphase. The optimized WPI-2 and WPI-3 systems formed continuous sizing layers and substantially enhanced interfacial adhesion. The modified CF/PI composites achieved an interlaminar shear strength of 126.99 MPa and an interfacial shear strength of 102.41 MPa at room temperature, representing increases of 42.1% and 32.7%, respectively. At 300 °C, the optimized composite retained an ILSS of 94.07 MPa, 24.9% higher than the unsized control. The improvement is attributed to a carborane-induced thermal locking effect, where bulky three-dimensional cages act as physical confinement nodes.

title: Predicting effective thermal conductivity of high-filled particulate composites from 3D microstructure via a hybrid CNN-transformer
abstract: The effective thermal conductivity (ETC) of high-filled particulate composites is critical for evaluating thermal management and thermo-mechanical integrity. However, severe structural heterogeneity creates tortuous heat transfer pathways, making rapid and accurate ETC prediction a formidable bottleneck for efficient material design. This study proposes an ETC prediction framework integrating microstructural modeling with a sequential CNN-transformer deep learning architecture. First, a microstructure generation strategy, termed DEM-EDF, is developed using a simplified discrete element method and the Euclidean distance field. Demonstrated on a ternary solid propellant (HTPB/AP/Al), it achieves high volume fractions up to 70%, and outperforms the Lubachevsky-Stillinger algorithm in efficiency by over 95% at medium-to-high volume fractions. Based on the generated microstructures, an ETC dataset is established via finite element analysis. Second, a sequential CNN-transformer model is constructed to directly predict the ETC using 3D microstructures. Each 3D structural sample is discretized into a series of 2D cross-sectional images as model inputs. A CNN extracts and dimensionally reduces these image features, which are then processed by a transformer module utilizing positional encoding and self-attention mechanism. The model achieves an excellent prediction accuracy of R2 > 0.98. Crucially, the self-attention mechanism effectively fuses image features across the 2D cross-sections, empowering the framework to robustly map high-volume-fraction microstructures to their ETC using remarkably sparse discretization (merely five cross-sectional images). Ultimately, this research provides a closed-loop framework from rapid microstructure generation to highly efficient ETC prediction, offering a powerful tool for low-cost thermal evaluation and material design.

title: Dielectric-tunable carbon-quartz blended fiber/silicone aerogel composites for ultra-broadband microwave absorption: Synergy of conductivity control and multilayered architecture engineering
abstract: Developing advanced carbon fiber-based electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorbing materials is crucial for electromagnetic protection and stealth. However, achieving broadband absorption remains challenging due to severe impedance mismatch arising from excessively high conductivity of carbon fiber. Herein, we report carbon-quartz blended fibers/silicone aerogel composites (CF-QF/SAs) with controlled conductivity and multilayered architecture to improve impedance matching for broadband EMW absorption. The graphitization degree and chemical components of carbon fibers are tailored via low-temperature carbonization of pre-oxidized polyacrylonitrile (PAN), enabling tunable electrical conductivity. Blending with quartz fibers at specific ratios further adjusts dielectric properties, establishing a continuously tunable permittivity system. When combined with silicone aerogel, the synergistic effects of conductive and polarization loss yield superior EMW absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of −56.1 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 6.6 GHz. Furthermore, an impedance-gradient incorporating a sandwich structure is innovatively proposed for fabricating multilayered composites. Simulation confirms that this design effectively improves impedance matching and attenuation capacity. The optimized composite achieves an ultra-broad EAB of 37.4 GHz, covering 2.5-39.9 GHz. The composite also demonstrates excellent mechanical properties with tensile strength of 12.2 MPa and thermal insulation properties with low thermal conductivity of 0.051 W m−1 K−1. Moreover, the composite exhibits outstanding high-temperature resistance, retaining superior absorption even after exposure to 800 °C for 1000 s. This work satisfies the multifunctional requirements for broadband stealth and thermal insulation in practical engineering applications.

title: Bridging the scales: From interfacial strength to macroscopic performance in chopped basalt fiber reinforced waterborne epoxy composites via integrated measurement and simulation
abstract: Achieving reliable reinforcement in waterborne epoxy (WEP) composites requires understanding how microscale interfacial properties translate into macroscopic damage tolerance. Here, a measurement-simulation-validation framework was developed for silane-modified chopped basalt fiber (CBF)/WEP composites. Interfacial normal strength and interfacial shear strength were quantified using cruciform specimen and microdroplet debonding tests, respectively, and the measured values were directly introduced into a cohesive-zone-based representative volume element model. The epoxy-functionalized silane KH560 provided the highest interfacial normal and shear strengths, reaching 20.76 and 33.19 MPa, respectively. However, simulations revealed that its relatively stiff interface promoted local stress concentration and interfacial microcrack initiation. In contrast, KH590 produced a thinner and more uniform interphase, leading to smoother stress transfer and reduced interfacial crack opening. Macroscopic tensile testing and dynamic mechanical analysis confirmed this prediction: KH590-CBF/WEP achieved the best overall reinforcement, with a tensile strength of 34.18 MPa and a storage modulus of 2036.13 MPa, corresponding to increases of 84.5% and 67.0% compared with neat WEP, respectively. These results demonstrate that maximizing interfacial strength alone is insufficient for optimizing composite performance; instead, an appropriate balance between interfacial bonding, interphase uniformity, and stress dissipation is required.

title: Tensile and interlaminar behaviour of brick-and-mortar carbon fibre thermoplastic composites
abstract: Brick-and-mortar carbon fibre structures have attracted considerable attention owing to their reliable mechanical performance, including high damage tolerance, multiple energy dissipation mechanisms and the potential to use carbon fibre scraps instead of pristine carbon fibre prepregs. Although numerous studies have focused on thermoset matrix systems, their behaviour under specific loading conditions, particularly Mode I and Mode II interlaminar fracture, remains unclear. To address this gap, the present study investigated the mechanical behaviour of brick-and-mortar laminates manually fabricated from carbon fibre/poly-ether-ether-ketone tapes with brick lengths of 50, 25 and 10 mm. Tensile, Mode I interlaminar fracture and Mode II interlaminar fracture tests were conducted to evaluate the mechanical response of the laminates. The brick-and-mortar structure retained approximately 88% of the stiffness of the continuous laminate, whereas the tensile strength decreased notably from 1860 MPa for the continuous laminate to 960 MPa for the strongest discontinuous configuration, corresponding to a brick length of 25 mm. In Mode I, the average fracture toughness was 1.75 kJ/m 2 for the 25-mm brick-length sample, compared with 1.76 kJ/m 2 for the continuous configuration. In Mode II, the fracture toughness increased by 33% for the 10-mm brick-length samples, reaching 5.10 kJ/m 2 compared with 3.83 kJ/m 2 for the continuous samples. Numerical simulations were performed to examine the underlying failure mechanisms, and the results demonstrated good agreement with the experimental observations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of brick-and-mortar configurations for thermoplastic composite structures.

title: Bioinspired 3D-structured reinforcement framework for enhancing the environmental resistance of particle-based composites
abstract: High-performance materials for extreme environments are often constrained by high cost, energy consumption, and limited sustainability, whereas low-cost, sustainable wood-based materials generally exhibit poor water resistance. Inspired by plant cell structures, we developed a three-dimensional fiber-reinforced polymer framework integrated with low-cost wood particles via stitching and hot pressing, and systematically investigated the underlying water-resistance mechanisms. Compared with conventional particleboard, the composite exhibits 14 times increase in water resistance, and after 6 aging cycles, the modulus of rupture decreases by only 34.9%. It retains high load-bearing capacity following water immersion and maintains excellent strength and impact resistance after freezing, highlighting its potential for extremely cold environments. Bending performance under high-temperature conditions is also improved. By optimizing the reinforcement material, the modulus of rupture and modulus of elasticity reach 106.12 MPa and 21.06 GPa, respectively, while impact toughness attains 309.2 kJ/m2, surpassing aluminum. Remarkably, its density and carbon emissions are only 30% and 19.44% of aluminum, respectively. For the first time, we demonstrate a positive correlation between the water resistance of a 3D structural reinforcement and the composite's overall water resistance and dimensional stability. CT imaging and finite element simulations reveal that the reinforcement's thickness-direction structure is the primary factor governing water resistance and clarify the contributions of different reinforcement regions to bending damage mechanisms. These findings provide experimental evidence and design guidance for the development of high-performance, durable structural composites.

title: Ultrahigh thermal conductivity and low thermal resistance carbon fiber thermal pad achieved by 3D printing
abstract: The advancement of high-power electronic devices has increased the need for thermal interface materials (TIMs) that combine high thermal conductivity, low thermal resistance, and high reliability. In this work, a three-dimensional (3D) printing–based manufacturing strategy was developed to fabricate carbon fibers (CFs) thermal pad with ultrahigh thermal conductivity and low thermal resistance. The shear stress generated during 3D printing vertically orients CFs as the thermally conductive backbone, while alumina (Al2O3) particles fill the gaps as thermally conductive bridges, synergistically constructing a continuous and compact 3D thermal conduction network. The through-plane thermal conductivity of the VCA/PDMS composite reaches 51 W m−1 K−1, which is 288 times that of pure PDMS. The composite also exhibited excellent thermal stability and an extremely low thermal resistance of 0.14 °C·in2·W−1. In a high-power LED application, the operating temperature was reduced by 15.6 °C using VCA/PDMS composite. The developed 3D printing method is scalable and cost-effective. It provides an effective material solution for the thermal management of high-performance electronic devices.

title: Waste skin collagen-derived carbon/graphene/fluorinated polyimide composite aerogel with directional thermal conduction and excellent mechanical properties
abstract: Materials combining directional thermal conductivity and mechanical flexibility are highly desirable for aerospace and microelectronic thermal management. However, achieving both properties simultaneously remains challenging. Waste skin collagen (Col) was enzymatically modified and mixed with graphene oxide (GO). Directional freeze-drying and high-temperature carbonization yielded collagen-derived carbon/graphene aerogel (CG). Fluorinated polyimide (FPI) was vacuum-impregnated into the skeletons to fabricate collagen-derived carbon/graphene/fluorinated polyimide composite aerogel (CGF). By tuning the GO incorporation and FPI concentration, the structure and properties of the composite aerogels were regulated. The results demonstrate that CGF-2 exhibits the optimal overall performance, achieving a maximum compressive strain of 78% under a load of 100 N and a permanent deformation rate below 0.4% after 20,000 compression cycles, while maintaining a relatively high vertical thermal conductivity of 5.12 W/(m·K), indicating an excellent synergistic optimization of thermal conductivity and mechanical performance. Moreover, the COMSOL simulation results further confirm that its vertical (⊥) heat transfer performance is superior to that in the horizontal direction (∥).

title: The effect of filler hybridization on reducing warpage in fused filament fabrication of polypropylene composites
abstract: This study investigated the key factors contributing to warpage reduction in polypropylene (PP)/talc/cellulose nanofiber (CNF) hybrid composites fabricated via fused filament fabrication (FFF). Experimental results demonstrated that this hybrid filler system exhibited a significant synergistic effect, achieving an 81.8% reduction in post-fabrication warpage compared to unfilled PP. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, a multiscale thermal deformation analysis combining the finite element method (FEM) with bulk-state solidification shrinkage rate testing was conducted. Although the simplified numerical model focused on the homogenized thermal expansion and elastic properties of the solidified material, it underestimated the warpage reduction rate at 6.35% because it did not account for layer-by-layer phase transformation, crystallization, or residual stresses. Nevertheless, the simulation accurately captured qualitative trends and confirmed the superior effectiveness of the hybrid filler system in suppressing thermal shrinkage. These findings suggest that warpage suppression arises from a complex mechanism involving increased structural rigidity, reduced thermal expansion, and the non-linear inhibition of crystallization shrinkage driven by microstructural interactions between the fillers, thereby providing practical guidelines for material design in automotive applications.

title: Cross-scale spatial and phonon-bridging synergy of 1D/2D boron nitride hybrids in highly thermally conductive and insulating films for electronic thermal management
abstract: The rapid evolution of 5G/6G communications and high-power-density electronic devices has severely exacerbated localized heat accumulation, creating an urgent demand for high-performance thermal management materials that simultaneously possess high thermal conductivity and reliable electrical insulation. Herein, we present a strategy for constructing highly efficient in-plane thermal conduction network through the cross-scale spatial synergy and phonon-bridging mechanism of one-dimensional boron nitride nanotubes (1D BNNTs) and two-dimensional boron nitride nanosheets (2D BNNSs) hybrid system. Micron-sized BNNSs serve as the primary skeleton of thermal conduction network, while high-aspect-ratio BNNTs functionalized via silane coupling agent act as structural thermal bridges to tightly span the interfacial gaps between adjacent 2D BNNSs. Induced by fluidic shear force, the 1D/2D hybrid fillers can achieve a highly in-plane ordered alignment, paving more direct and continuous pathways for phonon transport. Consequently, the resulting poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF)/BNNS/BNNT (PBST) composite film delivers an exceptional comprehensive performance: superior thermal conductivity of 6.65 W m−1 K−1, robust tensile strength of 41.52 MPa and outstanding electrical insulation properties. Practical applications in the smart-phone demonstrate that PBST composite film can effectively reduce hotspot temperature (ΔT = 5.31 °C). This study provides an innovative and viable solution to address the challenges of high-flux thermal dissipation in advanced electronic systems.

title: Self-healing and high-toughness continuous carbon fiber-reinforced polyamide 12 by multi-material 3D printing
abstract: It remains a significant challenge for fiber-reinforced composites to maintain consistent performance over their service lifetime due to the development of damage. Thus, timely repair of initial damage can effectively prolong the service life of composites. Self-healing composites can restore performance after damage in response to specific external stimuli, offering substantial benefits by reducing maintenance time and costs. Considering that delamination is the majority of damage in fiber-reinforced laminates, continuous carbon fiber-reinforced polyamide 12 (PA12-CCF) with soft poly(ether-block-amide) PEBA interlayers is designed with self-healing capacity and high toughness by multi-material 3D printing. This system achieves interlaminar self-healing by heating to a temperature above the interlayer's softening range (PEBA), thereby remelting the interlayers while preserving the integrity of the matrix and fibers. Double cantilever beam (DCB) tests reveal a 140% increase in the interlaminar fracture toughness GIc with the incorporation of PEBA interlayers, compared to pure PA12-CCFs. The multi-round self-healing capacity of PA12-CCF with PEBA interlayer is further studied. It exhibits 97% and 75% (2.20 kJ/m2) healing efficiencies in strength and fracture toughness for the first-time healing, and maintains more than 80% of its original strength and 60% (1.77 kJ/m2) of its toughness after the fifth self-healing, still superior to baseline PA12-CCF (0.99 kJ/m2). This design proposes a self-healing strategy for 3D-printed composites that not only enhances interlaminar toughness but also enables self-healing functionality for interlaminar damage.

title: Cellulose based Janus-aerogel composite as magnetically actuated thermal interface materials
abstract: With the miniaturization of electronic devices, interfacial thermal management encounters substantial challenges. However, conventional thermal dissipation materials incorporated with rigid thermal fillers fail to construct tight, durable, and tunable thermal conduction pathways, thereby limiting their application in electronic device heat dissipation. This work reports a magnetically actuated thermal-conductive NdFeB/cellulose nanofiber (CNF)/polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/liquid metal (LM) (MCPL) aerogel film with a Janus inner structure, in which the flexible LM-CNF/PVA constructs an efficient thermal conduction network, LM-enriched bottom surface provides higher in-plane conductivity, and the NdFeB particles-stratified layer endows the excellent magnetic actuation. The LM forms continuous thermal conduction pathways within the aerogel network, thus significantly reduces the intrinsic thermal resistance (3.16 cm2 K W−1) and achieves good in-plane thermal conductivity (1.632 W m−1 K−1). Unlike conventional thermal interface materials, the MCPL enables precise positioning and dynamic adhesion under magnetic regulation, which effectively realizes tunable interfacial thermal conductivity and enhances interfacial affinity. When deployed in LEDs, CPUs, and electrical transformer boxes, the MCPL exhibit controllable thermal conduction behavior, superior heat dissipation capacity and long-term operational stability. This material offers an innovative strategy for intelligent thermal management of electronic devices and facilities.

title: Self-healing glass fiber-reinforced epoxy thermoset with high strength, tear and impact resistance
abstract: Epoxy fiber-reinforced polymers (FRPs) are extensively utilized in high-performance structural parts owing to their outstanding strength and rigidity. Nevertheless, their inherent brittleness and irreparability significantly shorten their service life, especially in demanding environments. Herein, a novel class of epoxy FRPs featuring high strength, enhanced toughness, and self-healing was presented via a dual-network curing design incorporating both rigid and flexible curing agents. Precise tuning of the network structural parameter R yielded well-balanced mechanical attributes, including tensile strength surpassing 400 MPa, tearing energy up to 430 kJ/m2, and healing efficiencies exceeding 90% across multiple damage-healing cycles. Dynamic boronic ester linkages embedded in the matrix enabled molecular rearrangements at elevated temperatures while preserving the thermoset framework. Mechanical evaluations and fracture morphology analyses indicated that an optimal R window (115-250) synergistically enhanced energy dissipation, interfacial bonding, and fiber-matrix stress transfer. This work establishes a design paradigm that harmonizes strength, toughness, and reparability, facilitating the development of durable and maintainable thermosetting composites for advanced structural applications.

title: High-temperature electromagnetic absorption and multi-physics coupling simulation of ceramizable composites
abstract: High-temperature electromagnetic wave absorbing materials are crucial for electromagnetic protection and military stealth. Ceramizable composites are promising candidates for integrating microwave absorption, load-bearing capacity, and thermal protection in multi-field coupling environments; however, their high-temperature electromagnetic response remains poorly understood. This study presents the first systematic investigation of the effects of pretreatment temperature and in situ test temperature on electromagnetic wave absorption of quartz fabric-reinforced phenolic-based ceramizable composites. Experimental results show that increasing pretreatment temperature to 800 °C promotes pore development and heterogeneous interfaces, raising the average X-band reflection loss (RL) from −2 dB to −8 dB. Complete ceramization at 1100 °C forms a stable ZrO2/Al2O3 ceramic skeleton, achieving a minimum RL of −10 dB. For fully ceramized specimens, absorption first improves with test temperature up to 400 °C (RL ≈ −12 dB) due to activated polarization, then declines slightly at 600 °C owing to excessive thermal perturbation. To enable performance prediction, a thermal–chemical–electromagnetic multi-physics coupled simulation framework is established, based on thermogravimetric analysis and reaction kinetics. By mapping reaction progress to complex permittivity, the model successfully predicts RL under various service conditions and reveals parametric sensitivities of thickness, oxygen concentration, and holding time. This work provides a unified experimental and theoretical basis for the design of high-temperature microwave absorption materials.

title: Robust and transparent self-lubricating surface for anti-icing/de-icing via a multiscale puzzle complementary strategy
abstract: Surfaces of renewable energy infrastructure like wind turbine blades and photovoltaic panels are facing severe challenges under harsh service environments such as icing, sandstorms and contaminations. Protective outer coatings with low ice adhesion, superior mechanical durability, and high optical transmittance are urgently needed. Herein, we propose a multiscale puzzle complementary strategy to design transparent and mechanically robust self-lubricating surface (TRSS). The self-lubricating constituent (SLC) that synthesized via a molecular-scale puzzle assembly effect endows the surface with ultralow surface energy to achieve self-lubrication and low ice adhesion. Meanwhile, a macroscale interpenetrating polymer network puzzle via integrating reinforcing constituent and SLC drastically improves the composite's bulk mechanical integrity. The as-prepared TRSS exhibits excellent mechanical robustness, a low friction coefficient, high optical transparency, and outstanding dynamic anti-icing performance. Its remarkable light transmittance minimizes power generation loss when coated on photovoltaic panels, validating its promising applicability in photovoltaic industry. Systematic characterizations reveal that TRSS possesses prominent anti-icing and deicing efficacy with an ice adhesion strength of ∼30 kPa, and exceptional wear resistance where only ∼80 μm thickness loss is observed after 800 cycles of Taber abrasion. Collectively, these comprehensive functional merits establish TRSS as a dependable protective candidate for both aircrafts and renewable energy facilities, possessing great practical significance and broad engineering deployment prospects.

title: Microwave-assisted selective coalescence of PA12/CNT composite particles: coupled electromagnetic–thermal–phase-field modeling and property evolution
abstract: Microwave-assisted sintering offers a route to selectively fuse polymer composite powders, but the particle-scale coupling among electromagnetic absorption, localized heating, melt flow, and coalescence remains unclear. Here, carbon nanotube (CNT)-coated polyamide 12 (PA12) composite particles were prepared by ball milling and investigated through experiments and coupled electromagnetic–thermal–phase-field modeling. Thermal, dielectric, rheological, and thermal transport properties were characterized as model inputs. Hot-stage polarized optical microscopy was used to quantify thermally driven neck growth of particle doublets under spatially uniform heating, enabling calibration of an effective phase-field mobility that was validated in multi-particle assemblies. The CNT-rich coating increased dielectric loss and microwave responsiveness, but also increased melt-flow resistance and delayed neck growth under conventional heating. Under microwave irradiation, electromagnetic energy was preferentially dissipated in CNT-enriched surface and contact regions, generating localized temperature rise, reducing local viscosity, and promoting flow-driven neck growth through electromagnetic–thermal coupling. Prolonged microwave irradiation improved interparticle bonding and promoted the formation of a more continuous conductive network, leading to increased electrical conductivity and tensile modulus. This work clarifies the dual role of CNTs in microwave-assisted selective coalescence and provides a modeling-guided basis for controlling polymer composite powder microwave sintering.

title: Influence of layup configuration on through-thickness thermal conductivity of CFRP composites: Based on effective heat transfer volume theory and predictive modeling
abstract: The thermal performance of carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites is critical for engineering thermal management applications. This study investigates how layup configurations influence through-thickness (Z-direction) thermal conductivity and elucidates the underlying mechanisms. Thermal conductivity was measured using the laser flash method and the transient plane source technique. These measurements were validated through water droplet evaporation experiments and infrared thermal imaging. Cross-ply laminates exhibited higher Z-direction thermal conductivity than unidirectional laminates, with increases of 5.46% in thin specimens and 23.40% in thick specimens. Through finite element analysis (FEA), the regulation of heat flow distribution by carbon fibers in the resin matrix was investigated. Based on these results, the “effective heat transfer volume” concept was proposed for the first time. Specifically, the spatial arrangement and distribution of fibers influence the resin-matrix-dominated heat conduction pathways. At fiber spacings of 1–13 μm, cross-ply and angle-ply layups exhibit higher through-thickness thermal conductivity than unidirectional layups due to an increased effective heat transfer volume. Mathematical models were developed to predict the Z-direction heat flux for unidirectional, cross-ply, and angle-ply (±45°) configurations, based on the thermal conductivities of the carbon fibers and resin matrix as well as the fiber volume fraction. The models demonstrate excellent fit (R2 > 0.98) and high accuracy (errors < ±4%). These findings provide a theoretical foundation and practical guidance for structural optimization of CFRP composites in thermal management, such as electric vehicle battery encapsulation and 5G base station heat dissipation.

title: A closed-loop digital twin for online curing optimization of scarf-repaired composite laminates
abstract: This study develops a proof-of-concept closed-loop digital twin system for online curing optimization of scarf-repaired composite laminates. The system couples a physical entity, including the repaired specimen, in-situ sensors, and hot bonder, with a virtual entity driven by deep-learning surrogate models and multi-objective optimization. Real-time temperature data and adjustable curing parameters are used to predict the final degree of cure and residual stress field. The curing time and maximum von Mises stress are then minimized under a constraint on the final degree of cure. The optimized parameters are written once to the programmable logic controller (PLC) of the hot bonder to modify the subsequent temperature path during repair curing. Comparative experiments were conducted using the manufacturer-recommended cure cycle (MRCC) and the digital-twin-optimized cure cycle. The optimized cycle shortened the curing time from 17,330 s to 11,340 s, corresponding to a reduction of 34.6%. The residual strain at the center of the patch top surface was 934με in the MRCC experiment and averaged −221με across the four DT experiments, corresponding to a 76.3% reduction in strain magnitude. Across the four DT experiments, the average final DoC values at the top and bottom sampling locations of the repair patches were 99.28 ± 1.44% and 95.03 ± 6.17%, respectively, with a minimum bottom-surface DoC of 87.30%. In-situ strain measurements at the scarf interface further demonstrate the value of incorporating in-situ sensing and feedback execution into repair curing.

title: Physically-based strain criteria for mixed mode fracture and fatigue thresholds in orthotropic composite laminates
abstract: This study proposes a strain-based framework for predicting mixed mode fracture and fatigue threshold in orthotropic composite laminates. By analyzing the stress field at the crack tip and combining constitutive relations and compatibility conditions, maximum principal strain (MPε) and maximum shear strain (MSε) criteria for static crack initiation prediction are established. By introducing the anisotropy of the critical fracture distance, r-related criterion forms (r-MPε and r-MSε) that reflect both material anisotropy and characteristic damage length are obtained. Notably, the proposed criteria can not only perform forward predictions but also identify unknown parameters inversely and support model construction with limited experimental data. Furthermore, inspired by the evolution of the cohesive model, the proposed static fracture criterion is extended to the fatigue threshold prediction by assuming a similarity between the static fracture envelope and the fatigue threshold envelope. This enables the prediction of the fatigue delamination threshold under different stress ratios and mixed mode ratios. The proposed model has been validated using experimental results from different composite systems. The results show good agreement between the model and experimental results and demonstrate its ability to link fracture behavior to underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, a dimensionless parameter is introduced to characterize the combined effects of elastic anisotropy and fracture toughness. This parameter acts as a unified indicator for the occurrence of major failure mechanisms and overshoot phenomena.
