The proposed framework provides a physically meaningful and unified method for assessing mixed mode fracture and predicting fatigue life in composite structures.

title: Deep learning-assisted damage characterization in non-crimp fabric composites
abstract: Recent advancements in deep learning offer considerable potential for automated composite damage recognition. However, limited annotated datasets and complex material microstructures challenge pixel-level characterization of local damage mechanisms, while existing approaches provide limited integration of segmentation outputs with quantitative damage assessment. A deep learning-based convolutional neural network was integrated with digital imaging and automated crack counting algorithms to characterize damage in unidirectional non-crimp fabric glass fiber-reinforced reactive thermoplastic cross-ply laminates. Microscopic images of damage-containing material samples obtained in previous work were preprocessed and annotated with six feature-related classes for model training and testing. A U-Net architecture incorporating skip connections, dropout, and a weighted Dice loss function was employed to segment material features and damage. Results showed that smaller batch sizes produced the lowest weighted Dice loss and the highest Dice coefficients. Notably, the Dice coefficient improved significantly from ∼0.736 with equal class weights to ∼0.840 with optimized class weights, representing a 14.1% increase in the prediction accuracy of 90° tow cracks (the dominant damage mechanism). A controlled factorial ablation study further evaluated key model components across eight configurations and three random seeds. Removing skip connections from the full model reduced the mean Dice coefficient by approximately 51.6%, demonstrating their importance for multi-class segmentation. The trained model demonstrated a strong capability to identify damage initiation, progression, and interaction, and was integrated with automated crack counting algorithms for quantitative damage assessment. The resulting damage metrics could support analytical damage-mechanics models for predicting stiffness degradation and informing structural health monitoring and maintenance planning.

title: Fabrication of B,N-doped hollow carbon nanospheres/ MXene composite hydrogel for high-Performance microwave absorption
abstract: With the increasing severity of electromagnetic pollution and the limitations of conventional shielding technologies, microwave absorbing materials have attracted significant attention for their efficient conversion of electromagnetic energy into heat. In this work, boron/nitrogen-doped hollow carbon nanospheres (B,N-CNs) were prepared by oxidation polymerization. Subsequently, the B,N-CNs were loaded on MXene and incorporated into a polyurethane (PU) hydrogel matrix to fabricate a B,N-CNs/MXene/PU gel composite absorber. The synergistic combination of the high electrical conductivity of MXene and the hollow structure of B,N-CNs generates abundant heterogeneous interfaces, facilitating multiple polarization processes and enhanced electromagnetic wave attenuation. Moreover, B,N co-doping introduces abundant defects and heteroatomic sites, which strengthens defect-induced dielectric loss while optimizing impedance matching. Benefiting from this multi-component and multi-scale structural design, the B,N-CNs/MXene/PU gel exhibits improved microwave absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of −41.4 dB at 8.8 GHz, along with an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 2.5 GHz at a thickness of 2.5 mm. Furthermore, the incorporation of B,N-CNs significantly reinforces tensile properties of the composite, with the elongation at break increasing from 790% for MXene/PU gel to 1125% for B,N-CNs/MXene/PU gel.

title: Multiscale design of PEEK/MXene@Ni composites from microscale segregated network to macroscale non-gradient multilayer for ultra-broadband electromagnetic wave absorption
abstract: Broadband and strong absorption properties are desirable characteristics for electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorbing materials; however, simultaneously achieving both broad bandwidth and strong absorption remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a multiscale structural design strategy that integrates a microscale segregated network with a macroscale non-gradient multilayer structure. Typically, negatively charged MXene@Ni nanosheets were electrostatically assembled onto the surface of polyether ether ketone (PEEK) and subsequently hot-pressed to form the single-layer PEEK/MXene@Ni (PMN) composites with microscale segregated conductive network. At 5 wt% filler loading, the PMN composite achieved a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of −43.77 dB and a maximum effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 3.84 GHz due to the interfacial polarization and multiple reflection effects in the segregated network. To further broaden the EAB, an impedance matching-guided multilayer engineering was employed to develop the non-gradient multi-layer structure at the macroscale. Accordingly, the four-layer non-gradient composite (NG-4) exhibited an RLmin of −68.23 dB and a maximum EAB as high as 10.56 GHz. This exceptional performance is mainly attributed to the synergistic effect of impedance matching for EMW penetration and cascade dissipation through the multi-layer structure. Therefore, this multiscale design, ranging from microscale segregated networks to macroscale multilayer structures, provides a promising new pathway toward broadband and high-efficiency EMW absorbing materials.

title: Eco-friendly chitosan-derived carbon/cobalt composite aerogels with integrated electromagnetic wave absorption, radar stealth and thermal insulation properties
abstract: Chitosan-derived carbon aerogels have attracted significant attention in the field of electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorption due to their lightweight characteristic, simple preparation process and three-dimensional (3D) porous structure. However, the traditional manufacturing process still encounters numerous challenges in fabricating chitosan-derived carbon aerogels as multifunctional EMW absorbers. This highlights the necessity of developing simple and structurally sophisticated strategies. In this work, chitosan-derived carbon/cobalt (CDC/Co) composite aerogels with the low bulk density (42−57.2 mg/cm3) were prepared through a three-step method of physical crosslinking, freeze casting and high-temperature carbonization. The research results showed that the obtained binary composite aerogels had a unique 3D porous network structure, and numerous cobalt particles were grown in situ and distributed on the surface of the carbon framework. Furthermore, the abundant CDC/Co heterogeneous interfaces could induce the interfacial polarization under the alternating electromagnetic fields, thereby endowing CDC/Co composite aerogel with excellent EMW absorption performance. Significantly, the CDC/Co composite aerogel with the addition amount of cobalt salt of 0.4 mmol and a filling ratio of 10 wt% achieved the minimum reflection loss of −48.20 dB at a matching thickness of 3.34 mm and the maximum effective absorption bandwidth of 6.88 GHz under a thin thickness of 2.26 mm. Additionally, the CDC/Co composite aerogel also exhibited superior radar stealth and thermal insulation properties. Therefore, this study provides a new idea for the development of biomass chitosan-derived carbon-based composite aerogels as multifunctional EMW absorbers.

title: Mechanistic correlation between fiber-specific plasma activation and load transfer in hybrid 3D braided carbon fiber/epoxy vinyl ester composites
abstract: Hybrid 3D braided composites composed of high-strength T800 and high-modulus M55 carbon fibers must simultaneously coordinate stiffness utilization, strain mismatch, interface-mediated load transfer, and fiber integrity during surface activation. In this study, T800/M55 hybrid 3D five-directional braided composites with an epoxy vinyl ester resin matrix were investigated by integrating periodic unit-cell screening, fiber-specific plasma treatment, multiscale surface characterization, single-filament breaking-load and Weibull analyses, unidirectional short-beam shear (SBS) screening, and multi-mode mechanical validation. Model-guided screening showed that the M55 axial yarn/T800 braiding yarn configuration (H3) provided a favorable balance between axial stiffness gain and stress localization. Moderate T800-O2-4 min and M55-N2-3 min treatments each retained approximately 91% of the untreated mean single-filament breaking load, whereas prolonged treatment reduced load retention and/or Weibull statistical uniformity. These two controlled activation windows also maximized the SBS responses of the corresponding unidirectional composites. After these treatment windows were applied to H3, the mean values of SBS strength, flexural strength, tensile modulus, failure strain, and compressive strength increased, whereas the mean flexural modulus decreased. Fracture morphology progressively changed from clean fiber pull-out and interfacial debonding to greater resin coverage, matrix tearing, and mixed interfacial/cohesive fracture. These results reveal the competition between interfacial activation benefits and treatment-induced fiber degradation and establish an architecture–activation–load-transfer correlation in hybrid textile composites.
keywords: Hybrid 3D braided carbon fiber/epoxy vinyl ester composites

title: Harnessing the synergistic dielectric and magnetic loss in polypyrrole based nanocomposites for improving the EMI shielding behaviour in X-band
abstract: Polypyrrole-NiFe2O4-CaCu3Ti4O12 (PNC) nanocomposites are prepared via in-situ chemical oxidative polymerization. In this process, the weight ratio of pyrrole monomer and NiFe2O4 (NFO) is fixed to 1:1 whereas the concentration of CaCu3Ti4O12 (CCTO) is varied from 0 to 1 by weight fraction in the step size of 0.25 to study the influence of dielectric filler incorporation on electromagnetic shielding effectiveness of polymer-based nanocomposites in X-band. XRD and FTIR confirms the successful formation of a multi-phase nanocomposite structure. FESEM imaging reveals increased porosity and surface roughness with increasing CCTO content. Further, microscopic studies confirm the formation of cage-like structures where the nanofillers are attached with the polymeric chain. The nanocomposites exhibit ohmic electrical behaviour with DC conductivity of ∼0.2 S cm−1, and ferrimagnetic behaviour with a coercivity ∼330 Oe for PNC1. The electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding observations emphasis on enhanced absorption tendency of the nanocomposites with the inclusion of CCTO. The highest shielding effectiveness (SE) value is achieved for PNC1 (1 wt % of both nanofillers) ∼38 dB with absorption contribution ∼32 dB along with absorption efficiency ∼99.7%. Microwave dielectric analysis shows a significant increase in relative permittivity (εr) ∼ 65 and attenuation coefficient (α) ∼ 800 Np/m with CCTO loading. Reflection loss (RL) studies further confirm the microwave absorption capability of PNC1, which is approximately −10 dB. The synergistic contribution of dielectric and magnetic losses in PNC nanocomposites corresponds to superior EMI shielding performance, which could be useful in electronic, defence, communication, and aerospace applications.
keywords: Eddy current loss and EMI shielding

title: Coupled framework of machine learning and finite element for developing the outstanding carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites are crucial to manufacture the high load-bearing structures with lightweight, yet their mechanical performance depends on interacting design variables, such as fiber fraction, shape, and length. These factors are usually determined through expensive testing and simulations that require high computational cost and even induce an ultrahigh challenge. In this work, we introduce a coupled framework of machine learning (ML) and finite element method (FEM) to both predict and inversely design the mechanical properties under transverse and longitudinal tensile loading. FEM was used to generate a broad design-response space, and generative adversarial networks (GAN) were employed to augment the dataset to improve coverage, and mutual-information-based selection identified the most informative features. The trained ML regressor achieved high accuracy (R2 ≥ 0.9912) and showed strong agreement with independent experimental data. Model interpretability via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) reveals that Young's modulus is governed primarily by the volume fraction, followed by shape and length of fiber, providing the design-relevant insights rather than black-box fits. In addition to forward mechanical property prediction, Bayesian optimization (BO) is coupled with the trained machine learning model to implement target-driven inverse microstructural design. The resulting optimal microstructural candidates were further validated via FEM simulation. The findings indicate that the FEM-GAN-ML-BO framework is capable of efficiently forecasting, analyzing, and inversely designing CFRP composites. This framework minimizes the necessity for extensive experimental trials and large-scale numerical simulations, thereby aiding the advancement of high-performance composite materials for engineering purposes.

title: A focus on the agglomerates of nanodiamond surrounded by interphase zone to simulate the tensile modulus of polymer composites
abstract: Despite the presence of nanodiamond (ND) agglomeration in composites, this critical factor has been unnoticed in prior models predicting the tensile modulus of ND-filled systems. In the present study, the properties of agglomerates and their surrounding interphase are incorporated to state a predictive expression for the Young's modulus in the ND-reinforced samples. The operative volume share of reinforcement (ϕeff) is defined by agglomerate radius (Ragg), ND size, and the interphase thickness (t). Notably, ϕeff reaches a maximum value of 0.55 at ND radius of 5 nm (indicating no agglomeration), but significantly decreases to 0.015 at Ragg = 50 nm, indicating that larger agglomerates cause the least reinforcement. The nanocomposite modulus exhibits a 420% enhancement at Ragg = 10 nm; however, further increases in agglomerate size markedly reduce stiffness. Similarly, a 300% increase in modulus is attained at t = 20 nm, whereas thinner interphases lead to diminished reinforcement. A stiffer interphase also improves mechanical performance; 215% enhancement in the stiffness is seen at an interphase modulus of 30 GPa. In contrast, a lower interphase modulus of 5 GPa induces only a marginal 35% improvement of nanocomposite modulus. The proposed model substantially overestimates the modulus when assuming well-dispersed NDs, but accurately predicts the stiffness of real composites containing agglomerated NDs.

title: Experimental characterisation and damage-based modelling of 3D-printed continuous carbon-fibre-reinforced nylon laminates under tensile and shear-dominated loading
abstract: This study develops and experimentally validates a computationally efficient finite element model for predicting the mechanical response of 3D-printed continuous carbon-fibre-reinforced nylon laminates under tensile and shear-dominated loading conditions. The printed composite is represented within an equivalent single-layer formulation using homogenised theoretical plies. The constitutive formulation accounts explicitly for nonlinear transverse tensile and in-plane shear behaviour. Damage initiation is evaluated using the Hashin criterion. Depending on the identified failure mechanism, selective degradation of the relevant stiffness components is applied. For matrix-dominated failure modes, the formulation further distinguishes between transverse-tension- and shear-dominated failure and employs an additional strain-threshold criterion to govern degradation activation. Linear elastic, nonlinear constitutive and damage-related material parameters were identified from tensile tests on [0°] 4 , [90°] 4 and balanced [45°/-45°] s laminates. The parameter governing mixed transverse-tension/shear matrix failure was calibrated using the [45°] 4 configuration. The model was validated without further parameter adjustment using [0°/90°] s , [15°/-75°] s and [30°/-60°] s tensile and V-notched Iosipescu specimens. The consistency of the in-plane shear modulus identified from the balanced [45°/-45°] s laminate was verified using the [45°] 4 and V-notched Iosipescu configurations. Mechanical extensometers, strain gauges and digital image correlation provided the global stress-strain responses and local strain fields used for model identification and validation, confirming that characterisation procedures commonly employed for conventional composite laminates remain applicable to the investigated 3D-printed material. Compared with the built-in Abaqus Hashin damage model incorporating the experimentally observed nonlinear transverse-tension and in-plane shear constitutive relations, the proposed formulation provided more accurate predictions of the mechanical response of the investigated laminates.

title: Cellulose nanocrystals-regulated core-shell fibrous films for synergistic radiative cooling and phase change thermal management
abstract: Thermal comfort is increasingly challenged by heat waves and abrupt temperature fluctuations, requiring materials that dissipate heat while buffering thermal shocks. Existing combinations of radiative cooling and phase change systems are often achieved by stacking or mixing components, leaving structural design and performance regulation largely independent, which limits the mutual reinforcement of steady cooling and transient thermal regulation. Herein, we employ coaxial electrospinning to construct a core-shell fibrous film composed of polyethylene glycol@poly (vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene)/cellulose nanocrystals (PEG@PVDF-HFP/CNCs) for the synergistic regulation of radiative cooling and phase change performance. The shell achieves 94.91% solar reflectivity (0.3-2.5 μm) and 97.56% infrared emissivity (8-13 μm), while the core provides high thermal shock resistance with a phase change enthalpy of 47.3 J g−1. Crucially, CNCs enhance radiative cooling by optimizing structural scale and optical parameters, while simultaneously improving phase change thermal regulation by inducing PEG crystallization to enhance latent heat storage, achieving synergistic enhancement of both functions within the same material system. Outdoor measurements demonstrate a steady-state temperature reduction of 10.5°C together with effective buffering against abrupt ambient temperature fluctuations. This work achieves synergistic optimization of radiative cooling and phase change performance within one system, providing a novel pathway for thermal comfort regulation under dynamic environments.

title: Thickness-constrained PMIA nanofiber interlayers enabling integrated interlaminar toughening and in situ resistance-based delamination monitoring of CFRP laminates
abstract: Interlaminar delamination and integrated sensing remain challenges for carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates, particularly when functional interlayers must remain sufficiently thin and permeable for liquid-resin infusion. Here, poly(m-phenylene isophthalamide) (PMIA) nanofiber interlayers were incorporated into CFRP laminates fabricated by vacuum-assisted resin transfer molding. The mechanical response exhibited a property-dependent thickness effect rather than a universal optimum. PMIA-4 (∼24 μm) provided the highest Mode I fracture toughness and interlaminar shear strength, PMIA-8 (∼42 μm) achieved the highest Mode II fracture toughness, and PMIA-3 (∼18 μm) showed the most favorable in-plane response. At greater thickness, incomplete resin impregnation progressively offset the nanofiber-mediated toughening mechanisms. An electrically insulated PMIA-CNT-PMIA sensing interlayer (∼60-70 μm) was subsequently constructed by encapsulating a CNT-decorated PMIA membrane between two insulating PMIA membranes. The sensing architecture produced a mechanical trade-off: Mode I initiation and Mode II fracture toughness were higher than the Control mean values, Mode I propagation and flexural properties remained close to the Control, and moderate reductions occurred in interlaminar shear and tensile properties. Tensile and three-point-bending tests demonstrated a gauge factor of 7.1, repeatable resistance tracking over ten loading-unloading cycles, and opposite response polarities under tension and compression. During synchronized Mode I DCB tests on five valid specimens, abrupt resistance changes exhibited clear temporal correspondence with discrete crack-growth events and qualitatively tracked acoustic-emission activity, with the overall normalized resistance change ranging from 161.1% to 188.9%. These results establish a thickness-dependent strategy for balancing interlaminar performance and resistance-based Mode I delamination indication at a single instrumented interface.

title: Decoupling sensitivity–hysteresis trade-offs in printed ternary carbon nanocomposite sensors for human–machine interfaces
abstract: Stretchable strain sensors are central to wearable human–machine interfaces and smart rehabilitation systems, while they are limited by the intrinsic trade-offs among mechanical compliance, sensing range, and electrical hysteresis. In this work, we overcome this limitation by developing a screen-printable strain sensor enabled by dynamically reconfigurable ternary carbon nanocomposite conductive networks, comprising carbon black, carbon nanotubes, and lubricated carbon grease within a silicone matrix. The hybrid architecture introduces a sliding-percolation mechanism, where conductive pathways undergo reversible reconstruction under strain, enabling simultaneous suppression of electrical hysteresis and preservation of electrical continuity at large deformation. As a result, the sensor achieves a strain range of 200%, low electrical hysteresis, rapid response within 80 ms, a moderate gauge factor, and excellent cyclic durability. The strain sensors are further integrated into a smart glove system to enable remote control of a robotic hand. When deployed on a lower-limb rehabilitation platform, they can support motion-intent prediction for active rehabilitation in combination with a deep-learning model. This work demonstrates a screen-printing manufacturing strategy that reconciles robustness, sensitivity, and scalability through synergistic conductive networks, providing a practical route toward high-performance stretchable strain sensors for wearable human–machine interaction.

title: Development and experimental validation of strain rate-dependent failure criteria for unidirectional non-crimp fabric composites
abstract: In this study, two invariant-based failure criteria are proposed to predict failure of a unidirectional non-crimp fabric (UD-NCF) carbon fiber/epoxy composite. Three different failure modes, namely matrix failure, fiber tensile failure, and fiber compressive failure, are considered. The matrix failure functions are based on linear and quadratic transversely isotropic stress-invariants, while fiber failure is evaluated with a maximum stress criterion for tension and an adapted kinking criterion for compression. The main advantages of the invariant-based criteria are fewer required experiments for calibration and minimal computational effort in comparison with fracture plane-based criteria. Moreover, the chosen mathematical formulation ensures a non-negative Hessian and decoupled tensile and compressive behaviour. Furthermore, the strain rate dependency of the investigated UD-NCF composite is incorporated using empirical relations defined in previous work by the authors. For validation purposes, off-axis tests are performed at quasi-static and high strain rates. Overall, the observed agreement with experimental data presented here as well as from literature is excellent, highlighting the feasibility of the proposed criteria for design of UD-NCF composite structures.

title: MOF-on-MOF-derived GC/Co@CNTs with multiscale heterostructures for enhanced microwave absorption
abstract: Metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived electromagnetic wave absorption have attracted considerable interest because of their tunable composition, rich porosity, and structural versatility. However, conventional single-MOF-derived materials often have limited metallic components and single-dimensional structures, which hinder the simultaneous optimization of electromagnetic wave absorption performance. In this work, a ZIF-L@ZIF-67 precursor with a MOF-on-MOF architecture was designed. Through high-temperature pyrolysis, it was converted into Graphitized carbon/Co nanoparticles@carbon nanotubes (GC/Co@CNTs) composites composed of two-dimensional graphitized carbon, one-dimensional carbon nanotubes, and zero-dimensional Co nanoparticles. By tuning the pyrolysis temperature, the magnetic-dielectric response of the materials was effectively regulated. The minimum reflection loss reached −69.4 dB at a thickness of 1.85 mm, while an effective absorption bandwidth of 6.04 GHz at a thickness of 2.00 mm was obtained at 800 °C. During pyrolysis, the in-situ formation of a conductive carbon network, magnetic Co nanoparticles, and abundant heterogeneous interfaces synergistically promoted conduction loss, magnetic loss, and interfacial polarization. As a result, the electromagnetic attenuation capability of the composites was significantly improved. This study highlights the considerable promise of MOF-on-MOF-derived architectures for electromagnetic wave absorption and offers a viable structural engineering strategy for the development of next-generation microwave absorbers.

title: Dimension-dependent interfacial reinforcement mechanisms of carbon nanomaterials in CF/PI composites
abstract: To investigate the intrinsic relationship between the dimensional characteristics of carbon nanomaterials and the interfacial reinforcement mechanisms in carbon fiber/polyimide (CF/PI) composites, this study employed C60, graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to modify the PI matrix. By integrating microbond testing with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the mechanisms by which carbon nanomaterials with different dimensional structures regulate the interfacial structure and properties of CF/PI composites under external loading were systematically investigated. The experimental results show significant differences in the reinforcing effects of the three types of nanomaterials. Among them, the CNT-modified samples exhibited the most pronounced interfacial strengthening effect, achieving an interface shear strength of 136.46 MPa at a CNT loading of 0.5 wt%, corresponding to a 20.07% improvement compared with the pure-PI. In contrast, the C60 and GNP modified samples showed only limited enhancement at relatively low filler loadings. Fracture morphology analysis further demonstrated distinct CNT pull-out in the CNT-modified samples, accompanied by a transition in the failure mode from interfacial debonding to a coupled interface-matrix cooperative failure mechanism. The MD simulation results further elucidate the fundamental interfacial interaction mechanisms associated with nanomaterials of different dimensions. Benefiting from their one-dimensional high-aspect-ratio structure of CNTs, they can form a continuous bridging network within the interfacial region. Even under conditions where molecular chain mobility is restricted in high-temperature resin systems, CNTs can still effectively induce orientation, stretching, and partial disentanglement of PI molecular chains, while simultaneously introducing multiple energy dissipation mechanisms during interfacial failure.

title: Photothermal synergistic network and interphase regulation for thermoreversible carbon fiber-reinforced vitrimer composites
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites (CFRPs) are limited by the intrinsic brittleness of thermosetting resins and irreversible performance loss after damage. To address these challenges, a vitrimer containing β-hydroxyl ester linkages was designed based on epoxy acrylate resins and applied to photocurable resin and composite systems. A dual-curing strategy combining photocuring and thermal activation was developed to enable rapid room-temperature shaping and subsequent dynamic network activation. Considering the strong light absorption of carbon fibers, a hybrid ultraviolet and near-infrared curing approach integrated with filament winding was developed. This method enabled the fabrication of carbon fiber reinforced vitrimer composites with tailored interfacial structures and excellent mechanical properties. With vinyl ester sizing, the composites achieved a low porosity of 3.14 vol% and a high interlaminar shear strength of 51.4 MPa. The tensile strength and modulus reached 1686 MPa and 89.1 GPa respectively. During thermal activation, transesterification within the vitrimer matrix enhanced interfacial reconfigurability and enabled recovery of interfacial performance after cyclic loading. Further improvement was achieved with prolonged heating, with the ILSS increasing from 51.4 MPa in the pristine composite to 61.9 MPa after thermal healing, corresponding to an effective recovery of interfacial mechanical performance. The photocured network and thermally induced interfacial reconstruction synergistically regulated interfacial evolution. As a result, simultaneous interfacial reconstruction and performance recovery were achieved while providing a route toward recyclable and repairable carbon fiber composites.

title: High-temperature interface ageing of quartz fiber reinforced polyimide composites
abstract: Quartz fiber (QF) reinforced polyimide (PI) composites are highly desired for advanced aerospace applications, yet their long-term durability is severely constrained by high-temperature interfacial degradation. The underlying mechanisms, particularly the thermo-chemical role of the ubiquitous fiber sizing, remain a critical but unresolved issue. Here, through a joint study of an in-situ single-fiber push-out tests and reactive molecular dynamics simulations, the macroscopic-to-atomistic thermal deterioration behaviors of QF/PI composite interface were identified. The results show that complete sizing removal severely weakens the interface, whereas the water-washing strategy effectively mitigates early-stage physical damage, enabling an ∼85% retention of the interfacial shear strength at 300 °C for 80 h. However, upon exposure to 400 °C, the composite interfaces inevitably suffer a drastic strength drop and mechanical embrittlement. A temperature-dependent, two-stage interfacial degradation mechanism was revealed: (1) at moderate temperatures, additive volatilization triggers massive nano-void nucleation, which reduces the effective interfacial contact area; and (2) at temperatures near or above the peak decomposition temperature, the intrinsic pyrolysis of epoxy sizing transforms the cross-linked epoxy into porous char-like carbon clusters, and thus significantly weakens the interfacial interactions.

title: Core-shell structured nanocomposite microspheres for phase-adaptive burn wound treatment
abstract: Effective whole-cycle management of burn wounds remains a major challenge for modern dressings due to the need for simultaneous control of exudation, inflammation, infection, and tissue regeneration. Here, we designed and developed core–shell structured nanocomposite microspheres powder (PCSM) with spatiotemporal responsiveness to address the multifaceted therapeutic challenges arise at different stages of burn wound healing. Polyacrylamide (PA) microspheres were coupled with sodium alginate (SA) to create a core-shell structured nanocomposite powder through calcium-mediated crosslinking. The shell of the nanocomposite microspheres was further functionalized by incorporating polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)-decorated magnesium silicide (MNP), allowing hydrogen (H2) release in situ. The resulting microspheres, namely PCSM, can easily fills irregular wound surface, absorbs exudate, enable self-gelation, promotes coagulation. As exudate diffuses from the shell to the core, the embedded MNP is progressively activated, enabling sustained H2 release for up to 14 days to mitigate inflammation. This design not only manages exudate across the healing cycle but also uses it as a biological trigger for on-demand H2 generation, enabling personalized treatment of inflammatory burn wounds. Concurrently, Mg2+ and Si4+ ions released from MNP act with H2 to enhance cell migration and angiogenesis during tissue regeneration. During the skin remodeling stage, excessive exudate uptake weakens the interaction between microspheres, allowing PCSM to disintegration for painless detachment. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo evaluations demonstrate that PCSM provides a distinct spatiotemporal therapeutic response, enabling phase-adapted treatment that accelerates burn wound healing and underscoring its promise for clinical application.

title: Influence of fiber orientation on self-heating during fatigue of polymer matrix composites under low and ultrasonic cyclic frequencies
abstract: This work compares self-heating and its influence on fatigue strength and life of a quasi-isotropic CF-PAEK laminate with that of an orthotropic CF-PEKK laminate using thermographic approaches at low ( ≤ 40 Hz) and ultrasonic frequencies ( ≈ 20 kHz). The fatigue strengths were found to be approximately 47.9 MPa for CF-PAEK and 50.0 MPa for CF-PEKK at a low frequency of 40 Hz. At a cyclic frequency of 20 kHz, fatigue strength decreased by approximately 12% and 16%, respectively, reaching a value of 42 MPa for the CF-PAEK and CF-PEKK laminates. The total heat dissipation rates escalated from an order of magnitude of 10 5 J m − 3 s −1 at low to about 1 0 6 J m − 3 s − 1 at ultrasonic frequencies. A critical aspect of this work is the separation of damage-related heat dissipation rate from reversible internal friction in order to use it as a reliable physical indicator to characterize self-heating in polymer matrix composites (PMCs). The damage-related heat dissipation rate was higher for the CF-PAEK laminate under low frequency cyclic loading, leading to shorter fatigue lives in the high-cycle fatigue regime. In the very high-cycle fatigue regime, comparable damage-related heat dissipation rates between CF-PAEK and CF-PEKK laminates lead to comparable fatigue lives. These results, alongside literature data on the self-heating of PMCs with different fiber orientations, show that a major portion of the self-heating temperature rise associated with high heat-dissipation rates for off-axis fiber orientations under shear-dominated loading can be primarily attributed to contributions from internal friction.

title: Orientating graphene flakes in nanocomposites using rotating magnetic field and orientation evolution modeling
abstract: The orientation of 2D flakes in nanocomposites is of great value in determining the properties of nanocomposites, but their controlling and modeling are more difficult than those of microscale fillers therefore still remain challenging. External magnetic fields have been previously used to control the orientation of 2D materials in composites, but they only aligns flakes axially (only one degree of freedom constrained) instead of to an in-plane orientation state. Moreover, the evolution of orientation distribution of 2D materials during the orientating process has still been understood only empirically and phenomenologically, while a thorough understanding is needed to direct future manufacturing of nanocomposites. Herein, we present a rotating magnetic field (RMF) to orientate pre-magnetized graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) to achieve an in-plane orientation in nanocomposites and a dynamic orientation model is developed to describe and parameterize the orientation evolution of 2D flakes in nanocomposites. Mechanical properties of the magnetically controlled nanocomposites outperform those of uncontrolled ones, where the modulus of nanocomposites with high filler contents increased by ∼10%, the tensile strength and toughness increased by ∼50% and ∼250%, respectively. The theoretical model based on the probability density function starts from single flakes and follows through to cover a large number of flakes in nanocomposites. It is validated by the agreement with experimental results obtained using wide-angle X-ray scattering. The technique of using RMF and the orientation modeling are demonstrated to be powerful in controlling and understanding the orientation of 2D materials, which is crucial in improving the properties of their nanocomposites.

title: Laser-induced graphene architectures from MXene-PASS precursors for synergistic interfacial and functional enhancement of carbon fiber composites
abstract: Interfacial modification is key to enabling composites to meet the growing demand for structural-functional integration. This study introduces an innovative approach that uses an MXene-poly(arylene sulfide sulfone) (MXene-PASS) precursor to rapidly induce the in-situ formation of a high-quality, uniform porous graphene structure on carbon fiber (CF) surface, which greatly improves the interfacial and mechanical properties of the composites while also improving its electromagnetic interference shielding performance. A small amount of MXene enables the gradual release of concentrated energy, allowing gentle carbonization of PASS and preserving abundant high-quality graphene structures on the carbon fiber by limiting consumption of the resin-derived carbon source. This graphene architecture establishes a graded interfacial transition layer between fiber and resin through strong mechanical interlocking and chemical interactions, acting as an efficient load-transfer bridge. Its porous structure facilitates stress dispersion and extends crack propagation paths. The resulting composite exhibits a tensile strength of 508.8 MPa, an interfacial shear strength (IFSS) of 98.1 MPa, and an interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) of 52.7 MPa-improvements of 36.2%, 82.7%, and 168.9%, respectively, over composites based on desized carbon fiber. Moreover, the high-quality porous graphene network interconnects carbon fibers within the composite, forming a three-dimensional conductive pathway that provides electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding effectiveness exceeding 40 dB across the X-band. This interfacial modification strategy opens a new avenue toward the rapid development of structural-functional integrated composites and provides valuable insights for the industrial implementation of interfacial modification technologies.

title: Editorial Board
Quantitative X-ray tomography and deep learning analysis of damage topology in impact-loaded 3D-printed Bouligand composites
abstract: It is well known that Bouligand structures derive their impact tolerance from low-pitch helicoidal fibre architectures that steer cracks and regulate damage growth. This study examines the low-velocity impact response of continuous aramid fibre-reinforced nylon composites manufactured by dual-extrusion fused filament fabrication (FFF) with pitch angles of 5°, 10°, 20°, and 45°. Instrumented impact testing is combined with post-mortem high-resolution X-ray computed tomography (XCT) to characterise how pitch angle influences impact response and damage topology. In particular, we use a DNN-assisted segmentation framework to classify through-thickness cracking, delamination, and filament fracture. While previous studies have demonstrated the beneficial influence of low-pitch Bouligand architectures on impact resistance, the present work provides volumetric quantification of intralaminar cracking, delamination, and filament fracture within continuous-fibre FFF Bouligand structures, revealing how their interaction evolves with pitch angle. The results show that the lowest-pitch laminate exhibits the highest peak load and absorbed energy, while low-pitch architectures also promote more distributed damage and suppress filament fracture.

title: Asymmetric filler engineering of PVDF nanocomposites for high-energy-storage density via synergistic MXene/Al2O3 hybrids
abstract: Traditional polymer-based dielectric energy storage materials are typically limited by the compromise between low dielectric permittivity and inadequate breakdown strength. This trade-off represents a major bottleneck that severely restricts the enhancement of energy storage performance. In this work, we introduced a ternary composite design that synergistically integrates two-dimensional MXene nanosheets and insulating Al2O3 nanoparticles into a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) matrix. In this structure, the MXene component induces strong interfacial polarization, significantly enhancing the effective dielectric constant, while the Al2O3 filler acts as a nanoscale barrier, inhibiting charge injection and leakage conduction, thereby maintaining high breakdown strength. With a low filler loading of 0.2 wt%, the film demonstrated a dielectric permittivity of 18.15 and a dielectric loss of 0.028. Moreover, the breakdown strength attained 124% of that measured for pure PVDF, and the maximum discharge energy density increased to 4.76 J/cm3. This design provides a novel route for energy storage utilizing advanced dielectric materials.

title: Revealing the effect of damage interaction on the compressive behavior of Double-Double laminates under double low-velocity impacts
abstract: Double-Double (DD) laminates have recently received attention as a flexible alternative to conventional quadriaxial (Quad) laminates for stiffness tailoring and lightweight composite design. However, their damage evolution and underlying mechanisms during multiple impact events and subsequent compression after impact (CAI) have not been fully elucidated. This paper investigated the effect of distance between impact positions (DBIP) on damage interaction, buckling evolution, and residual compressive performance in quadriaxial laminates and their in-plane stiffness-equivalent DD laminates under double impacts. Ultrasonic C-scan, three-dimensional digital image correlation, and strain monitoring techniques were combined to characterize the damage morphology, out-of-plane deformation, and failure modes. Results showed that the DD laminates outperformed the Quad laminates in impact resistance, exhibiting a higher delamination initiation threshold, shallower dent depth, and up to a 32.3% reduction in delamination area. Furthermore, increasing the DBIP reduced the interaction between adjacent damage zones, delayed local buckling, and shifted the failure mode from localized damage-driven instability toward more stable global buckling. These findings provide a reference for the damage-tolerant design of lightweight composite structures.

title: Interfacial engineering of graphene-reinforced NBR composites via SDS: Molecular dynamics insights into structural transformation and enhanced mechanical performance
abstract: Advanced graphene (Gr) and its derivatives hold considerable promise for enhancing the mechanical performance of nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR). However, the graphene-reinforced NBR chronically suffers from the agglomeration tendency of functionalized Gr, as well as the insufficient mechanism understanding of Gr-NBR interfacial interactions, thus resulting in limited interfacial stress transfer and hindering the rational structural design of high-performance Gr-NBR nanocomposites. In this context, we demonstrate a multicomponent graphene-reinforced NBR composite through facile and scalable mechanical delamination and blending methods. Specifically, the sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) is employed to promote the dispersion of Gr in NBR via non-covalent interactions. Concurrently, the carbon black (CB) is embedded onto the surface of Gr@SDS nanosheets to form hybrid clusters, thereby promoting the uniform stress distribution. The influence of SDS incorporation on interfacial interactions of Gr-NBR is systematically elucidated through molecular dynamics simulations, revealing the interfacial binding energy, as well as the compactness and conformational dynamics of polymer chains. The as-achieved Gr@SDS/CB-NBR composites deliver the maximum tensile strength of 19.93 ± 0.61 MPa and elongation at break of 537.51 ± 15.22%, demonstrating a remarkable 40.95% increase in tensile strength compared to the Gr/CB-NBR composite. Molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that the enhanced mechanical properties originate from an SDS-induced structural transformation from compact multilayer adsorption to a loosely packed arrangement, enabling simultaneous interfacial strengthening and ductility retention. This work provides molecular-scale insights into high-performance rubber nanocomposites.

title: Bridge-coupled multitask learning for non-circular fiber-reinforced composites: Joint prediction of crack propagation and transverse mechanical response
abstract: Jointly characterizing microcrack evolution and macroscopic mechanical response in non-circular fiber-reinforced composites remains challenging due to the high computational cost and coupled failure mechanisms. Therefore, this study proposes a multitask deep learning framework for the simultaneous prediction of microscopic crack paths and macroscopic stress–strain responses. First, a dataset was constructed using the finite element method, including five fiber cross-sectional shapes: circle, ellipse, kidney, square, and triangle. Subsequently, with microstructure images as input, ResNet34 was adopted as the shared encoder, and two task-specific branches were constructed for crack segmentation and curve regression. To strengthen the physical correlation between the two tasks, a Bridge mechanism was further designed. Under the random-split setting, the proposed model accurately predicts both crack path and stress–strain responses, with an average R2 > 0.9 for curve prediction. LOSO validation further demonstrates useful generalization to unseen fiber geometries, although accurate pixel-level crack reconstruction and prediction of the complete post-peak response become more challenging, while peak load-carrying characteristics remain accurately predicted. Further mechanistic analysis indicates that fiber cross-sectional shape significantly affects local stress concentration and crack deflection behavior, with square fibers exhibiting better toughness and triangular fibers being more prone to rapid failure within the two-dimensional finite element setting considered in this study.

title: A modelling framework for additively manufactured parts reinforced with curvilinear fiber trajectories
abstract: The additive manufacturing of continuous fiber reinforced polymers is a very promising technology, due to the possibility of deposing the fibers along optimized trajectories. Such a high design complexity makes the modelling and simulation of parts quite challenging, as a consequence of their large-scale heterogeneity. Indeed, components can be designed and manufactured with multiple materials, and their deposition paths result in locally varying anisotropic properties. In this work, an efficient strategy is proposed for conducting finite element simulations of printed components, accounting for the peculiarities of their bead-based architecture. The approach employs an analytical model for the assignment of elastic properties to the finite elements, and enables the computation of the bead meso-scale stresses, that are viable for strength and damage assessments. The accuracy of the model has been validated through comparison with experimental tests on a plate with a hole, reinforced with curvilinear fiber paths following the maximum principal stress trajectories. Longitudinal and transverse strain maps predicted by the simulation resulted in agreement with those obtained from DIC acquisitions. The damage onset and failure locations were also well captured, though the strength assessment is out of the scope of the present work.

title: Gel-like metamaterial percolation composite N-butyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide-multi-walled carbon nanotubes
abstract: The dielectric spectra of a percolation composite based on the ionic liquid N-butyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (BMPyrrTFSI) and 4.1 wt% multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) were investigated in the temperature range from −40 to +80 °C and AC frequencies (f) from 1 kHz to 1 MHz. Using dielectric spectroscopy and differential scanning calorimetry, it was established that two types of crystalline phases of the ionic liquid form near the nanotube surface at subzero temperatures. It was shown that electronic conductivity through the MWCNT network dominates at negative temperatures, while the contribution of ionic conductivity begins to manifest at temperatures above 10 °C. A transition from positive to negative dielectric permittivity with increasing frequency, characteristic of metamaterials, was observed. The experimental frequency dependences of ε′(f) were approximated using the Drude–Lorentz model. The temperature dependences of the resonant frequency ω0, plasma frequency ωp, and damping coefficient γ were determined. It was found that with increasing temperature, the values of ω0 and ωp increase monotonically, while γ decreases. These effects are associated with the “unfreezing” of ionic mobility, a decrease in viscosity, and the restructuring of the electrical double layer at the MWCNT-ionic liquid interface. These results demonstrate the potentialof pyrrolidinium-based ionic liquids for creating tunable metamaterials with controllable negative dielectric permittivity.

title: A skin-comfortable and service durable SiR/POE Thermoplastic Vulcanizate (TPV) for intelligent wearables
abstract: With the rapid advancement of intelligent wearables, the development of wearable polymer materials that simultaneously combine skin comfort, mechanical robustness, recyclability, and service durability remains challenging. Guided by application-driven materials design, silicone rubber/polyolefin elastomer (SiR/POE) thermoplastic vulcanizate (TPV) was prepared through hydrosilylation dynamic vulcanization for intelligent wearable applications. To address the intrinsic incompatibility between SiR and POE, polyolefin elastomer-graft-polysiloxane was introduced as a compatibilizer, which acted as a molecular bridge by interacting with both the SiR and POE phases. After effective compatibilization, the interfacial thickness increased from 90 to 193 nm, while the median size of the dispersed SiR phase decreased from 2.17 μm to 0.72 μm, indicating markedly improved interfacial compatibility. During dynamic vulcanization, the phase morphology evolved from a continuous SiR phase to a co-continuous structure and finally to a fine dispersed sea-island morphology with a median domain size of 0.96 μm. The optimized SiR/POE 50/50 TPV with good reprocessability exhibited well-balanced mechanical properties, including a tensile strength of 8.3 MPa, an elongation at break of 600%, low hysteresis loss, and low compression set. More importantly, a scientific evaluation framework for wearable-related properties was established. The optimized TPV demonstrated multiple key performances required for intelligent wearables, including appropriate hardness, good compressive resilience, favorable frictional behavior, improved breathability, and excellent resistance to sweat, abrasion, yellowing, and staining. These results demonstrate the potential of SiR/POE TPV as a sustainable material for intelligent wearables and provide guidance for the application-driven design of high-performance silicone-based TPVs.

title: Endowing carbon fiber/ poly (ether ether ketone) composites with excellent mechanical and EMI shielding performance via interfacial transition structure
abstract: The next-generation aviation and aircraft raise imperious demands of advanced carbon fiber (CF) reinforced thermoplastic (CFRTP) composites with integrated structural-functional performance, synchronously possessing such as excellent mechanical properties and remarkable electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding performance. Owing to the designability of interfacial layers of composites, constructing an interfacial transition layer to increase the wettability between CF and matrix, as well as endowing the functional characteristic for composites is an advisable strategy to overcome the inherent interfacial obstacle of CFRTP. Herein, a multi-dimensional sizing agent containing Fe3O4 in-situ synthesized on MXene (Fe3O4@MXene), along with a polymeric component (polyetherimide) is utilized to decorate CF. The uniformly dispersed sizing components enhance the interfacial interactions and mechanical interlocking between CFs and poly (ether ether ketone) (PEEK), ultimately boosting the interfacial properties of CF/PEEK composites. Besides, the increment of crystalline degree of PEEK, along with the formation of a gradient interfacial modulus-stage synergistically increases the mechanical properties of CF/PEEK composites via introducing proper concentration of sizing agents. Concurrently, the EMI shielding effectiveness of modified composites exhibit a significant improvement due to the enhanced multiple reflections and conduction loss by introducing the nano-particles. This feasible and effective sizing approach could direct a pathway to fabricate advanced CFRTP with structural-functional integrated performance.

title: Torsional damage behaviour of double-layer braided composite tubes with varying braid angles studied by in situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT)
abstract: Braid angle is a key design variable for braided composite tubes, yet its role in governing damage evolution in multilayer tubular architectures under torsion remains insufficiently understood. Here, time-resolved in-situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT) has been used to investigate the torsional behaviour of double-layer 1/1 braided CFRP tubes with braid angles of 30° (DL30), 45° (DL45) and 60° (DL60). Increasing braid angle progressively increased wall thickness and tow crimp, while the effective fibre volume fraction varied only modestly and non-monotonically. These architectural changes produced distinct mechanical responses: DL45 and DL60 exhibit higher tube-level torsional stiffness whereas DL30 displays the highest shear modulus and torsional strength. Damage accumulation is strongly braid-angle dependent. At higher strain levels, intra-tow cracking, inter-tow debonding and inter-laminar debonding all markedly reduce as braid angle increases. The predominant damage mechanism also changes: DL30 develops a rapidly connected damage network (intra-tow cracking and inter-tow/laminar debonding) promoting microscale fibre kinking/buckling and further fibre breakage, leading to an abrupt post-peak loss of strength; DL45 showed more distributed damage accumulation and the highest post-peak strength; while DL60 exhibited delayed, weakly connected damage evolution with the lowest overall level of damage accumulation. These results suggest that angle-graded multilayer designs could combine lower-angle regions for reduced tow crimp, higher shear modulus and strength, with intermediate or higher-angle regions for damage suppression and stable post-peak performance.

title: Effect of yarn contact on high voltage damage of 3D braided carbon fiber/epoxy composites
abstract: Accurately predicting the high-voltage damage of three-dimensional (3D) braided carbon fiber composites is still a challenge for lightning protection design due to the complex microstructures. This paper presents a phase field-electrical-thermal coupled model accounting for yarn contact to reveal the high-voltage damage and dielectric breakdown behavior. The results show that the randomness of the damage depends on the yarn contact. The electric field in the composite concentrates at the yarn knots. The local electric field strength exhibits a 1.0%-6.3% increase at the surface knots of the contacting braided yarns, which leads to a shift in the initial breakdown locations. The current induced by high voltage propagates through the pathway established by the yarn contacts and the intrinsic electrical breakdown inside the epoxy resin. A temperature rise of over 400 °C caused by Joule heating leads to pyrolysis damage of the epoxy resin in the composite. Finite element analyses show that elliptical damage occurs at the braided knots, as shown in the tests. Furthermore, the intrinsic electric breakdown, the conductive pathway, and the thermal damage change accordingly with the yarn contact locations and quantities.

title: Experimental and numerical characterisation on open-hole compression of fibre-reinforced plastic laminated with hybridisation of carbon/glass fibres
abstract: This paper presents the first experimental and numerical investigation to explore the effect of hybridisation of 0° plies in a cross-ply laminate on the failure response of open-hole composites in compression. In this study, open hole compression (OHC) tests are conducted in accordance with the ASTM D6484 test standard. A three-dimensional ply-by-ply finite element model (FEA) employing cohesive layers, and Hashin and Quads damage criteria, was created to perform the analysis. The effect of varying the position of the 0° glass fibre ply within the stacking sequence was explored. Experimentally, the failure sequences were investigated via Digital Image Correlation (DIC) to detect the initiation and propagation of the damage events on the surface. Post-mortem X-ray computed tomography (CT) was undertaken to identify the three-dimensional damage morphology and to compare the spatial distribution of damage modes between the different configurations. Among the configurations investigated, we identified a particular hybrid configuration maintained an OHC strength comparable to that of the unhybridised carbon-fibre baseline while increasing the displacement at failure by 13.9%. This improvement is associated with the overall H3 laminate architecture, including the position of the glass plies, the distribution of local sublaminate stiffness, and the arrangement of ply interfaces. The FEA results were in good agreement with the experimental results and helps to understand failure mechanism. This work illustrates the key benefit of optimised ply hybridisation when aiming to maximise the global compressive strength response at the structural detail level.

title: Bioinspired catechol-based sizing agents featuring substrate-independent adhesion and vinyl reactivity for synergistically reinforced carbon fiber/vinyl ester composites
abstract: The interfacial properties of carbon fiber-reinforced vinyl ester resin (CF/VE) composites are critical for their performance in extreme environments. Inspired by mussel adhesive chemistry, a series of polyethylene glycol-modified epoxy (EPE)-based sizing agents were designed with controlled catechol functionalities and vinyl grafting ratios. The optimized formulation, 0.15Vi/0.2Mu, contained catechol and vinyl groups occupying 20% and 15% of EPE hydroxyl sites, respectively. AFM force-distance measurements using sizing agent-modified probes showed a catechol content-dependent increase in adhesion force, confirming the substrate-independent adhesive capability of catechol moieties on the carbon fiber surface. Meanwhile, vinyl groups copolymerized with the VE matrix during curing, forming covalent crosslinks. Owing to the synergistic effects of catechol-mediated adhesion and vinyl-induced copolymerization, 0.15Vi/0.2Mu-CF/VE composites exhibited significantly improved interfacial performance. The interlaminar shear strength, interfacial shear strength, and fracture toughness reached 69.25 MPa, 66.94 MPa, and 78.35 J/m2, representing increases of 35.0%, 107.6%, and 371.4%, respectively, compared with untreated D-CF/VE composites. This work provides an effective strategy for interfacial engineering of high-performance VE-based composites.
keywords: Carbon fiber reinforced vinyl ester resin composite

title: Creating the multilevel structure in the aramid fiber-reinforced epoxy composites for improved mechanical performance and environmental durability
abstract: Aramid fiber (AF) has been employed as a reinforcement for fiber-reinforced polymer composites (FRPCs) in recent years, owing to its light weight and excellent mechanical performance. However, the problems of the limited interfacial interaction between fiber and polymer resin and lack of functionality constricted the wider application. Herein, a multilevel structure like the mouth structure of a sea anemone composed of zinc oxide nanowires (ZnO NWs) and SiO2 particles was successfully constructed on the AF surface through a hierarchical surface modification strategy. It significantly increased the surface roughness of AF, and promoted the interfacial interlocking and improved the interfacial interaction between AF and epoxy (EP), thus enhancing the mechanical performance of AF/EP composites. After modification, the tensile strength and impact strength were increased by about 42% and 33%, in comparison to the unmodified composite. Besides, the AF/EP composites were endowed with good environmental durability including UV shielding and anti-icing performance, widening the potential application especially in complex practical environments.

title: Flexible, thin PDMS composites embedded with graphene nanoplatelets-polyaniline reinforced electrospun carbon nanofiber networks for broadband EMI shielding
abstract: Advancements towards nanoscale device architectures has aggravated the challenges related to Electromagnetic Interference (EMI). Hence modern electronics demands engineering of thin, mechanically flexible, and lightweight materials for effective EMI shielding for which metals are a limitation. In this work, we developed a thin, hydrophobic and highly flexible electrospun PAN based carbon nanofibers (PCNF) incorporated with graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) and coated with emeraldine salt of polyaniline (PANI) which is conducive for constructing hierarchical conductive networks for high-performance broadband EMI shielding (8 GHz-26.5 GHz). PCNF with an optimized loading of 7 wt% GNP (GPCNF) exhibited electrical conductivity of 0.9 S cm−1, total EMI SE value of 58.7 dB at a thickness of 70 μm with absolute shielding effectiveness value reaching 29,942 dB cm2 g−1 while its PANI coated sample (GPCNF-PANI) exhibited electrical conductivity 4.3 S cm−1, total EMI SE value of 73.8 dB at a thickness of 90 μm with an absolute shielding effectiveness value of 16,007 dB cm2g−1 outperforming the state-of-art GNP/C/polymeric systems reported in literature. The present study adopts simultaneous optimisation of conductive network formation, impedance mismatching, dielectric polarisations and multiple internal scattering pathways leading to effective EMI shielding. Also, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite of GPCNF-PANI (GPCNF-PANI-PDMS) prepared by hand lay-up technique showed excellent mechanical robustness with a storage modulus of 123 MPa, elongation at break of 26.3%, pronounced hydrophobicity with contact angle of 116° which is convenient to reduce moisture dependent degradations. This research offers an effective design pathway for next generation shielding materials suitable for advanced and wearable electronics.

title: Physics-guided uncertainty-aware neural network for off-axis fatigue life prediction of composite laminates with limited experimental data
abstract: Off-axis fatigue life prediction of composite laminates remains challenging because of material anisotropy, life scatter, and limited experimental data. This study proposes a GPR-enhanced physics-guided uncertainty-aware neural network for predicting the off-axis fatigue life of T700/7901 composite laminates. Unlike purely data-driven models, the proposed framework incorporates mechanics knowledge through material-coordinate stress components, the Tsai-Wu stress-severity descriptor, and monotonicity regularization. Gaussian process regression is first used to reconstruct orientation-dependent S-N relationships and generate probabilistic augmented samples with uncertainty estimates. Material-coordinate stress components and the Tsai-Wu failure index are then introduced as descriptions of stress severity, while an uncertainty-weighted loss function is designed to reduce the influence of highly uncertain augmented samples. Fatigue tests of T700/7901 composite laminates with different fiber orientations are used to train and validate the model. The results show that 200 augmented samples per fiber orientation provide a suitable balance between prediction accuracy, training stability, and data redundancy. The proposed model achieves an R2 of 0.940, outperforming conventional data-driven models. Beyond the improvement in prediction accuracy, monotonicity regularization discourages locally unreasonable stress-life trends, while uncertainty-weighted learning reduces the influence of relatively uncertain augmented samples. Moreover, validation on unseen fiber orientations further confirms the generalization capability of the proposed model, demonstrating its effectiveness for fatigue life prediction of composite laminates with limited experimental data.

title: Coiling dynamics of composite laminated parabolic shell: Modeling, validation and failure analysis
abstract: Traditional metal mesh deployable antennas suffer from performance bottlenecks due to the inherent “pillowing effect” that is difficult to eliminate. This work investigates a Semi-Rigid Reflector Deployable Antenna (SRRDA) configuration, which employs a composite laminated parabolic thin shell to replace the flexible metal mesh, thereby fundamentally eliminating the pillowing effect. The composite laminated parabolic shell exhibits strong geometrically nonlinear dynamic characteristics during the stowage and deployment of the SRRDA. Based on the absolute nodal coordinate formulation (ANCF), the geometrically nonlinear governing equations of the composite laminated parabolic shell are established to accurately describe its large-deformation behavior. A prototype is fabricated in-house and a coiling experimental platform is constructed. Through cross-validation between theoretical predictions, experimental results, and FEM simulations, the accuracy of the proposed model in predicting nonlinear responses is verified. Furthermore, the Tsai–Wu failure criterion is introduced to systematically analyze the effects of structural geometric parameters, layup sequences, and roller dimensions on the coiling torque and failure index, yielding theoretical criteria for parameter sensitivity. The proposed model offers theoretical reference for other deployable mechanisms.

title: Unraveling the effects of prebuckling nonlinearity on the initial buckling response of spherical cap-cylindrical shells: the roles of geometry and composite reinforcement
abstract: Although extensive studies have been devoted to the buckling of isolated spherical shells and cylindrical shells under external pressure, the nonlinear buckling behavior of the composite spherical cap-cylindrical shell—a crucial structure that is commonly used in submarines, launch vehicles, and pressurized industrial vessels—remains relatively underexplored. In this study, a semi-analytical method is developed to solve the governing nonlinear equations for the buckling of the composite spherical cap-cylindrical shells under external pressure, and the approach is well validated through finite element simulations. The method employs the perturbation technique in conjunction with the quasilinearization method to handle nonlinearities, while the precise integration method is adopted to ensure high accuracy. A parametric study quantifies the effects of the spherical shallowness parameter and the length-to-height ratio between cylindrical and spherical segments on the knockdown factor and the nonlinear buckling resistance per unit mass. The results reveal two noteworthy observations. First, similar to isolated spherical shells, the spherical cap-cylindrical shells appear to possess a region characterized by the spherical shallowness parameter, wherein the knockdown factor tends to drop markedly, implying a potential instability-sensitive regime. Second, within this region, the incorporation of composite materials seems to alleviate the detrimental influence of geometric nonlinearity, and this improvement can be attained without the need for geometric redesign.

title: Enhancing high-frequency magnetic properties of nanocrystalline powder - epoxy resin composites via computer-assisted size distribution optimization
abstract: Size distribution of powder fillers plays a paramount role in governing the microstructure and macroscopic performance in fields of composite materials. Conventional trial-and-error powder gradation approaches, hampered by intrinsic inefficiencies and poor precision, have long bottlenecked the development of high-performance composite materials. Here, we proposed a computer-assisted strategy for optimizing powder size distribution and validated it using Fe-based nanocrystalline soft magnetic powders as a model. Leveraging a mathematical framework derived from the Modified Andreasen and Andersen model, we performed high-throughput calculations of the compactness index R2 across a diverse set of gradation schemes, enabling efficient and precise identification of the optimal size distribution schemes. Implementation of this strategy produces substantial synergistic improvements in both microstructure and magnetic properties of Fe-based nanocrystalline soft magnetic composites (FNSMCs): low-grey-value phase fraction (similar to porosity) is reduced by 37.6% to 11.6%; core loss (Pcv) at 2 MHz/20 mT decreased by 16.7% to 2139.2 mW/cm3; permeability at 1 MHz increased by 10.7% to 18.7; quality factor (Q) at 1 MHz rosed by 6.7% to 104.3; and DC bias performance at 100 Oe improved by 5.1% to 88.2%. Mechanistically, the optimized size distribution — where fine powders fill interstitial non-ferromagnetic voids between coarse powders — promotes the expansion of magnetic domains and magnetization process, and then enhances permeability and suppresses hysteresis loss. Additionally, the tailored coarse-fine powder interfaces significantly enhance the electrical resistivity of the FNSMCs, and then markedly attenuating both inter-powder and total eddy current losses.

title: Exploring the hidden influence of crack parallel tension on interlaminar fracture toughness in quasibrittle composites
abstract: Interlaminar fracture in composite structures rarely occurs under idealized pure Mode I conditions; instead, delamination often develops in the presence of substantial in-plane stress parallel to the crack. Yet, the effect of crack parallel tension on interlaminar fracture resistance remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce a novel Half Open-I (HOI) test that generates Mode I opening and crack parallel tensile stress simultaneously using a standard uniaxial tensile testing machine. The target stress state is induced intrinsically through specimen geometry and controlled by the inserted tab thickness, eliminating the need for biaxial loading systems, specialized fixtures, or high-strength bonded pads. Experiments on IM7/977-3 carbon/epoxy laminates, combined with nonlinear J-integral evaluations, reveal that the measured R-curves initially converge to a plateau near the conventional interlaminar fracture energy of approximately 0.21 N/mm. However, once the crack parallel tensile stress exceeds roughly 50% of the unidirectional tensile strength, the apparent fracture resistance decreases systematically. At 60% of the unidirectional tensile strength, the resistance is reduced by approximately 29%, demonstrating a substantial degradation in delamination resistance under tensile stress states that are invisible to conventional Mode I fracture tests. Fractographic observations indicate a corresponding transition in fracture morphology, consistent with reduced fiber-bridging effectiveness and premature bridging-fiber failure. These results show that crack parallel tension is an active driver of fracture-process-zone evolution. The proposed HOI test therefore provides a practical route for quantifying stress-state-dependent delamination resistance and offers new data for damage-tolerant design of lightweight composite structures.

title: Application guide for bio-inspired helicoidal composites: Relationship between layup configuration and impact performance
abstract: Bio-inspired helicoidal design has attracted widespread attention in improving the impact resistance of fiber-reinforced composites in recent years. However, it remains unclear whether this design offers sufficient advantages in terms of impact resistance and damage tolerance under variable impact conditions, which hinders its advancement in industrial applications. To this end, basalt fiber reinforced bio-inspired helicoidal laminates with the pitch angles of 12° (H-12°), 24°(H-24°), or 36° (H-36°) are designed and prepared, and the traditional cross-ply (CP) and quasi-isotropic (QI) laminates are also prepared as the references. Their low-velocity impact performances at the impact energies of 30 J and 50 J (including impact responses, damage modes and residual properties) are investigated by experimental, numerical and theoretical methods. The results show that the helicoidal laminate with a small pitch angle (H-12° and H-24°) has a higher impact resistance (high peak force and low absorbed energy) than other laminates at relatively high impact energy of 50 J. The lateral delamination damage and the along-the-thickness damage (including fiber breakage) can be inhibited in the H-12° helicoidal laminate at the impact energy of 50 J. This is attributed to the fact that the sub-critical damage mechanism, involving helicoidal cracking and helicoidal delamination, is specifically activated in the helicoidal laminate with a small pitch angle at relatively high energy impact. Furthermore, the Bayesian method is also applied in this study to build a quantitative relationship between layup configuration and impact performances to provide the guidance on design and application of helicoidal laying.

title: Bioinspired interfacial crosslinking for functional polymer composites with high adhesion and thermal conductivity in low-pressure packaging
abstract: Interfaces are critical for heat/force transfer in applications, especially in electronic packaging. Interface materials require high thermal conductivity and strong adhesion to ensure electronic device stability, yet achieving heat dissipation and adhesion poses a constant challenge due to conflicting material requirements. Inspired by Sharpey's fibers in tendon-bone adhesion, herein, we propose an interfacial crosslinking strategy by integrating borate ester bonds and aluminum (Al) filler networks into epoxy polymer composites to enhance heat/force transfer ability. Borate ester bonds enhance intrinsic adhesion energy via B-O covalent bonds, while Al networks improve bulk dissipation energy and suppress cracks. The obtained polymer composites exhibit the highest adhesion strength of 11.72 MPa, adhesion energy of 8146.4 J m−2 with an ultra-low thermal resistance of 0.28 K cm2 W−1 under low pressure. Meanwhile, the composites with the highest thermal conductivity of 4.97 W m−1 K−1 still maintain a high adhesion strength of 11.18 MPa. We also clarify the mechanism underlying high adhesion performance of the interfacial crosslinking at the molecular scale by surface energy calculations, Kraus' model, Chaudhury's model and molecular dynamics. Moreover, the fabricated polymer composites show effective heat dissipation and mechanical stability under low pressure packaging. This work addresses the critical need for balanced heat/force transfer at the interface in next-generation advanced electronic devices.

title: Cryogenic microcrack suppression and gas-barrier retention enabled by plasma-engineered PET nanomaterial
abstract: Cryogenic carbon/epoxy structures for composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs) must resist thermally induced microcracking while maintaining mechanical and gas-barrier performance. Here, electrospun PET nanofibers were activated by atmospheric plasma to improve epoxy compatibility without disrupting their porous morphology and were interleaved into IM7/8552 laminates. Plasma-treated PET increased short-beam strength by up to 27.2% at room temperature and −196 °C relative to the corresponding baselines. Mode II ENF testing further showed a 44.6% increase in precracked GIIc relative to the baseline. After 50 cycles between −196 and 100 °C, baseline and polyamide-modified laminates developed microcracks and lost low-temperature storage modulus, whereas the PET-modified laminates showed substantially reduced observable microcrack formation within the inspected regions and retained their modulus. Helium permeability also remained nearly unchanged after cycling, while that of the baseline increased by approximately 8.4-fold. These results demonstrate that plasma-treated PET nanofibers simultaneously improve short-beam strength, suppress cryogenic-cycling damage, and preserve gas-barrier performance in carbon/epoxy laminates for COPV applications.

title: Anisotropic conductive paste based on PS@Au core–shell microspheres: Controllable preparation, contact resistance modeling, and RFID packaging performance
abstract: The miniaturization of radio frequency identification (RFID) devices and the growing use of flexible substrates require reliable interconnections at low bonding forces. Conventional anisotropic conductive pastes (ACPs) can exhibit unstable conduction when the applied force is insufficient. Here, monodisperse 3 μm PS@Au core–shell microspheres with a dense Au coating were prepared by dopamine-assisted electroless plating. The minimum powder-compaction resistivity was 8.8 × 10−5 Ω cm at 2 N. A temperature- and force-dependent contact-resistance model was established using Hertzian contact mechanics, Holm constriction theory, multiparticle parallel conduction, and a phenomenological post-critical electrical-continuity correction. Within the validated range of 1.2–1.6 N, the calculated interconnection resistance agreed with the measurements to within 10%. Voronoi and nearest-neighbor analyses revealed local spatial heterogeneity but no dominant macroscopic agglomeration within the analyzed field of view. The resulting ACP formed low-resistance through-thickness interconnections within the selected processing window and maintained stable RFID performance after reliability testing. These results provide a material–modeling framework for low-force RFID interconnection.

title: From multiscale homogenization to large-amplitude vibration analysis of multiphase nanocomposite plates
