abstract: This study investigates the large-amplitude nonlinear free vibration behavior of multiphase nanocomposite rectangular plates reinforced with carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), and short carbon fibers (SCFs) embedded in a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) matrix. The nanocomposite plate is embedded on an elastic foundation. A finite element (FE)-based multiscale homogenization framework is first employed to determine the effective mechanical properties of the multiphase nanocomposite by accounting for the coupled contributions of nanoscale and microscale reinforcements. The geometrically nonlinear formulation of the plate is then developed based on von Kármán strain-displacement relations and Hamilton's principle, leading to the governing equations of motion under various boundary conditions. To solve the resulting nonlinear system, an advanced numerical approach combining the variational differential quadrature (VDQ) method, Galerkin reduction, time-periodic discretization, pseudo-arc length continuation, and the modified Newton-Raphson method is implemented. The nonlinear vibration response is characterized in terms of the frequency-amplitude relationship for different reinforcement parameters and structural configurations. The results demonstrate a pronounced hardening-type nonlinear behavior, where the nonlinear frequency increases with vibration amplitude. Parametric studies further reveal that increasing CNT, GNP, and SCF contents, as well as enlarging filler aspect ratios, significantly increase the stiffness and nonlinear frequency response of the multiphase nanocomposite plates.

title: Mechanical performance and damage mechanism of bio-inspired Directional-Biased-Helicoidal (DBH) laminates under out-of-plane and CAI loads
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates with full-revolution bio-inspired helicoidal layups have demonstrated outstanding impact resistance and out-of-plane strength. However, as most aerospace applications demand CFRP laminates with high mechanical performance along the primary in-plane loading direction, a segmented Directional-Biased-Helicoidal (DBH) laminate that offers superior in-plane strength, stiffness, and Compression-After-Impact (CAI) strength along one direction is more practical than conventional full-revolution helicoidal laminates. This study investigates the out-of-plane and CAI performance of DBH laminates to assess their potential in aerospace applications. The results show that the spiraling matrix split damage developed in DBH laminates can effectively reduce fiber fracture and increase their out-of-plane peak load between 24% and 33.6% compared to the conventional directional biased quadriaxial (Quad) laminate. Under impact loading, unlike conventional quasi-isotropic (QI) laminates, delaminations in Quad laminates tend to concentrate and grow excessively at a few interfaces due to stiffness mismatch between ply clusters. In contrast DBH layups can restrict such extensive delamination formation. The experimental result shows that the CAI strength (based on ASTM D7137/D7137M test standard) of the DBH laminate with an inter-ply angle of 30 o outperforms the Quad counterpart by a remarkable 35.3%. More surprisingly, further experiments showed that the CAI strength of the full-revolution helicoidal laminate with the same inter-ply angle was 23.2% lower than one of its QI counterparts. The impact-induced damage patterns and CAI performance of these laminates were investigated with the aid of CT scanning and numerical simulation.

title: Graphite nanoflake/polydimethylsiloxane conductive composite digital sensors for muscle spindle-inspired structural health monitoring
abstract: A real-time health assessment is imperative for ensuring the reliable and safe operation of all structures. Considerable uncertainty, however, remains regarding the monitoring of structures made from advanced metals. In this study, polymer nanocomposite-based structural health monitoring (SHM) sensors are explored as a means to enhance both the adaptability of SHM sensors to different structures and the robustness and reliability of the monitoring process. Graphite nanoflake (GnF)-reinforced polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) conductive polymer nanocomposites (GnF/PDMS CPnCs) with tailorable elongation at electrical disconnection are used for multiple sensing elements in the SHM sensors, enabling them to match the deformation behavior of a structure, regardless of the material from which it is made. The SHM sensors, bioinspired by muscle spindles, convert the deformation of a structure into discrete binary signals on the electrical disconnection of their sensing elements. This allows the SHM sensors to detect the deformation and failure onset of the structure in a digital manner, achieving high robustness to environmental variations and exceptional reliability. Twelve kinds of GnF/PDMS CPnCs with varying GnF contents were experimentally characterized with an emphasis on the effects of GnF content and porosity on elongation at break, electrical conductivity, and elongation at electrical disconnection. Subsequently, a series of prediction models on mechanoelectrical properties vs. GnF content and porosity are developed and validated to facilitate the design of the sensing elements. The biological detection mechanism by which muscle spindles perceive the stretch of skeletal muscles is analyzed. The electrical disconnection of sensing elements, induced by either increased filler-to-filler distance or mechanical fracture, is also extensively addressed to establish a method that is long-term useable and relatively insensitive to environmental variations. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the development of a polymer nanocomposite-based SHM strategy for structures and their components.

title: Bio-inspired Bouligand-corrugated-sandwich structure for high-performance wood-based composites: Flexural properties, impact resistance and dimensional stability
abstract: Multi-structural design is an effective approach to enhancing the mechanical performance of composite materials. In this study, a bio-inspired composite integrating Bouligand helicoidal layup, corrugated architecture, and sandwich configuration is proposed, using wood-based composites as the validation platform. The design synergistically combines the crack deflection mechanism of Bouligand structures, the geometric constraint effect of corrugated architecture, and the high-strength face layer load-bearing capacity of sandwich structures. The flexural properties, impact resistance, and dimensional stability of the composites were systematically evaluated. The results demonstrate that although individual structures exhibit certain improvements, the Bouligand-corrugated-sandwich composite (BSC) demonstrates a balanced enhancement of mechanical performance among the investigated configurations: it achieves the highest flexural load and stiffness with the most uniform stress distribution; its impact peak load reaches 1204.5 N, which is 4.72 times that of the orthogonal laminate (P); fracture morphology reveals that BSC simultaneously exhibits crack deflection characteristic of Bouligand structures and high-strength face layer load-bearing characteristic of sandwich structures; under humid conditions, BSC retains the highest flexural load. The combined effects of Bouligand layup, corrugated architecture, and sandwich configuration contribute to the balanced enhancement of mechanical performance compared with individual structural designs. This design strategy provides a potential approach for developing high-performance composite materials and offers insights into the design of advanced composites where high load-bearing capacity and impact resistance are simultaneously required.

title: Promotion of Si3N4/SiC whisker aerogel with superior oxidation resistance, low thermal conductivity and wide temperature range via dual network design
abstract: Lightweight ceramic aerogels with outstanding high-temperature oxidation resistance and measurable mechanical stiffness have emerged as promising thermal barrier materials for extreme thermal management in energy systems. Nevertheless, developing dual-whisker ceramic aerogels that simultaneously deliver ultralow thermal conductivity, adequate mechanical stiffness and broad thermal shock tolerance remains a persistent technical bottleneck. Herein, we synthesize a dual-network Si3N4/SiC ceramic aerogel by coupling carbothermal reduction with directional freeze-drying technology. Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that electrostatic interactions, van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds synergistically promote the dispersion and assembly of precursor components prior to calcination. After heat treatment, the resulting ceramic aerogel exhibits a compressive modulus of 1.017 MPa, attributed to its interwoven fibrous network. Complementary finite element simulations further illustrate the continuous stress transfer pathways within its intricate hierarchical nanostructure. Notably, we systematically clarify the relevant working mechanisms from both microscopic and macroscopic perspectives. The prepared aerogel possesses a low density of 42.5 mg/cm3, a high porosity of 98.3%, and room temperature thermal conductivity of 0.0334 W/(m·K). Impressively, the material maintains macroscopic integrity under short duration thermal exposure from −196 °C up to 1300 °C, demonstrating broad thermal shock tolerance. Numerical simulations of transient heat conduction are performed to systematically interpret its unique internal heat transfer behaviors. Its low thermal conductivity arises from three coordinated structural features: the dense in-situ generated SiO2 outer oxide layer, mutually connected nano-fibrous architecture, and directionally arranged lamellar shielding structure, which collaboratively restrain solid-phase thermal conduction, gas-phase heat transfer and radiative heat loss under variable temperature conditions.

title: Tailoring void structure and sound absorption properties of 3D-Printed plant fiber reinforced composites via gradient force-controlled deposition
abstract: Plant fiber reinforced composites are emerging as sustainable sound-absorbing materials, yet their acoustic performance is highly sensitive to void structures, which are strongly influenced by the inherent diameter irregularity of plant fiber bundles. Conventional 3D printing controlled by fixed layer heights cannot accommodate such variations, resulting in uncontrolled compaction and unpredictable porosity. To address this limitation, a robotic 3D printing system integrating position control with real-time force feedback control was developed in this study, enabling precise regulation of the normal contact force. Thus, the degree of compaction during deposition is directly controlled, allowing adaptive response to the diameter irregularity. Secondly, continuous flax fiber reinforced composites (CFFRCs) were printed under different normal printing forces of 3, 6, and 9 N, along with a gradient-force specimen. Microstructural and acoustic characterizations were performed via optical microscopy, mercury intrusion porosimetry, and impedance tube measurements, supplemented by acoustic simulations incorporating actual void structures to reveal the underlying mechanisms. The results showed that the force-controlled method could progressively refine the void network with high spatial precision, effectively accommodating the irregularity. As printing force increased, the primary absorption peak shifted from 520 to 444 Hz. Furthermore, CFFRC printed with gradient force exhibited enhanced low-frequency sound absorption when sound entered from the side printed at 3 N, demonstrating that the gradually densified structure facilitated a favorable impedance transition. This work highlights that force-controlled deposition provides better adaptability than conventional layer-height approaches, particularly for processing plant fibers, and opens a new route for functionally graded acoustic composites.

title: Resolving the strength-cryostability trade-off in PVA organogels through solvent-ion compaction and magnetic nanocrystal alignment
abstract: Poly(vinyl alcohol) gels are attractive for soft electronics, wearable sensors, and soft robotics, but their low-temperature application remains challenging because mechanical strength and deformability are difficult to retain simultaneously. This limitation originates from two coupled effects: solvent crystallization disrupts the continuous soft phase, while restricted chain relaxation in a compact network promotes brittle failure. Here, these issues are addressed through a cooperative strategy that integrates solvent- and ion-induced network compaction with magnetic alignment of Fe3O4-functionalized cellulose nanocrystals. Solvent exchange from DMSO to an EG/H2O medium suppresses low-temperature crystallization and simultaneously drives contraction and dense packing of PVA chains. Al3+/SO42− further stabilizes the compact network through salting-out effects and reversible coordination with oxygen-containing groups on PVA and the nanocrystals. To counteract the brittleness typically associated with densified networks, magnetically aligned nanocrystals create anisotropic reinforcing pathways that enhance stress transfer, deflect cracks, and preserve damage tolerance. Consequently, the optimized organogel achieves a tensile strength of 20.3 MPa, an elongation at break of 820%, and a fracture energy of 0.64 MJ m−2, while remaining flexible and ionically conductive down to −60 °C.

title: Hygrothermal aging behavior and multi-scale damage evolution of pultruded GFRP composites characterized by acoustic emission and digital image correlation
abstract: The long-term service reliability of composite insulators is critically dependent on the durability of pultruded glass fiber reinforced polymer (GFRP) core rods under harsh environmental conditions. This study investigates the hygrothermal aging behavior and damage evolution of unidirectional GFRP composites exposed to an 85°C/85%RH environment. Physicochemical characterizations (FTIR/DMA) reveal degradation driven by synergistic matrix plasticization and chemical hydrolysis, accelerating interfacial weakening, ultimately reducing static tensile strength by 15.03% and fatigue life by 59.07% at 60 days. In-situ monitoring using coupled Acoustic Emission (AE) and Digital Image Correlation (DIC) uncovers a failure mechanism transition: from matrix-dominated brittle fracture in unaged specimens to interface-dominated structural decoupling in severely aged ones under static and fatigue loading. This transition is evidenced by step-wise stiffness degradation, ratcheting effects, and high-energy interfacial splitting signals. Furthermore, a synergistic structural health monitoring framework is established. By integrating qualitative b-value analysis with a novel quantitative prediction model based on ultra-early AE counts, residual tensile strength is estimated with high precision at low stress levels. This research provides deep insights into the interfacial degradation mechanics and offers a robust, quasi-non-destructive strategy for the safety assessment of in-service composite insulators.

title: Lotus leaf microstructure bio-inspiration: Design and preparation of compatible stealth materials with multiband radar wave absorption and ultra-low infrared emissivity
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in the performance of radar/infrared compatible stealth materials, achieving multiband radar stealth while maintaining extremely low infrared emissivity remains challenging. Therefore, inspired by the anti-reflective microstructure of lotus leaf, this work proposes a biomimetic structure dominated by random linear patterns. This design enables the infrared stealth layer—a thin aluminum film—to achieve an emissivity of 0.09–0.13, after integrating the radar layer (composed of carbonyl iron/polyurethane), the effective absorption bandwidth (reflection loss, RL ≤ −10 dB) covers 15.26–17.83 GHz, 24.93–30.75 GHz, and 38.85–39.73 GHz. Moreover, the introduction of the infrared stealth layer eliminates the radar cross-section (RCS) enhancement observed in the pure radar stealth layer and achieves omnidirectional stealth performance. The RCS value is reduced below −27.5 dB at θ = 90° across the range of −180° < φ < 180°. Simulation demonstrates that the tiny gaps in the infrared layer allow effective transmission of radar waves, thereby facilitating magnetic resonance absorption in the radar stealth layer, thus overcomes the design limitations of conventional stealth structures. This biomimetic strategy achieves a breakthrough in radar stealth performance under ultra-low infrared emissivity, offering a novel design route for advanced radar/infrared compatible stealth materials.

title: Bioinspired external patch configuration for enhancing mechanical performance of repaired composite laminates
abstract: Adhesively bonded external patch repairs are widely applied in the aerospace industry, as they can restore the structural integrity of damaged composite components and accommodate complex shapes. However, traditional straight-edge patches often induce high peel stresses at the patch termination due to stiffness discontinuities, leading to premature debonding and reduced repair efficiency. This study proposes an innovative patch edge profiling design inspired by biological suture structures to enhance adhesive strength and delay debonding failure between the patch and the parent laminate for better load transfer. A combination of quasi-static tensile experiments and numerical simulations was used to analyze and compare the mechanical response and failure modes of repaired specimens with different patch configuration parameters, including stacking sequences, patch lengths, and edge profiling designs. The results indicate that adjusting patch configuration parameters significantly influences mechanical performance by redistributing stress and altering failure modes. Remarkably, for a patch length of 50 mm and a [0/90]s stacking sequence, rectangular- and elliptical-edge patches increased the peak load by 18.7% and 12.2%, respectively, compared with the straight-edge patches, significantly enhancing failure stability. These improvements arise from the distributed stiffness transition and extended load-transfer path provided by the profiled edges, which alleviate local stress concentrations and delay interfacial debonding. This study introduces a novel approach to the repair of lightweight aerospace components, offering significant potential for enhancing component durability and reliability.

title: Dual-template engineered hierarchical porous SiCw/epoxy composites with fast dielectric response and enhanced insulation performance
abstract: Polymeric dielectrics with both low dielectric constant and excellent insulation performance are required for high-frequency integrated circuits and compact high-voltage insulation systems. Herein, a silicon carbide whisker (SiCw)/epoxy resin (EP) composite with hierarchical porous structures was carefully designed using NH4HCO3 and ground sugar as porogens. The size-complementary filling concept, namely, the spatial packing effect of porogens with different sizes, was introduced to construct hierarchical porous structure composed of large and small pores. The hierarchical porous structure improved flashover strength by promoting surface charge dissipation and retarding streamer propagation. Moreover, the dielectric constant was reduced by the abundant air phase introduced into the pores, while SiCw contributed to electric-field homogenization and mechanical reinforcement. The relative dielectric constant of the composites decreased to approximately 1.5–1.6, and the signal delay in a 20 cm microstrip line was reduced from 21.5 ns to 4.4 ns. The surface flashover voltage increased by 78% compared to the EP sample, and the tensile strength was improved by 72% after SiCw incorporation. This work provides a structural design strategy for low-permittivity and high-flashover-strength epoxy composites for high-frequency integrated-circuit insulation systems.

title: Temperature-driven transition from stress hysteresis to synchronous brittle fracture in elastomer-enhanced sandwich structures under impact
abstract: Elastomeric interlayers improve composite impact resistance, but temperature-dependent changes in local load transfer and their relationship with failure modes remain insufficiently understood. We investigate the low-velocity impact behavior of elastomer-enhanced CFRP/aluminum honeycomb sandwich structures from −30 °C to 80 °C. The local load-bearing stress lag time (Δt) is proposed as a structural response quantity extracted from finite element stress histories, quantifying the time difference between CFRP regions below and above the elastomer reaching the same reference stress. Combining Δt with stress fields, energy distribution, and experimental damage morphology links local response timing to temperature-dependent failure modes. At a reference stress of 600 MPa, Δt increases from 0.10 ms to 0.67 ms between −30 °C and 80 °C. At −30 °C, Δt is 68.8% shorter than at 25 °C, accompanied by stress concentration, localized fiber fracture, and an approximately 52.7% post-peak load drop. From −10 °C to 50 °C, Δt increases from 0.24 ms to 0.40 ms alongside wider in-plane stress distributions. At 80 °C, Δt reaches 0.67 ms, but the stress diffusion region does not expand further and diagonal stress concentration appears. Thus, a longer local response lag does not necessarily indicate wider load diffusion. This framework adds a temporal dimension to understanding elastomeric load transfer and supports impact-resistant structural design through joint analysis of response timing, stress distribution, and damage.

title: Gradient yolk-shell resonators structures with frequency tunable absorption bands for underwater acoustic absorption
abstract: Conventional underwater acoustic absorption materials suffer from fixed frequency bands and significant performance degradation under high pressure. In this study, we propose a composite functional gradient acoustic structure (CFAS) fabricated by incorporating yolk-shell BCZT@SiO2 nanoparticles with graded cavity sizes and controllable interfacial microstructures into a polyurethane matrix. The layered gradient architecture induces sequential resonance, broadening the effective absorption band from 3-4 kHz to 1-9 kHz, and the average absorption coefficient of the CFAS material increases by more than 30% compared with that of pure resin. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the broadband absorption arises from the synergistic interplay of yolk-shell cavity resonance, piezoelectric energy conversion, and multi-interface damping within the gradient structure. The rational interfacial design and layer-by-layer curing process also ensure excellent mechanical stability. This work clarifies the structure-interface-performance relationships of yolk-shell-based gradient materials and provides a versatile multi-scale fabrication route for high-performance broadband acoustic attenuation materials.
